lessons.title: What Is Systems Analysis and Design?
lessons.content:
Imagine a small pharmacy on Mirpur Road. Every sale is written by hand in a thick register. When a customer asks for a medicine, the shop boy climbs a ladder, searches three shelves and comes back to say "sold out". At month end the owner sits until midnight adding numbers to find out what he must reorder. One day his nephew says, "Uncle, let's buy software." But which software? What should it do? Who will type the data? What happens to the old registers? Answering those questions carefully, before anyone writes code or spends money, is exactly what systems analysis and design is about.

What it is: Systems analysis and design (SA&D) is a step-by-step way of studying how an organization works today, finding what problems or chances it has, and then planning a better system to solve them. Analysis means understanding the problem: what is happening now and what is needed. Design means deciding how the new system will meet those needs: screens, reports, data, programs and hardware. The person who does this work is called a systems analyst.

Why it exists: In the early days of business computing, programmers often jumped straight into coding. The result was systems that ran but did not do what the business needed, cost far more than planned, or were rejected by the people who had to use them. Organizations learned that most failures came from misunderstanding the problem, not from bad code. SA&D grew as a discipline to fix that: understand first, design second, build third.

What a system is: A system is a set of related parts that work together toward a common goal. Your body is a system. A cricket team is a system. A pharmacy is a system: the counter, the shelves, the staff, the register, the suppliers and the cash box all work together so that customers get the right medicine and the owner makes a profit. In the next lesson we will look at systems thinking in depth: boundaries, inputs, outputs and feedback.

What an information system is: An information system (IS) is a system that collects, stores, processes and shares information to support an organization's work and decisions. It is not only a computer. It has six parts. People are the users and the IT staff. Procedures are the rules and steps people follow, such as "check the prescription before selling an antibiotic". Data is the raw facts, such as medicine names, prices and quantities. Software is the programs. Hardware is the computers, printers, barcode scanners and phones. Network is what connects them, such as the shop Wi-Fi and the internet. If you change only the software and forget the procedures and the people, the system usually fails.

Data and information: Data is raw facts: "Napa, 50 strips, 12 taka". Information is data processed into something useful for a decision: "Napa will run out in 3 days at the current selling rate". An information system turns data into information for the right person at the right time.

Types of information systems in one paragraph: Organizations use different kinds of IS. A transaction processing system (TPS) records daily business events, like every sale at the pharmacy counter. A management information system (MIS) produces regular reports for managers, like weekly sales by branch. A decision support system (DSS) helps with less routine choices, like "which new branch location is best?". Executive systems give top leaders a summary dashboard. Your Management Information Systems course covers these in depth; here you only need to know that the analyst must first understand which kind of system the organization actually needs.

The systems analyst: The systems analyst is the bridge between the business people and the technical people. The pharmacy owner speaks the language of sales, stock and profit. The programmer speaks the language of tables, APIs and code. The analyst understands both, asks the right questions, writes down what is needed in a clear form, and makes sure the system that gets built actually solves the real problem. In small companies the same person may analyse, design and even program. In big companies analysts often focus only on requirements and design.

What an analyst actually does day to day: Meets users and managers to find out how work is done now. Observes the work in person. Studies forms, reports and old files. Draws diagrams of how data moves. Estimates costs and benefits. Compares options such as building new software or buying a ready-made package. Writes specifications that developers can follow. Helps with testing, training and moving to the new system. Listens to complaints after launch and plans improvements.

Skills of an analyst, part 1, technical: An analyst needs to understand how computers, databases, networks and software development work, even if they do not write all the code. They must read and draw models such as data flow diagrams, entity relationship diagrams and UML diagrams. They should know what is technically possible, what is risky and roughly what it costs.

Skills of an analyst, part 2, business and people: They must understand how the business makes money, what the rules are and what the managers worry about. Communication is the biggest skill: interviewing, listening, writing clearly and presenting. Problem solving matters too: breaking a messy situation into smaller pieces. Finally, ethics: analysts see confidential data such as salaries and patient records, and must keep it safe and be honest about costs and risks.

Stakeholders: A stakeholder is anyone who is affected by the system or can affect it. System owners pay for the system and approve it, such as the pharmacy owner. System users use it every day, such as the counter staff and the stock keeper; there are also external users, such as customers checking an order online. System designers decide the technical solution, such as database and interface designers. System builders construct it, such as programmers and network engineers. The analyst coordinates all of them. A project sponsor is the senior person who pushes the project forward and protects its budget.

Why stakeholders matter: Different stakeholders want different things. The owner wants low cost and better profit. The counter staff want fast, simple screens. The accountant wants correct tax reports. The supplier wants clear orders. If the analyst listens only to the owner, the staff may hate the system and quietly go back to the paper register. Good analysis means finding and balancing all these needs.

Analysis vs design, a worked view: Take one need in the pharmacy: "know which medicines to reorder". Analysis asks: how is reordering done now, who decides, what data is used, how often, what goes wrong? We may discover that the owner reorders by memory and often runs out of fast-moving items. The requirement becomes: "The system shall list every medicine whose stock is below its reorder level." Design then asks: where is the reorder level stored, which screen shows the list, is it printed or shown on a phone, how often is it calculated? Analysis is the "what"; design is the "how".

SA&D vs software engineering: These two subjects overlap. Software engineering focuses on how to build good software: process models, coding practice, testing and project management. SA&D focuses on the bigger business system: understanding the organization, deciding what to build, and designing how people, procedures, data and software fit together. Your Software Engineering course covers process models, testing and project management in depth, so in this course we look at them only from the analyst's point of view.

Real life example 1, a pharmacy chain: Imagine a chain of 12 pharmacies in Dhaka, which we will call ShasthoPharma and use as our running example. Each branch keeps its own paper stock register. Head office does not know which branch has extra stock of insulin while another branch is out of it. The analyst interviews the owner, branch managers and counter staff, observes a busy evening at one branch, and studies the registers. She finds the real problem is not "we need a computer" but "we cannot see stock across branches, so we lose sales and medicines expire". The design that follows is a central stock database, a simple sales screen with barcode scanning at each branch, and a daily reorder and expiry report for head office.

Real life example 2, a university admission system: A university in Bangladesh used to take admission forms on paper and print results on a notice board. Thousands of students travelled to the campus just to submit a form. An analyst studying this would identify stakeholders (students, guardians, the admission office, departments, the bank or mobile payment provider), gather requirements (online form, fee payment through mobile financial services, admit card download, result by SMS), and then design screens, the database and the payment integration. Many universities in Bangladesh now run admissions online in exactly this way.

Course map: Here is our journey. First we build foundations: systems thinking and the systems development life cycle (SDLC). Then planning: how projects start, feasibility study and cost-benefit analysis. Then analysis: what requirements are and how to gather them with interviews, questionnaires, observation and JAD sessions, and how to organize them. Then modeling: data flow diagrams for processes, structured English, decision trees and decision tables for logic, the data dictionary and ER diagrams for data, and UML use case, activity, sequence, class and state diagrams for objects. Then design: architecture, outputs, inputs and user interfaces. Finally implementation, conversion to the new system and maintenance.

How an analyst thinks: A good analyst is curious and a little suspicious, in a friendly way. When the owner says "we need an app", the analyst asks "why?" and "what happens today?". When a clerk says "this is how we always do it", the analyst asks "what would go wrong if we stopped?". The goal is not to impress anyone with technology. The goal is to find the simplest change, in people, procedures, data or software, that solves the real problem at a cost the organization can afford. Sometimes the best answer is a better paper form or a clear rule, not new software at all.

How big the effort should be: SA&D is not only for huge government or bank projects. For a small shop, the whole analysis may be a few conversations and one page of notes. For a national system, such as a hospital network or a tax system, it may take a team of analysts many months. The steps are the same; only the depth and the amount of documentation change.

Common mistakes: Students often think SA&D is about writing code; it is mostly about understanding and planning. Another mistake is thinking an information system is just a computer program; remember the six parts. Many also treat users as an afterthought; in practice, ignoring users is one of the most common causes of system failure. And some confuse a symptom ("sales are falling") with the real problem ("customers leave because medicines are out of stock").

What exams ask: Define system and information system, and list the components of an IS. Explain the role and skills of a systems analyst. Who are the stakeholders of an information system? Distinguish between systems analysis and systems design. Differentiate data and information with examples.

Recap: Systems analysis and design is the disciplined way of understanding a business problem and planning an information system to solve it. An information system has people, procedures, data, software, hardware and network. The systems analyst is the bridge between business and technology and needs technical, business, people and ethical skills. Many stakeholders are involved and their needs must be balanced. Next lesson: systems thinking, the way analysts look at any organization as a set of connected parts.
key_points: Systems analysis is understanding what is needed; systems design is deciding how the new system will meet those needs.
A system is a set of related parts working together toward a common goal.
An information system has six parts: people, procedures, data, software, hardware and network.
Data is raw facts; information is processed data that helps a decision.
The systems analyst is the bridge between business people and technical people.
Analysts need technical, business, communication, problem-solving and ethical skills.
Stakeholders include system owners, users, designers, builders and the project sponsor, and their needs often conflict.
Many system failures come from misunderstanding the problem or ignoring users, not from bad code.
lessons.tip: For every topic in this course, keep one real organization in mind (a pharmacy, your university, a bKash agent shop) and apply each new idea to it. SA&D makes sense only when you picture real people doing real work.
lessons.task: Pick a small business near you (a pharmacy, a grocery shop or a photocopy shop). On paper, list its six IS parts (people, procedures, data, software, hardware, network) as they are today, and write down three problems you think a better system could solve.

quiz.explain: The analyst understands both business needs and technical options and translates between them.

quiz.explain: It is data processed into something useful for a decision, which is information.

quiz.explain: System owners sponsor, pay for and approve the system.

lessons.title: Systems Thinking: Seeing the Whole and Its Parts
lessons.content:
Think about a Dhaka traffic jam at Farmgate. One car stops to pick up a passenger. The bus behind it stops. A rickshaw squeezes into the gap. Within five minutes the whole road is locked, and the cause was one small stop far away from where you are stuck. Nobody planned the jam; it came from many parts affecting each other. Systems thinking is the habit of seeing situations like this: not as a pile of separate things, but as connected parts where a change in one place shows up somewhere else.

What systems thinking is: Systems thinking is a way of looking at an organization, a machine or any situation as a whole made of interacting parts, with a purpose, a boundary and an environment. Instead of asking "which part is broken?", a systems thinker asks "how do the parts work together, and what happens around them?". For an analyst this matters because an information system is always placed inside a bigger business system. If you only look at the screen and the database, you will miss why things really go wrong.

Why analysts need it: Suppose ShasthoPharma, our pharmacy chain, complains that medicines expire on the shelves. A narrow view says "add an expiry date field to the software". A systems view asks more: who orders stock, how much, from which supplier, how is stock moved between branches, what does the counter staff sell first, the old box or the new box? The real fix may be a "first expiry, first out" rule plus a weekly report, not just a new field. Systems thinking stops you from solving the wrong problem.

The characteristics of a system: Textbooks list a set of characteristics that every system has. We will go through them one by one using the pharmacy: components, interrelationships, boundary, purpose, environment, interfaces, input, output and constraints. Some books group them differently, but the ideas are the same.

Components: A component is a part of the system. It can be simple, like the cash box, or itself a whole system, like the stock room. In ShasthoPharma, components include the counter, the stock room, the purchasing desk, the accounts section, the staff and the paper registers. Each component does a job.

Interrelationships: Components do not work alone. The counter depends on the stock room; the purchasing desk depends on sales figures; accounts depend on both. These links are the interrelationships. Most problems an analyst finds live in these links, for example the counter selling an item that the stock register still shows as available, because the two are not updated together.

Boundary: The boundary is the line that separates what is inside the system from what is outside. Drawing the boundary is one of the analyst's first decisions. Is the supplier inside our system or outside? Usually outside: we cannot change how the supplier works, we only exchange orders and deliveries with them. Is the doctor who writes the prescription inside? Outside too. A clear boundary tells everyone what the project will change and what it will not.

Purpose: Every system exists for a reason. The pharmacy's purpose is to sell the right medicines safely and profitably. A new stock system's purpose might be "never run out of the top 200 medicines and cut expired stock by half". When a purpose is fuzzy, nobody can tell whether the system is working, so analysts try to write it in measurable words.

Environment: The environment is everything outside the boundary that affects the system or is affected by it: customers, doctors, suppliers, the drug regulator, competitors, the electricity supply, even the weather (dengue season raises demand for certain medicines). The system cannot control its environment, but it must react to it.

Interfaces: An interface is a point where the system meets its environment or where two components meet. The counter is an interface with customers. The purchase order is an interface with suppliers. Inside the system, the stock transfer slip is an interface between two branches. Interfaces are where data crosses a boundary, so they are where errors, delays and security problems often appear. Analysts study them carefully.

Input, process, output: A system takes inputs from its environment, transforms them, and produces outputs. For the pharmacy, inputs include medicines from suppliers, prescriptions and money from customers. The process is checking, selling, recording and restocking. Outputs are medicines in customers' hands, receipts, purchase orders and reports. A tiny worked view: input "prescription for Amoxicillin 500 mg, 21 capsules" plus "stock 300 capsules"; process "check prescription, pick, bill 21 x 8 taka = 168 taka, reduce stock"; output "medicine, receipt for 168 taka, stock now 279".

Constraints: A constraint is a limit the system must work within. Some come from inside, such as a small budget or staff who are not comfortable with computers. Some come from outside, such as laws that say certain medicines need a prescription, or unreliable internet in a branch. A good design respects constraints; for example, a branch with weak internet may need an offline mode that syncs later.

Open and closed systems: An open system interacts with its environment: it takes inputs and gives outputs and adapts to change. Every business is an open system. A closed system, in theory, does not interact with its environment at all. Truly closed systems are rare; a sealed experiment or a fully self-contained program with no input is the usual textbook example. Some books also say "relatively closed" for a system that only interacts in controlled ways, like a payroll program that only accepts data through one approved file. The lesson for analysts: information systems are open, so they must be designed to handle change.

Subsystems and decomposition: A big system is easier to understand if we break it into smaller systems, called subsystems. ShasthoPharma can be split into sales, inventory, purchasing, accounts and human resources. Inventory can be split again into receiving, storage, transfer and expiry control. This breaking down is called decomposition. It is the same idea you will use later when drawing level 0 and level 1 data flow diagrams. A good rule: break down until each piece is small enough that one person can understand it fully.

Coupling and cohesion: Once you split a system, two questions decide whether the split is good. Cohesion asks: does everything inside one subsystem belong together? High cohesion is good; the inventory subsystem should only handle stock, not salaries. Coupling asks: how much do subsystems depend on each other? Low coupling is good; if sales and accounts only exchange one daily sales summary, a change in one rarely breaks the other. A small test: if changing the format of a receipt forces you to rewrite the payroll module, coupling is too high.

Feedback and control: Feedback is when part of the output is measured and sent back as input to adjust the system. The pharmacy compares actual stock against a target level; if Napa falls below 100 strips, a reorder is triggered. That is feedback control. Negative feedback corrects a difference and keeps the system stable, like the reorder rule bringing stock back to target, or a thermostat keeping a room cool. Positive feedback pushes the system further in the same direction, like a popular product getting more shelf space, selling more, and getting even more space. Analysts design reports and alerts as feedback loops for managers.

Entropy: Entropy means a system's natural tendency to become disordered and decay if nobody maintains it. A neat stock register slowly fills with mistakes, crossed-out entries and missing pages. Software decays too: business rules change, quick fixes pile up, data gets messy. The fix is maintenance and regular review, which is why the last stage of the SDLC, support and maintenance, never really ends.

Effectiveness and efficiency: Two words help you judge any system. Effectiveness means doing the right thing: does the system meet its purpose? Efficiency means doing it with little waste: how much time, money and effort does it take? A pharmacy that never runs out of stock but keeps three times more stock than needed is effective but not efficient, because money is locked up in boxes on shelves. A pharmacy with tiny stock and low cost that often says "sold out" is efficient but not effective. Analysts look for designs that balance both.

Systems inside systems: Every system is part of a bigger one, and every component may be a system itself. ShasthoPharma is one company inside the larger healthcare system of the country, which includes hospitals, doctors, drug companies and regulators. Inside ShasthoPharma, the inventory subsystem has its own components and its own purpose. This nesting is why analysts always ask "at what level are we looking?". A change that looks small at the branch level, such as a new prescription rule, may come from a decision made far up in the bigger system.

Real life example 1, a bKash agent shop: A bKash agent in a market takes cash from customers and sends money digitally (cash in), or gives cash for digital money (cash out). Components: the agent, the phone app, the cash drawer, the agent's e-money balance. Boundary: the shop. Environment: customers, the bKash company, the bank where the agent refills cash, the regulator. Input: cash and requests; output: transactions, receipts by SMS. Feedback: when the e-money balance gets low, the agent refills it; when cash gets low, the agent visits the bank. A constraint is the transaction limits set by rules. Every part of systems thinking is visible in one small shop.

Real life example 2, a hospital emergency room: A government hospital emergency room in Dhaka has doctors, nurses, beds, a registration desk and a pharmacy counter. If the registration desk is slow, patients pile up; if the pharmacy counter is far away, nurses spend time walking; if beds are full, ambulances wait outside. An analyst who only computerises the registration desk may simply move the queue to the doctor's room. Systems thinking says: look at the whole flow from arrival to discharge, find the real bottleneck, and then design.

Common mistakes: Drawing the boundary too wide, so the project tries to change everything and never finishes, or too narrow, so it ignores the part that causes the problem. Treating the information system as separate from the people and procedures around it. Forgetting the environment, such as laws or seasonal demand. Splitting a system into pieces that are tightly coupled, so every small change ripples everywhere. Thinking a system, once built, will stay healthy without maintenance.

What exams ask: Define a system and list its characteristics with an example. Explain open and closed systems. What is a boundary and why is it important? Explain feedback and control with an example. What are coupling and cohesion? Explain entropy in the context of information systems. Draw a simple diagram of a system with its input, process, output and environment.

Recap: Systems thinking means seeing any organization as connected parts with a purpose, a boundary and an environment. Every system has components, interrelationships, interfaces, inputs, processes, outputs and constraints. Business systems are open systems that interact with their environment. We break big systems into subsystems, aiming for high cohesion and low coupling. Feedback keeps systems under control, and entropy reminds us that every system needs maintenance. Next lesson: the systems development life cycle, the road map an analyst follows from idea to working system.
key_points: Systems thinking looks at a situation as connected parts with a purpose, boundary and environment.
Main characteristics: components, interrelationships, boundary, purpose, environment, interfaces, input, output and constraints.
The boundary decides what the project will change and what stays outside.
Business and information systems are open systems that exchange inputs and outputs with their environment.
Decomposition breaks a system into subsystems, the same idea used later in levelled DFDs.
Good subsystems have high cohesion and low coupling.
Feedback uses measured output to adjust the system; negative feedback keeps it stable.
Entropy is the natural decay of a system, which is why maintenance never ends.
lessons.tip: Before any analysis job, draw one box for the system, write its purpose inside, and draw arrows for every input and output with the outside party at the other end. This one-minute sketch prevents many boundary mistakes.
lessons.task: Choose your university library or canteen. On paper, list its components, boundary, environment, three inputs, three outputs, one constraint and one feedback loop. Then split it into three subsystems.

quiz.q: What does the boundary of a system tell us?
options: What is inside the system and what is outside it
How many users the system has
quiz.explain: The boundary separates the system from its environment and defines the scope of change.

quiz.q: A pharmacy reorders Napa automatically when stock falls below 100 strips. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: Output (stock level) is measured and fed back to trigger a correcting action.

quiz.q: Which pair describes a well-designed set of subsystems?
quiz.explain: Each subsystem should do one related job (high cohesion) and depend little on others (low coupling).

quiz.q: Why are business information systems called open systems?
options: They interact with and adapt to their environment
quiz.explain: Open systems take inputs from and give outputs to their environment and must adapt to change.

quiz.q: A stock register slowly filling with errors and missing entries is an example of:
quiz.explain: Entropy is the tendency of a system to become disordered unless it is maintained.

lessons.title: The SDLC from the Analyst's View
lessons.content:
Think about building a house in your village. Nobody starts by pouring cement. First the family decides they need a house and how much money they have. Then they talk about how many rooms, where the kitchen goes, whether there will be a second floor later. Then a mistri draws a plan. Then the building starts. Then the family moves in, and for years afterwards they repair the roof, paint the walls and maybe add a room. An information system goes through the same journey. That journey has a name: the systems development life cycle, or SDLC.

What the SDLC is: The systems development life cycle is the set of phases an information system goes through from the first idea until it is retired. Most SA&D textbooks describe four or five main phases: planning, analysis, design, implementation, and support (also called maintenance or operation). Some books split them differently, for example separating "preliminary investigation" from planning or "testing" from implementation, but the logic is the same: decide why, then what, then how, then build and deliver, then keep it running.

Why we need a life cycle: Without a common map, every project invents its own steps, people forget important work such as training or data conversion, and managers cannot tell how far a project has come. The SDLC gives everyone a shared vocabulary ("we are still in analysis"), a checklist of what must be produced, and natural points where managers can decide to continue, change or stop the project.

Phase 1, planning: Planning answers the question "why build this system, and is it worth it?". It starts with a request, such as the ShasthoPharma owner saying "we keep running out of stock". The analyst does a preliminary investigation to understand the problem and its scope, checks feasibility (technical, economic, operational and others), and helps make a rough plan of time, people and cost. The main outputs are a system request, a feasibility report and a project plan. Lessons 4, 5 and 6 cover this phase.

Phase 2, analysis: Analysis answers "what exactly must the new system do?". The analyst studies the current system (the as-is system), gathers requirements from users with interviews, questionnaires, observation and group sessions, and then models the requirements with diagrams such as data flow diagrams, decision tables, ER diagrams and use cases. The main output is a requirements document, sometimes called the system requirements specification or system proposal. Most of this course, lessons 7 to 20, lives in this phase.

Phase 3, design: Design answers "how will the system do it?". The analyst and designers choose an architecture (for example a central server with browser screens at each branch), decide whether to build, buy or outsource, and design the database, inputs, outputs, screens and programs. The main output is a design specification that builders can follow. Lessons 21 to 23 cover design.

Phase 4, implementation: Implementation turns the design into a working system that people actually use. Programmers build or configure the software, testers test it, data is moved from the old system to the new one, users are trained, documentation is written, and the organization switches over using a conversion strategy such as parallel running or a pilot branch. Lesson 24 covers this.

Phase 5, support and maintenance: After go-live the system must be kept healthy: fixing bugs, adapting to new laws or business rules, improving performance and adding small features. This phase is usually the longest and, over the life of a system, often costs more than the original development. Eventually the system becomes too old or costly and a new SDLC begins to replace it. Lesson 25 covers this.

Deliverables and gates: Each phase produces deliverables, meaning documents or products that prove the work is done. A gate (also called a milestone review or phase review) is a meeting at the end of a phase where the system owner or a steering committee looks at the deliverables and decides: go ahead, go back and fix, or stop. For example, after the feasibility report ShasthoPharma's owner may say "the cost is too high for 12 branches; start with 3 branches". Gates protect the organization from spending more money on a project that no longer makes sense.

A tiny worked map for ShasthoPharma: Planning, two weeks: system request, feasibility report, approval. Analysis, six weeks: interviews with 15 staff, observation at 3 branches, requirements document with 40 requirements, DFDs and an ER diagram. Design, four weeks: choose a cloud-hosted system with browser screens, design 12 screens and 8 reports. Implementation, eight weeks: build, test, load 3,000 medicine records, train 60 staff, pilot in one branch, then roll out. Support: ongoing. The numbers are only an example, but every real plan looks something like this.

The analyst's role in every phase: The analyst is busiest in planning and analysis, but does not disappear later. In design, the analyst checks that every requirement is covered by some screen, report or program. In implementation, the analyst helps write test cases from the requirements, answers developers' questions about business rules and often helps train users. In support, the analyst studies change requests and decides whether each one is a small fix or the start of a new project. Think of the analyst as the person who carries the users' voice through the whole life cycle.

Why early mistakes are expensive: A misunderstood requirement is cheap to fix while it is still a sentence in a document: you just rewrite the sentence. If it is found during design, screens and tables must change. If it is found after go-live, code, data, reports, training material and user habits may all need to change. Many studies of software projects have reported that fixing a defect late costs many times more than fixing it early, although the exact multiplier varies a lot between projects. This is the main reason analysis is worth the time.

How the phases are arranged, the waterfall approach: The simplest arrangement runs the phases once, in order, each finishing before the next starts, like water falling down steps. Waterfall is easy to manage and produces clear documents. Its weakness is that users see the system only near the end, and requirements that were misunderstood in analysis are found very late, when fixing them is expensive. It works best when requirements are clear and stable, such as a government form whose rules are fixed by law.

Iterative and phased approaches: Instead of one big delivery, the system can be built in versions. In a phased (incremental) approach, ShasthoPharma might get sales and stock in version 1, purchasing in version 2 and accounting in version 3, each going through analysis, design and implementation. Users get value earlier and lessons from version 1 improve version 2. The risk is that early design choices may not suit later versions.

Prototyping: In prototyping, the analyst quickly builds a rough working model, often just screens with little real logic, shows it to users, collects feedback and improves it. A throwaway prototype is used only to discover requirements and is then discarded. An evolutionary prototype is improved step by step until it becomes the real system. Prototyping is very good when users cannot describe what they want but can react to something they see.

RAD and agile in brief: Rapid application development (RAD) combines user workshops, prototyping and tools that generate code quickly to deliver systems in short time frames. Agile methods such as Scrum deliver working software in short cycles, often two to four weeks, with the customer involved all the time and less heavy documentation. Your Software Engineering course studies these process models in depth. For an analyst, the main difference is when and how much analysis is done: in waterfall most analysis happens up front; in agile, analysis happens a little in every cycle, often written as short user stories.

Structured vs object-oriented approach: There are also two main ways of modeling a system. The structured approach looks at the system as processes that transform data, and uses data flow diagrams, the data dictionary, structured English, decision tables and ER diagrams. The object-oriented approach looks at the system as objects that combine data and behaviour, and uses UML diagrams such as use case, class, sequence and activity diagrams. Many real projects mix both. This course teaches both because exams and workplaces in Bangladesh use both.

Choosing an approach: A few simple questions guide the choice. How clear are the requirements? Clear and stable suggests waterfall; unclear suggests prototyping or agile. How familiar is the technology? New technology suggests building small pieces first. How soon is value needed? Urgent needs suggest phased or agile delivery. How available are users? Agile needs users who can join meetings often. How big and risky is the project? Large, regulated projects often need more formal documents and gates.

Real life example 1, a mobile banking feature: A bank in Dhaka wants to add bill payment for electricity and gas in its app. Requirements depend on each utility company's rules and the users' habits, which are not fully known. The team builds a clickable prototype of the payment screens, tests it with twenty customers at a branch, and then develops the feature in short cycles, releasing one utility at a time. Planning and analysis still happen, but in small slices rather than one big document.

Real life example 2, a land record system: A government office computerising land records follows detailed rules set by law. Requirements are known and stable, approvals are formal, and mistakes are costly. Here a more waterfall-like approach with full documentation and formal gates makes sense, even if it is slower, because the organization needs a clear record of every decision.

Common mistakes: Thinking the SDLC is just "coding and testing"; most of the effort and most of the value comes from planning and analysis. Believing support is a minor afterthought; it is usually the longest phase. Treating a phase as a box that can never be reopened; in practice teams go back when they discover something new. Confusing the phases (planning, analysis, design...) with the approaches (waterfall, prototyping, agile); the phases are the work to be done, the approach is how that work is arranged in time.

What exams ask: Define the SDLC and explain its phases with their deliverables. Compare waterfall and prototyping, with advantages and disadvantages. What is a throwaway vs evolutionary prototype? Differentiate structured and object-oriented analysis. Why is maintenance often the most expensive phase? When would you choose an iterative approach?

Recap: The SDLC is the life journey of an information system: planning (why), analysis (what), design (how), implementation (build and deliver) and support (keep it running). Each phase produces deliverables and ends at a gate where owners decide whether to continue. The phases can be arranged as a waterfall, in phases, with prototypes, or in agile cycles, and the choice depends on how clear the requirements are, how risky the project is and how soon value is needed. Next lesson: how a project begins, from a request to a clear problem statement.
key_points: The SDLC is the set of phases a system goes through from idea to retirement.
Common phases: planning (why), analysis (what), design (how), implementation (build and deliver), support (keep running).
Each phase produces deliverables and ends at a gate where owners decide go, fix or stop.
Support and maintenance is usually the longest phase and often the most expensive over a system's life.
Waterfall runs phases once in order; it suits clear, stable requirements.
Phased, prototyping, RAD and agile approaches deliver in smaller pieces and suit unclear or changing requirements.
Throwaway prototypes discover requirements; evolutionary prototypes grow into the real system.
Structured analysis models processes and data; object-oriented analysis models objects with UML.
lessons.tip: Memorise the phases as questions: Why? What? How? Build it. Keep it alive. If an exam question describes an activity, ask which question it answers and you will know the phase.

quiz.explain: Analysis studies the current system and gathers and models requirements.

quiz.explain: A system is maintained for years after go-live, so support usually lasts longest and often costs the most.

quiz.explain: A throwaway prototype is used to learn requirements and is not kept as the final system.

options: Users cannot describe what they want
Value is needed within two weeks
quiz.explain: Waterfall works best when requirements are well understood and unlikely to change.

options: Data flow diagrams, data dictionary and decision tables
quiz.explain: Structured analysis models processes and data with DFDs, the data dictionary and logic tools.

lessons.title: Project Initiation: From a Request to a Clear Problem
lessons.content:
A patient walks into a doctor's chamber and says, "Doctor, give me a strong painkiller." A good doctor does not just write the prescription. She asks: where does it hurt, since when, what did you eat, do you have fever? The headache may come from high blood pressure, poor sleep or a sinus infection, and each needs a different treatment. Projects start the same way. Someone asks for "new software", and the analyst's first job is to act like that doctor: find the real problem behind the request before anyone agrees on a cure.

What project initiation is: Project initiation is the very start of the planning phase. It covers how an idea for a new or improved system arrives, how it is written down, how the organization decides whether to look into it, and how the analyst investigates enough to describe the real problem, its scope and its constraints. The outputs are a system request, a short preliminary investigation report and, if approved, a project charter.

Where requests come from: Requests for systems come from many directions. Users complain about slow or error-prone work ("the counter takes ten minutes to find a medicine"). Top managers see a strategic chance ("let's sell online"). The IT department sees that hardware or software is too old to support. And the outside world forces change: a new law, a competitor launching home delivery, a supplier demanding electronic orders, or a bank changing its payment system. Analysts often group these reasons as improved service, better performance, more information, stronger controls and reduced cost.

The system request: A system request is a short document that describes the business reason for a project and the value it is expected to bring. A common template has five parts. Project sponsor: the person who wants it and will champion it. Business need: the reason, in business words. Business requirements: the main capabilities needed, in broad terms. Business value: the benefits, tangible ("cut expired stock by 5 lakh taka a year") and intangible ("happier customers"). Special issues or constraints: deadlines, budget limits, laws.

A worked system request for ShasthoPharma: Sponsor: the managing director. Business need: branches often run out of fast-selling medicines while other branches hold extra stock, and medicines worth a noticeable amount expire every month. Business requirements: see stock of every branch in one place, record each sale, alert when stock falls below a reorder level, list items near expiry. Business value: fewer lost sales, less expired stock, faster month-end reports. Special issues: must work in branches with weak internet; must be ready before the next financial year.

Who decides: Most organizations have more requests than money and people. Many use a steering committee, a group of senior managers from different departments, to review requests and choose which ones become projects. They compare requests by business value, cost, risk, how well they fit the company's strategy and whether they are required by law. A request required by law, such as a new VAT reporting rule, usually jumps the queue even if its business value is low.

Problems, symptoms and opportunities: A symptom is what people see and complain about. A problem is the underlying cause. An opportunity is a chance to do better even when nothing is broken. "Customers are angry" is a symptom. "The stock register is updated only at night, so the counter does not know what is really on the shelf" is a problem. "We could take orders on WhatsApp and deliver" is an opportunity. If you treat the symptom, for example by training staff to apologize politely, the real problem stays.

Cause-and-effect analysis, the fishbone diagram: A fishbone diagram, also called an Ishikawa diagram, helps find the possible causes of a problem. Write the problem (the effect) at the head of the fish on the right, such as "medicines expire on shelves". Draw a backbone to the left and add bones for categories of causes. A common set of categories is people, methods (procedures), machines (equipment), materials, measurement and environment. Then, with the users, write possible causes on each bone.

Fishbone worked for ShasthoPharma: People: new staff do not know to sell older stock first. Methods: reorders are based on memory, not data; no rule for transferring stock between branches. Machines: no system shows expiry dates. Materials: some suppliers deliver short-dated stock. Measurement: nobody counts expired stock until year end. Environment: demand jumps during dengue season and drops afterwards, leaving extra stock. Now the team can see that software alone fixes only some causes; procedures and supplier rules must change too.

The 5 whys: Another simple tool is to ask "why?" repeatedly, about five times, until you reach a root cause. Why did we lose this sale? Because the medicine was out of stock. Why? Because we did not reorder on time. Why? Because nobody noticed stock was low. Why? Because stock is only counted at month end. Why? Because the register is kept on paper and counting takes a full day. Root cause: no continuous stock tracking. The number five is a guideline, not a rule; stop when the answer is something you can actually fix.

Scope: Scope is the boundary of the project: what it will include and what it will not. A good scope statement lists the business functions covered, the departments or branches involved, and what is explicitly out of scope. For example: "In scope: sales, stock and reordering at all 12 branches and head office. Out of scope: payroll, accounting and online sales, which may be future projects." Writing "out of scope" items is just as important as writing what is in.

Scope creep: Scope creep is the slow growth of a project's scope after it has started, through small extra requests that each seem harmless. "Can it also print staff duty rosters?" "Could customers see their old prescriptions?" Each addition takes time and money, and together they can sink the project. The cure is not to refuse every idea but to record each request, judge its cost and value, and either add it formally with more time and budget or save it for a later version.

Constraints: During initiation the analyst also lists constraints, the limits the solution must respect. They can be present or future (must handle 3 more branches next year), internal or external (staff skill vs government regulations), mandatory or desirable, and about time, budget, technology or people. Constraints shape every later choice, so finding them early saves painful surprises.

Preliminary investigation: Before a full analysis, the analyst does a short preliminary investigation, often taking days rather than weeks. The usual steps are: understand the problem or opportunity, define the project scope and constraints, do some quick fact-finding (a few interviews, reading reports, a short visit), analyze how much the project might cost and gain, and present results and a recommendation to management. Possible recommendations are: do nothing, do a quick fix, start a full project, or study further.

The project charter: If management approves, a project charter is written. It is a short, formal document that authorizes the project and names the sponsor and project manager, states the objectives, scope and key deliverables, gives a high-level budget and timeline, and lists major risks and assumptions. It is the project's birth certificate: everyone can point to it when arguing about what was agreed.

A Gantt chart in brief: Planning also needs a simple schedule. A Gantt chart is a bar chart where each task is a row and a bar shows when it starts and ends along a timeline. For ShasthoPharma, rows might be "interviews, weeks 1-2", "observation, weeks 2-3", "requirements document, weeks 4-5". Gantt charts are easy for managers to read. Detailed scheduling methods such as PERT and critical path analysis are covered in your Software Engineering course.

Why initiation matters so much: Starting a project on the wrong problem is the most expensive mistake an organization can make, because every later phase builds on it. A beautiful system that solves the wrong problem is still a failure. Initiation is also cheap: a few conversations, a fishbone drawn on a whiteboard and a two-page request cost almost nothing compared with months of development. Spending a little extra time here is the best investment in the whole life cycle.

Who should be involved: At initiation the analyst should already talk to more than just the sponsor. A quick word with two or three front-line users, the person who handles the money, and someone from IT usually reveals problems the sponsor never mentioned. For ShasthoPharma, a ten-minute chat with a counter salesman revealed that many "out of stock" medicines were actually in the stock room but in the wrong place, which changed the business need from "buy more" to "know where everything is".

Real life example 1, a college fee collection: A private college in Chattogram receives a request from the accounts office: "We need software for fees." The analyst investigates and finds that the real pain is that students pay at three banks and through mobile financial services, and matching payments to students takes days. The scope becomes "collect and match fee payments automatically" rather than "full college management software", which keeps the project small, cheap and finished in one semester.

Real life example 2, a garment factory: A garment factory in Gazipur wants "a new attendance system" because salaries are often wrong. A 5 whys session shows that attendance is captured correctly by the card machine, but overtime hours are entered by hand into a spreadsheet, where errors creep in. The fix is to connect the attendance data to the payroll calculation, a much smaller change than replacing the attendance machines.

Common mistakes: Accepting the user's first solution ("we need an app") as the problem. Writing scope without an out-of-scope list. Skipping the constraints until design. Trying to do a full analysis during the preliminary investigation, which wastes time before the project is even approved. Letting extra requests slip in without recording them, which leads to scope creep.

What exams ask: What are the main reasons for systems requests? Describe the contents of a system request. Distinguish a problem from a symptom with an example. Draw a fishbone diagram for a given problem. What is scope creep and how can it be controlled? List the steps of a preliminary investigation. What is a project charter?

Recap: Projects begin with requests from users, managers, IT or the outside world. A system request captures sponsor, need, requirements, value and constraints, and a steering committee often decides which requests go ahead. The analyst separates symptoms from real problems with fishbone diagrams and the 5 whys, defines scope with clear in and out lists, notes constraints, and runs a short preliminary investigation. An approved project gets a charter and a simple schedule. Next lesson: the feasibility study, where we check whether the project can and should be done.
key_points: Project initiation turns an idea or complaint into a clear, approved project.
Requests come from users, top management, the IT department and outside forces such as laws and competitors.
A system request states the sponsor, business need, business requirements, business value and special issues.
A steering committee often selects projects by value, cost, risk, strategic fit and legal need.
A symptom is what people notice; a problem is the underlying cause; an opportunity is a chance to improve.
Fishbone diagrams and the 5 whys help find root causes.
Scope must list what is in and out; scope creep is uncontrolled growth of scope.
A preliminary investigation ends with a recommendation; an approved project gets a project charter.
lessons.tip: Whenever someone names a solution ("we need an app"), politely ask "What problem would that solve, and how do you know?". Write their answer down; it often becomes the business need in your system request.
lessons.task: Pick a problem you face at university, such as long queues at the registration office. Draw a fishbone diagram with at least two causes on each of four bones (people, methods, machines, environment), then do a 5 whys on the cause you think is most important.

quiz.q: Which of these is a symptom rather than a root problem?
options: Stock is counted only at month end
No rule exists for transferring stock between branches
quiz.explain: Complaints are what people notice; the other options are underlying causes.

quiz.q: The part of a system request that explains the benefits in money and other terms is the:
quiz.explain: Business value lists the tangible and intangible benefits expected from the project.

quiz.q: A fishbone diagram is mainly used to:
options: Identify possible causes of a problem
quiz.explain: The Ishikawa or fishbone diagram groups possible causes of an effect into categories.

quiz.q: Scope creep means:
options: The slow, uncontrolled growth of a project's scope
quiz.explain: Small extra requests added without control make the project bigger, later and costlier.

quiz.q: Which document formally authorizes a project and states its objectives, scope, budget and sponsor?
quiz.explain: The charter is the formal start of the project, written after approval.

lessons.title: The Feasibility Study
lessons.content:
Before a family in Sylhet decides to send a son abroad for work, they ask a few hard questions. Can we afford the agency fee? Is the visa process legal and safe? Will he cope with the language and the job? Can it all be done before the job offer expires? If any answer is a clear "no", the plan is dropped or changed, however attractive it looked at first. A feasibility study asks exactly these kinds of questions about a proposed information system, before the organization commits serious money.

What a feasibility study is: A feasibility study is an evaluation of whether a proposed project can be done successfully and whether it is worth doing. Feasible means "possible and sensible under the real conditions". The study looks at the project from several angles: will it work technically, will people use it, can the organization afford it and gain from it, can it be done in time, is it legal, and will the organization support it. It ends with a recommendation and a go or no-go decision.

Why do it at all: Projects are expensive and risky. Studies of IT projects over many years have reported that a large share run over budget, run late or are cancelled. A feasibility study does not remove risk, but it brings the biggest risks into the open early, while changing course is still cheap. It also forces the team to write down assumptions, so that later, if something goes wrong, everyone can see which assumption failed.

When it happens: A first, quick feasibility check is part of the preliminary investigation in the planning phase. But feasibility is not a one-time event. It should be reviewed at every gate: after analysis, when requirements are clearer, costs may look different; after design, when the real architecture is chosen, technical risk may change. Some organizations even stop projects in the middle of design because a new law or a cheaper ready-made product changes the picture.

The main types: Textbooks usually list operational, technical, economic and schedule feasibility, and many add legal and organizational (or political) feasibility. A popular memory aid is TELOS: Technical, Economic, Legal, Operational and Schedule. In this lesson we cover all except economic feasibility, which needs its own lesson for cost-benefit calculations.

Operational feasibility: Operational feasibility asks: if we build it, will it actually be used and will it solve the problem? It looks at users, procedures and the organization. Will the counter staff accept a new sales screen? Do they have the skills, or will training be needed? Does the system fit the way work flows, or will it fight against it? Will managers really use the reports? A system that works perfectly in a demo but that staff avoid or work around is operationally infeasible.

The PIECES framework: To study the current system and see whether a change is needed, many analysts use PIECES, a checklist created by James Wetherbe. Each letter is a category of problems or opportunities. P is Performance: throughput and response time, for example a sale takes four minutes to record. I is Information: inputs, outputs and stored data, for example reports are late, wrong or missing. E is Economics: costs and profits, for example expired medicines waste money. C is Control and security: too little control lets fraud and errors in, too much slows work down. E is Efficiency: wasted time, effort or materials, for example the same data is written in three registers. S is Service: to customers, staff and partners, for example customers wait long or get wrong medicines.

PIECES worked for ShasthoPharma: Performance: finding a medicine and writing the bill takes about five minutes at peak hours. Information: head office gets branch stock figures only at month end, often with mistakes. Economics: expired stock and lost sales cost money every month. Control: cash and stock are not matched daily, so leaks go unnoticed. Efficiency: each sale is written in the sales register and again in the stock register. Service: customers are told "not available" when another branch has the item. With this list, the analyst can show managers that a change is clearly needed and which kind of change.

Technical feasibility: Technical feasibility asks: can we build and run it with available technology and skills? It considers whether the required hardware, software and network exist, whether the organization or its vendor has experience with them, how large the project is, and whether the new system must connect with existing systems. Risk grows with three things: unfamiliar technology, an unfamiliar business area, and a large project. For ShasthoPharma, a web-based stock system on a cloud server is mature technology, but weak internet in some branches is a technical risk that the design must handle.

Questions for technical feasibility: Does the technology exist and is it reliable? Do we or our vendor have people who know it? Can it handle the expected volume, say 5,000 sales a day across 12 branches, and growth to 20 branches? Can it integrate with the barcode scanners, the accounting software and mobile payment services? Can it provide the needed security? If the answer to several of these is "we are not sure", a small proof-of-concept or prototype is a cheap way to find out.

Schedule feasibility: Schedule feasibility asks: can the system be ready by the date it is needed? A deadline may be fixed by law (a new tax reporting rule from July), by business events (the system must be live before the dengue season peak), or by contracts. The analyst estimates how long each phase may take and compares it with the deadline. If the timeline is impossible, options include reducing scope for the first version, adding resources, or moving the deadline. Adding people to a late project does not always help, because new people need time to learn.

Legal feasibility: Legal feasibility asks: does the project break any laws, regulations or contracts? Examples include data protection and privacy rules, rules on keeping financial and tax records, software licensing (are we allowed to install this product on 12 computers?), copyright, and industry rules. A pharmacy, for instance, must follow drug regulations such as keeping records of certain controlled medicines and selling some only with a prescription. The system must support these rules, not make it easy to break them.

Organizational and political feasibility: Organizational feasibility asks: will the important people support it? Is there a strong project champion, usually a senior manager? Do the departments affected agree with the goals, or will some lose power, staff or influence and resist quietly? Political problems are real: a branch manager who controls ordering may resist a system that makes ordering automatic and visible to head office. Good analysts identify such stakeholders early and involve them, rather than being surprised later.

A tiny scoring example: Some teams rate each feasibility type on a simple scale to make discussions clearer. Suppose for ShasthoPharma: operational 4 out of 5 (staff are willing, training needed), technical 3 out of 5 (internet risk), schedule 3 out of 5 (tight but possible), legal 5 out of 5 (no conflicts), organizational 4 out of 5 (strong sponsor, one worried branch manager). The scores themselves are judgments, not facts, but they quickly show where the risks are: internet and schedule. The team can then plan offline mode and a phased rollout.

Feasibility of alternatives, not just one idea: A common trap is to study only the solution someone already has in mind. A better study compares a few alternatives under the same headings. For ShasthoPharma the alternatives could be: do nothing; improve the paper system with a daily stock sheet and a phone call to head office; buy a ready-made pharmacy package; or build custom software. "Do nothing" always belongs on the list, because it shows the cost of the current problems. Sometimes the cheapest alternative, a better paper procedure, solves most of the problem, and the study saves the organization from an expensive system it did not need.

The feasibility report: The results are written in a feasibility report for management. A typical report includes an introduction and the problem statement, the scope, a short description of the current system and its problems, the alternatives considered (for example do nothing, improve the paper system, buy a package, build custom software), the feasibility of each alternative under each heading, the costs and benefits, and a recommendation with reasons. It should be short enough that busy managers actually read it, with details in appendices.

Go, no-go, or change: The decision after a feasibility study is not always yes or no. Management may approve the project, reject it, ask for a smaller first version, ask for more study in one risky area, or put it on hold until a better time. A "no" is not a failure of the analyst; stopping a bad project early saves the organization money and time.

Real life example 1, a rural clinic telemedicine system: An NGO wants to connect village clinics in northern Bangladesh to doctors in Dhaka by video. Technical feasibility: video needs stable internet that some villages lack, so the team checks network coverage and considers recorded consultations or phone calls as a backup. Operational: health workers need training to use tablets and take good photos. Legal: patient data must be kept private. Schedule: the donor's funding ends in 18 months. The study recommends starting in a few unions with good coverage, then expanding.

Real life example 2, a school result publishing system: A board of education wants students to get results by SMS and on a website. Technical feasibility looks good, since SMS gateways and web hosting are mature. Schedule feasibility is critical, because results day is fixed and huge numbers of students check at the same moment. The study points out that the website must handle a sudden traffic spike, so load testing and extra server capacity become required parts of the plan.

Common mistakes: Doing only economic feasibility and ignoring whether people will use the system. Treating feasibility as a single checkbox at the start instead of revisiting it. Confusing operational feasibility (will it be used and work in practice) with technical feasibility (can it be built). Forgetting the legal side, especially licensing and data privacy. Writing a feasibility report so long that nobody reads it.

What exams ask: Define a feasibility study and explain its types. What does TELOS stand for? Explain the PIECES framework with examples. Distinguish operational and technical feasibility. What factors raise technical risk? What should a feasibility report contain? Why should feasibility be re-evaluated during the SDLC?

Recap: A feasibility study checks whether a project can be done and should be done. Operational feasibility asks if it will be used and solve the problem, and PIECES helps describe current problems. Technical feasibility asks if it can be built with available technology and skills. Schedule feasibility asks if it can be ready in time, legal feasibility asks if it follows laws and contracts, and organizational feasibility asks if key people support it. The results go into a short report with a recommendation, and feasibility is reviewed again at every gate. Next lesson: economic feasibility, where we put numbers on costs and benefits.
key_points: A feasibility study checks whether a project is possible and worth doing under real conditions.
TELOS: Technical, Economic, Legal, Operational and Schedule feasibility; organizational or political feasibility is often added.
Operational feasibility asks whether people will use the system and whether it will solve the problem.
PIECES (Performance, Information, Economics, Control, Efficiency, Service) is a checklist for problems in the current system.
Technical risk rises with unfamiliar technology, an unfamiliar business area and a large project.
Schedule feasibility compares realistic estimates with fixed deadlines.
A feasibility report compares alternatives and ends with a recommendation.
Feasibility should be reviewed at every gate, not only at the start.
lessons.tip: Remember PIECES with a picture: a puzzle with six pieces. If any piece of the current system is broken, you have a reason for change; if no piece is broken, question whether the project is needed.
lessons.task: Take your university's course registration process. Write one PIECES problem for each letter, then rate a proposed mobile registration app from 1 to 5 on technical, operational, schedule and legal feasibility with one sentence of reason for each score.

quiz.explain: TELOS is Technical, Economic, Legal, Operational and Schedule feasibility.

quiz.explain: Operational feasibility asks whether the system will actually be used and fit the way people work.

quiz.q: In PIECES, the same data being written in three registers is mainly a problem of:
quiz.explain: Repeated, wasted effort is an efficiency problem.

quiz.q: Which situation raises technical risk the most?
options: Medium project in a familiar business area
Large project using technology the team has never used
quiz.explain: Size and unfamiliar technology are two of the main drivers of technical risk.

quiz.explain: Licensing, contracts, privacy and regulations fall under legal feasibility.

lessons.title: Economic Feasibility: Costs, Benefits, Payback, ROI and NPV
lessons.content:
A rickshaw puller in Rangpur is thinking about buying a battery-powered auto-rickshaw. It costs a lot of money up front. Every day he must pay for charging and sometimes repairs. But he can carry more passengers, travel further and earn more each day. Before borrowing money he wants to know three things: how many months until the vehicle pays for itself, how much he will gain overall, and whether that gain is worth more than simply keeping the money safe in a bank. Economic feasibility asks those same three questions about an information system.

What economic feasibility is: Economic feasibility, also called cost-benefit analysis, checks whether the expected benefits of a system are greater than its costs, by enough to justify the investment and the risk. It is the part of the feasibility study that managers usually look at first, because it speaks their language: taka, months and returns. The analyst's job is to list the costs and benefits honestly, put numbers on them where possible, and calculate a few standard measures.

Costs: one-time and recurring: Costs are usually split into two groups. One-time costs, also called development or start-up costs, are paid once to build and launch the system: analysts' and programmers' time, buying hardware and software licences, setting up the network, converting old data, training staff and consultants' fees. Recurring costs, also called operating costs, continue every year the system runs: software maintenance and support, cloud hosting or server costs, internet bills, electricity, replacement parts, supplies such as receipt paper and the salary of the person who looks after the system.

Benefits: tangible and intangible: A tangible benefit can be measured in money: fewer expired medicines, fewer lost sales, less overtime, lower printing costs, fewer errors that cost money to fix. An intangible benefit is real but hard to put a taka value on: happier customers, better decisions, a better reputation, less stress for staff, faster response to a health emergency. Costs can be intangible too, for example lower staff morale during the change. Intangibles should not be ignored; they are written in the report in words, even if they are not in the calculations.

Estimating with care: Estimates are guesses supported by evidence. For costs, analysts use vendor quotations, salary rates and experience from similar projects. For benefits, they use data from the current system. For example, if the registers show that about 40,000 taka of medicine expires every month across ShasthoPharma, and the new expiry report is expected to cut that by roughly 80 percent, the benefit is about 32,000 taka a month, or about 3.8 lakh taka a year. Writing down how each number was estimated lets managers challenge it, which is healthy.

Our worked case: Let us use simple round numbers for ShasthoPharma. One-time costs: software development or setup 8 lakh taka, hardware such as computers, barcode scanners and printers 4 lakh, training and data conversion 2 lakh, total 14 lakh. Recurring costs: hosting, support and internet, 2 lakh per year. Tangible benefits per year: less expired stock 4 lakh, profit from sales no longer lost 3 lakh, staff time saved on registers 1 lakh, total 8 lakh per year. So the net yearly benefit, after recurring costs, is 8 minus 2, which is 6 lakh per year. We will look at five years of use.

Payback period: The payback period is the time it takes for the cumulative net benefits to equal the initial investment. It answers "when do we get our money back?". Track the running total. Start: minus 14 lakh. After year 1: minus 14 plus 6 equals minus 8. After year 2: minus 2. After year 3: plus 4. The balance turns positive during year 3. To find the exact point, take the 2 lakh still needed at the start of year 3 and divide by that year's 6 lakh net benefit: 2 divided by 6 is about 0.33. So payback is about 2.33 years, roughly 2 years and 4 months. When the yearly net benefit is the same every year, you can also simply divide: 14 divided by 6 equals 2.33.

Strengths and weaknesses of payback: Payback is easy to calculate and easy for managers to understand, and a short payback means lower risk, because the money comes back quickly. But it ignores everything that happens after the payback point, so a system that keeps giving benefits for ten years looks no better than one that stops after three. It also ignores the time value of money, which we will fix with NPV.

Return on investment: Return on investment (ROI) compares the total net gain with the total cost over the life of the system. The formula is ROI equals total benefits minus total costs, divided by total costs, times 100 percent. Over five years, total benefits are 8 lakh times 5, which is 40 lakh. Total costs are 14 lakh one-time plus 2 lakh times 5 recurring, which is 24 lakh. ROI equals 40 minus 24, divided by 24, which is 16 divided by 24, about 0.667, or 66.7 percent. In words: over five years, every taka spent brings back that taka plus about 67 paisa of gain. ROI is useful for comparing projects of different sizes, but like simple payback it ignores when the money arrives.

The time value of money: A taka today is worth more than a taka next year, because today's taka can be invested and earn interest, and because the future is uncertain. If a bank pays 10 percent a year, 100 taka today grows to 110 taka in one year. Turn this around: 110 taka received one year from now is worth only 100 taka today. This "today's value" of future money is called its present value. The formula is present value equals future value divided by (1 plus r) to the power n, where r is the yearly discount rate and n is the number of years.

Discount factors: With a 10 percent discount rate, the factor 1 divided by 1.1 to the power n is about 0.909 for year 1, 0.826 for year 2, 0.751 for year 3, 0.683 for year 4 and 0.621 for year 5. Multiply any future amount by the factor to get its present value. For example, 6 lakh received in year 3 is worth about 6 times 0.751, which is 4.51 lakh today. The discount rate is chosen by the organization, often based on its cost of borrowing or the return it could get elsewhere.

Net present value: Net present value (NPV) adds up the present values of all future net benefits and subtracts the initial investment. If NPV is positive, the project earns more than the discount rate and is economically worth doing; if it is negative, the money would do better elsewhere. For our case: present value of 6 lakh per year for five years equals 6 times (0.909 plus 0.826 plus 0.751 plus 0.683 plus 0.621), which is 6 times 3.790, about 22.74 lakh. NPV equals 22.74 minus 14, which is about 8.74 lakh taka. Positive, so the project passes the economic test at a 10 percent discount rate.

Discounted payback: We can also find payback using present values instead of plain amounts. Year 1 brings 6 times 0.909, about 5.45 lakh in today's money; year 2 about 4.96 lakh, running total 10.41; year 3 about 4.51 lakh, running total 14.92, which passes 14. The exact point is 2 plus (14 minus 10.41) divided by 4.51, about 2.8 years. Discounted payback is always a little longer than simple payback, because future money counts for less.

Break-even analysis: Break-even is the point where the cumulative benefits of the new system equal its cumulative costs. On a graph, draw a line of cumulative costs and another of cumulative benefits over time; where they cross is the break-even point. Before it, the project has cost more than it returned; after it, it is in profit. For a system with a big one-time cost and steady yearly flows, the break-even point is essentially the payback point, which is why the two ideas are often taught together.

Comparing alternatives: Economic feasibility is most useful when comparing options. Suppose ShasthoPharma can buy a ready-made pharmacy package with a one-time cost of 6 lakh but recurring costs of 3.5 lakh per year, giving a net yearly benefit of 8 minus 3.5, or 4.5 lakh. Its NPV over five years at 10 percent is 4.5 times 3.790, about 17.06 lakh, minus 6, which is about 11.06 lakh. That is higher than the custom option's 8.74 lakh, and its payback, 6 divided by 4.5 or about 1.33 years, is shorter. The economic answer favours the package, but the final choice will also weigh fit with requirements, vendor support and other feasibility types.

A quick sensitivity check: Our estimates may be wrong. Suppose yearly benefits turn out 30 percent lower, 5.6 lakh instead of 8 lakh. The net yearly benefit becomes 5.6 minus 2, which is 3.6 lakh. NPV becomes 3.6 times 3.790, about 13.64, minus 14, which is about minus 0.36 lakh. So if benefits fall by 30 percent, the custom project roughly breaks even and slightly loses. This kind of "what if" test is called sensitivity analysis. It tells managers how solid the estimates must be and which number deserves the most care.

Real life example 1, a coaching centre: A coaching centre in Dhanmondi considers an online system for admissions and fees costing 1.5 lakh taka once and 30,000 taka a year to run. It expects to save one part-time clerk's pay of 1.2 lakh taka a year. Net yearly benefit is 1.2 lakh minus 0.3 lakh, which is 0.9 lakh, so payback is 1.5 divided by 0.9, about 1.7 years. An intangible benefit, parents paying from home by mobile banking, may matter even more for attracting students.

Real life example 2, solar irrigation pumps: Agricultural projects in Bangladesh compare solar irrigation pumps with diesel pumps in the same way. The solar pump has a higher one-time cost but almost no fuel cost, while the diesel pump is cheaper to buy but costly to run every season. Over many years, the comparison of payback and present values often decides which is better for a village. Information systems are judged with exactly the same tools.

Common mistakes: Forgetting recurring costs, so the system looks cheaper than it is. Counting intangible benefits as huge taka amounts without evidence. Mixing up ROI and payback: payback is a time, ROI is a percentage. Ignoring the time value of money when comparing projects with very different timing. Using a single "best guess" without checking what happens if benefits are 30 percent lower; a quick sensitivity check makes the report more honest.

What exams ask: Distinguish tangible and intangible benefits, and one-time and recurring costs, with examples. Calculate payback period, ROI and NPV for given cash flows. Explain the time value of money and present value. Why is NPV considered better than simple payback? What is a break-even point? Compare two alternatives using NPV.

Recap: Economic feasibility compares costs with benefits. Costs are one-time or recurring; benefits are tangible or intangible. Payback period tells how soon the investment is recovered, ROI tells the overall percentage gain, and NPV tells the gain in today's money after accounting for the time value of money. Positive NPV means the project is economically worth doing at the chosen discount rate. Use these measures to compare alternatives, and always explain your estimates and intangibles in words. Next lesson: requirements, the heart of systems analysis.
key_points: Economic feasibility (cost-benefit analysis) checks whether benefits outweigh costs enough to justify the investment.
One-time costs are paid to build and launch; recurring costs continue every year of operation.
Tangible benefits can be measured in money; intangible benefits are real but hard to value.
Payback period = time until cumulative net benefits equal the initial investment.
ROI = (total benefits - total costs) / total costs x 100%.
Present value = future value / (1 + r)^n; money today is worth more than the same money later.
NPV = sum of present values of net benefits - initial investment; positive NPV means economically worthwhile.
Compare alternatives with the same measures, and state assumptions and intangibles in words.
lessons.tip: Always draw a small table with years as columns and rows for costs, benefits, net and cumulative. Once the table is right, payback, ROI and NPV become simple arithmetic and you avoid most exam mistakes.
