lessons.task: Imagine your family shop buys a 30,000 taka computer and billing software, costs 5,000 taka a year to run, and saves 20,000 taka a year in errors and time. Make a 3-year table and calculate payback, ROI over 3 years and NPV at 10 percent using the discount factors 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751.

quiz.q: A system costs 12 lakh once and gives a net benefit of 4 lakh every year. What is the simple payback period?
quiz.explain: 12 divided by 4 equals 3 years.

quiz.q: Which of these is an intangible benefit?
options: Fewer expired medicines worth 3 lakh taka
quiz.explain: Reputation is real but hard to measure directly in money.

quiz.q: Over five years, total benefits are 30 lakh and total costs are 20 lakh. What is the ROI?
At a 10% discount rate, what is the present value of 110 taka received one year from now?
Why is NPV usually preferred to simple payback for judging a project?
options: It accounts for the time value of money and all years of benefits
It only looks at the first year
quiz.explain: NPV discounts every future cash flow and counts benefits after the payback point too.

lessons.title: Requirements: What the New System Must Do
lessons.content:
Suppose you ask a tailor in Islampur to make a panjabi for Eid. If you just say "make a nice panjabi", you may get the wrong size, the wrong colour and a collar you hate. A good tailor asks: what length, which fabric, which colour, what kind of collar, how many pockets, and when do you need it? Each of those answers is a requirement. If even one is missed or misunderstood, the customer is unhappy, however skilful the tailor. Systems analysts face the same challenge, only with hundreds of requirements and many customers at once.

What a requirement is: A requirement is a statement of what a system must do, or a quality or characteristic it must have, to meet the needs of its users and the organization. "The system shall record each sale with date, medicine, quantity and price" is a requirement. "The system shall show search results within 2 seconds" is also a requirement. Requirements are the bridge between the analysis phase and the design phase: designers design to satisfy them, testers test against them, and users accept the system when they are met.

Why requirements matter so much: Many project failures are traced back to requirements: they were incomplete, wrong, vague, or kept changing without control. A misunderstood requirement found after go-live costs far more to fix than one corrected on paper. That is why the analysis phase spends so much effort finding, writing and checking requirements, and why the next four lessons are about gathering and organizing them.

Levels of requirements: Requirements exist at different levels of detail. Business requirements state what the organization wants to achieve: "Reduce expired stock by half within a year." User requirements describe what users need to do with the system, in their own terms: "As a branch manager, I want to see which items will expire in the next 60 days." System requirements are the detailed, precise statements that designers and programmers work from, and they are divided into functional and non-functional requirements.

Functional requirements: A functional requirement describes a process the system must perform or information it must provide. In other words, it is something the system does. For ShasthoPharma: the system shall let a salesperson find a medicine by brand name or generic name; the system shall calculate the bill including discount and VAT; the system shall reduce stock when a sale is saved; the system shall produce a daily list of medicines below their reorder level; the system shall block the sale of prescription-only medicines unless a prescription number is entered.

Non-functional requirements: A non-functional requirement describes a quality or constraint on how the system works, rather than a specific function. Common categories are: operational (the physical and technical environment, for example "must run in a web browser on the existing branch computers" and "must keep working when the internet is down and sync later"); performance (speed, capacity and reliability, for example "search results within 2 seconds for 95 percent of searches" and "support 50 users at the same time"); security (who can access what, for example "only managers can change prices"); and cultural and political (for example "screens must support Bangla and English" and "reports must follow the tax authority's format"). Usability, maintainability and availability are also often listed.

A quick test to tell them apart: Ask "is this something the system does, or how well or under what conditions it does it?". "Print a receipt" is functional. "Print a receipt within 3 seconds" adds a non-functional performance requirement. "Only cashiers can reprint receipts" is a security requirement. Both kinds matter: a system with every function but painfully slow screens will be abandoned just as surely as one that is fast but missing key functions.

Writing good requirements: A good requirement is clear and unambiguous (only one reasonable meaning), complete (says everything needed), consistent (does not contradict another requirement), verifiable or testable (you can check whether it is met), feasible (can be done within budget and technology), necessary (really needed, not gold plating) and traceable (has an ID and a source, so you know who asked for it and why). Many teams write each one starting with "The system shall..." and give it a number, such as R-12.

From bad to good, worked: Bad: "The system should be fast." Fast for whom, doing what? Better: "R-21: The system shall display medicine search results within 2 seconds for at least 95 percent of searches during opening hours." Bad: "The system should be easy to use." Better: "R-30: A new salesperson shall be able to record a sale of three items without help after 30 minutes of training." Bad: "The system shall handle stock." Better: split into several requirements, for receiving stock, transferring stock between branches, adjusting stock after a count, and so on. Words like "fast", "easy", "user friendly", "flexible" and "etc." are warning signs.

User stories, a lighter format: Teams that work in an agile way often write user requirements as short user stories in the form "As a [role], I want [something] so that [reason]". For example: "As a counter salesperson, I want to scan a barcode instead of typing the medicine name, so that I can serve customers faster." Each story is later given acceptance criteria, such as "the scanned medicine appears in the bill within 1 second", which play the same role as testable system requirements. The format is different, but the goal is the same: a clear, checkable statement of need.

Where requirements come from: Requirements are discovered, not invented by the analyst. Sources include interviews with users and managers, questionnaires, watching people work, existing forms, reports and manuals, laws and regulations, complaints and error logs, and competitors' systems. Each requirement should record its source, for example "R-17, from interview with the Gulshan branch manager, 12 March", so that questions can go back to the right person later.

Requirements vs design: A requirement says what is needed, not how to build it. "The system shall store customer phone numbers" is a requirement. "Store phone numbers in a VARCHAR(15) column in MySQL" is a design decision. Mixing them too early limits designers and can lock the project into a poor solution. Sometimes, however, a "how" is a genuine constraint, for example "must use the bank's payment gateway", and then it belongs in the non-functional list.

As-is and to-be: Requirements analysis compares two pictures. The as-is system is how things work today, with all its problems. The to-be system is how things should work after the change. The analyst first understands the as-is system well enough to know what must be kept, what must be fixed and what can be dropped, then describes the to-be system. Spending too long on as-is wastes time; skipping it means you may forget an important rule that the old system handled quietly, such as a branch manager who always checks the narcotics register on Fridays.

How much change: BPA, BPI and BPR: The size of the gap between as-is and to-be depends on how ambitious the project is. Textbooks describe three levels. Business process automation (BPA) keeps the business process mostly the same but uses computers to do it faster and with fewer errors. Business process improvement (BPI) makes moderate changes to how the process works to make it more efficient or effective. Business process reengineering (BPR) radically redesigns the process, often starting from a blank page. More change means more potential value but also more cost and risk.

BPA techniques: Two common techniques support BPA. Problem analysis asks users to list problems with the current system and how they would solve them; the resulting ideas are usually small fixes. Root cause analysis goes deeper, finding the underlying causes of problems, as we did with the fishbone and 5 whys. For ShasthoPharma, BPA would mean computerising the existing sales and stock registers, with the same steps, just faster and accurate.

BPI techniques: For BPI, duration analysis compares the total time a process takes from start to finish with the time spent on actual work. If a purchase order takes 3 days from request to dispatch but only 40 minutes of actual work, the process is full of waiting and handoffs and can be improved, for example by letting one person do several steps. Activity-based costing finds the cost of each step to target the most expensive ones. Informal benchmarking looks at how other organizations, often seen as customers, do the same thing, for example how a large online pharmacy lets customers upload prescriptions.

BPR techniques: For BPR, outcome analysis asks what the customer truly wants as the end result and works backwards; a patient really wants the right medicine quickly, not to visit a shop. Technology analysis lists new technologies and asks how each could transform the business, such as mobile apps, e-prescriptions or delivery partners. Activity elimination imagines removing each activity one at a time and asks what would happen; sometimes a step that everyone assumed was needed turns out to be useless. BPR for ShasthoPharma might lead to an online ordering and home delivery model with stock managed centrally.

Real life example 1, a passport application: In Bangladesh, passport applications moved from handwritten forms to machine-readable and then e-passports with an online application step. A functional requirement of such a system is "the applicant shall submit personal details online and choose an appointment". Non-functional requirements include identity data security, handling very large numbers of applicants and support for Bangla and English names. Moving paper forms to online forms alone would be closer to automation; redesigning the whole flow around online appointments and biometrics is closer to reengineering.

Real life example 2, a restaurant delivery service: A restaurant in Uttara wants to take orders through food delivery apps. User requirement: "As the kitchen manager, I want new orders to appear on a screen in the kitchen." Functional: "The system shall display each new order with items, notes and pickup time." Non-functional: "Orders shall appear within 10 seconds of being placed" and "The screen shall be readable from 2 metres away." Clear requirements like these let any developer build the right thing.

Common mistakes: Writing vague requirements with words like "fast" and "easy". Mixing several requirements in one sentence, which makes testing hard. Forgetting non-functional requirements entirely. Writing design decisions as requirements too early. Gathering requirements only from managers and ignoring the people who will use the system daily. Assuming requirements will not change; they always do, and lesson 11 shows how to manage that.

What exams ask: Define a requirement. Distinguish functional and non-functional requirements with examples. List the characteristics of a good requirement. Rewrite a vague requirement into a testable one. Explain BPA, BPI and BPR and give techniques for each. What is the difference between the as-is and to-be system?

Recap: A requirement is a statement of what a system must do or a quality it must have. Requirements exist at business, user and system levels; system requirements are functional (what it does) or non-functional (how well and under what constraints). Good requirements are clear, complete, consistent, testable, feasible, necessary and traceable. Analysts compare as-is with to-be, and the level of change can be automation, improvement or reengineering, each with its own techniques. Next lesson: the first and most common way of finding requirements, the interview.
key_points: A requirement states what a system must do or a quality it must have.
Levels: business requirements, user requirements and detailed system requirements.
Functional requirements describe what the system does; non-functional requirements describe how well and under what constraints.
Non-functional categories include operational, performance, security and cultural or political requirements.
Good requirements are clear, complete, consistent, testable, feasible, necessary and traceable.
Requirements say what, not how; design decisions come later unless they are real constraints.
As-is is today's system; to-be is the improved system.
BPA automates, BPI improves and BPR radically redesigns business processes.
lessons.tip: After writing any requirement, ask: "How would a tester prove this is met?" If you cannot describe a test, rewrite the requirement until you can.
lessons.task: Write five functional and five non-functional requirements for your university's online result system. Number them (R-1, R-2...), start each with "The system shall", and underline any vague word you used, then remove it.

quiz.q: "The system shall show search results within 2 seconds" is an example of a:
quiz.explain: It describes how well the system performs, not a new function.

quiz.q: Which requirement is written best?
options: The system should be user friendly
A new salesperson shall record a 3-item sale without help after 30 minutes of training
The system should be fast and flexible
The system shall handle stock etc.
quiz.explain: It is specific and testable; the others use vague words.

quiz.q: Radically redesigning a business process, often from a blank page, is called:
quiz.explain: BPR makes fundamental, radical changes to how the business works.

quiz.q: Duration analysis is a technique mainly used for:
quiz.explain: Duration analysis compares total process time with actual work time to find waiting and handoffs to improve.

quiz.q: The description of how the business works today, before any change, is the:
quiz.explain: The as-is system is the current situation that the analyst studies first.

lessons.title: Fact-Finding I: Interviews
lessons.content:
Think about a new doctor meeting a patient. The doctor does not start writing a prescription the moment you walk in. She asks: "What is the problem? Since when? Does it hurt more at night? Have you taken any medicine?" Each answer leads to the next question, and slowly the real illness becomes clear. A systems analyst does the same thing with an organization. The most common and most powerful tool for this is the interview: a planned conversation with the people who know how the work is really done.

What fact-finding is: Fact-finding, also called requirements elicitation or information gathering, is the set of techniques an analyst uses to collect facts about the current system and the needs for the new one. The main techniques are interviews, questionnaires, observation, document analysis, JAD sessions and prototyping. This lesson covers interviews in depth. The next two lessons cover the others and compare them.

What an interview is: An interview is a direct, usually face-to-face conversation between the analyst and one person or a small group, with a clear purpose: to learn facts, opinions, feelings and ideas about the system. Interviews let you see reactions, ask follow-up questions on the spot and build trust. Their downside is that they take a lot of time, both yours and the interviewee's, and the quality depends heavily on the skill of the interviewer.

Why interviews matter: Documents tell you what is supposed to happen. Interviews tell you what actually happens, and why. In the ShasthoPharma pharmacy chain, the official rule may say "stock is counted every Friday". A branch manager in an interview may admit, "Honestly, we count only when head office calls, maybe once a month." That one sentence explains why the stock data is unreliable. No document would have told you that.

Step 1, decide who to interview: You cannot talk to everyone, so you choose people from different levels and roles. At ShasthoPharma that means the owner (goals and budget), the head office accountant (reports and tax), two or three branch managers (stock and staff), several counter staff (daily sales), the stock keeper, and perhaps a supplier's sales representative. Talking to only top managers gives a pretty picture; talking to only clerks misses the goals. You need both. An organization chart helps you pick.

Step 2, plan the interview: Before each interview, set clear objectives: what exactly do you want to learn from this person? Read available documents first so you do not waste time asking things you could have read. Prepare a list of questions, but stay flexible. Book a time and place that suits the interviewee, ideally at their workplace so they can show you forms and screens. Tell them in advance the purpose and roughly how long it will take, for example 45 minutes. Plan to record notes, and if you want to make an audio recording, ask permission first.

Open-ended questions: An open-ended question lets the person answer in their own words, with no fixed choices. Examples: "How do you decide which medicines to reorder?" or "What is the most frustrating part of closing the shop each night?" Open questions give rich detail, reveal feelings and surprises, and make people feel heard. The downside is that answers can be long, wander off topic and are hard to compare between people.

Closed-ended questions: A closed question limits the answer to a specific fact or a choice. Examples: "How many sales do you make on a typical day?", "Do you check expiry dates when receiving stock, yes or no?", "Which is slower: billing or searching for the medicine?" Closed questions are quick, precise and easy to compare across many interviews. The downside is that they cannot uncover what you did not think to ask, and too many of them can feel like an interrogation.

Probes: A probe is a follow-up question that digs deeper into an answer. "Why?", "Can you give me an example?", "What happens then?", "You said it is often late; how late, roughly?" Probing is where the real facts appear. Suppose a counter staff member says, "The register is a headache." A good analyst probes: "Which part exactly?" Answer: "Finding yesterday's sale when a customer comes back to return a strip." Now you have a specific requirement: searching past sales by date and customer.

Bipolar and leading questions: A bipolar question allows only two answers, usually yes or no. Use them sparingly, mainly to confirm facts. A leading question pushes the person toward an answer, such as "You agree the new system will be much faster, don't you?". Avoid leading questions completely; they give you the answer you wanted instead of the truth. Also avoid questions full of jargon, like "Would you prefer a normalized relational schema?". Speak the interviewee's language.

Pyramid structure: The way you order questions is called the interview structure. In the pyramid structure you start with very specific, closed questions and gradually move to general, open ones. Example: "How many prescriptions did you fill yesterday?" then "Which kinds of prescriptions take longest?" then "How do you feel about the way prescriptions are handled overall?" Use a pyramid when the interviewee seems reluctant or needs warming up, because concrete facts are easy to answer.

Funnel structure: The funnel is the opposite: start with broad, open questions and narrow down to specific, closed ones. Example: "Tell me how a normal day at your branch goes" then "What happens when a medicine is out of stock?" then "How many times last week did that happen?" Use a funnel when the person is comfortable and enjoys talking. It is easy to start and lets them tell you what they think is important.

Diamond structure: The diamond combines both. You start specific and easy, widen out to general open questions in the middle, then close again with specific questions to confirm details. It takes longer but often gives the most complete picture. It works well for long interviews with key people, such as the owner.

Unstructured vs structured interviews: In an unstructured interview, the analyst has only a topic and lets the conversation flow. It is great early on, when you know little. In a structured interview, the questions and their order are fixed in advance, and every interviewee gets the same questions. It is great later, when you need comparable answers from many branch managers. Many real interviews are semi-structured: a prepared list, with freedom to probe.

Individual vs group interviews: Most interviews are one-to-one, which makes people more open about problems, especially problems with their boss. A group interview brings two to five people from the same area together, for example three counter staff from different branches. It saves time, and one person's answer often reminds another of something important. But in a group, quiet or junior people may hold back, and a senior person can dominate. A practical rule: use one-to-one interviews for sensitive topics and group interviews for checking common procedures.

Phone and video interviews: When branches are far apart, such as a ShasthoPharma branch in Chattogram, a phone or video call can replace a visit. It saves travel money but you lose body language and cannot see the forms and shelves yourself. Ask the person to send photos of the register or forms before the call so you can talk about them together.

Respect and language: In Bangladesh, people may be polite and avoid saying "no" or criticising a senior colleague directly. A counter staff member may say "everything is fine" while the boss is in the room. Choose a quiet place, assure them their answers are used to improve the system and not to blame anyone, and speak in the language they are most comfortable with, often Bangla rather than English.

Step 3, conduct the interview: Arrive on time and dress appropriately. Start with a short introduction and explain the purpose. Begin with easy questions. Listen far more than you talk; a rough guide is that the interviewee should speak most of the time. Take notes, and repeat key points back to check you understood: "So, if I understand correctly, reorders are placed only on Sundays?" Watch body language: hesitation or a glance at the boss may mean there is more to the story. Keep to the agreed time. End by thanking them, asking "Is there anything I should have asked but didn't?", and asking whether you can contact them again.

Step 4, write it up: Write the interview report the same day, while memory is fresh. Include who, when, where, the objectives, the main facts learned, opinions, problems raised, and open questions to follow up. Many analysts send a short summary back to the interviewee to confirm accuracy. This step is often skipped, and then three weeks later nobody remembers who said what.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma branch manager: The analyst plans a 45-minute funnel interview with the Dhanmondi branch manager. She starts broad: "Walk me through how stock arrives at your branch." She learns that suppliers deliver directly to branches, not to head office. She narrows: "How do you record a delivery?" Answer: "We sign the supplier's challan and file it." She probes: "Does anyone add it to the stock register?" Pause. "When we have time." Then closed questions: "How many deliveries per week?" About 15. "How often is the register updated the same day?" Maybe half. Requirement discovered: goods received must be recorded at the moment of delivery, perhaps by scanning the challan items.

Real life example 2, a union parishad service centre: Imagine an analyst designing a system for issuing birth registration and trade licence documents at a union digital centre. Interviewing the entrepreneur who runs the centre gives the official steps. Interviewing villagers waiting in line, using simple Bangla and open questions like "What made today's visit difficult?", reveals that many had to come back twice because a document was missing and nobody told them the full list in advance. That turns into a requirement: show a complete checklist of required documents before the visit, for example by SMS or on a printed notice.

Advantages and disadvantages summary: Interviews give rich, deep information, allow follow-up, reveal feelings and politics, and build relationships with users. But they are time-consuming and costly, answers depend on the interviewer's skill, people may say what they think you want to hear, and results from many interviews are harder to combine than questionnaire numbers.

Common mistakes: Talking too much and listening too little. Asking leading questions. Not preparing, so you ask things the documents already answer. Interviewing only managers. Forgetting to write up notes promptly. Treating the first answer as the full truth instead of probing. Using technical jargon. Promising features in the interview that may never be built; this creates false expectations.

What exams ask: Define fact-finding and list its techniques. Explain the steps of conducting an interview. Distinguish open-ended and closed-ended questions with examples, plus their advantages. Explain pyramid, funnel and diamond structures with diagrams. Compare structured and unstructured interviews. List the advantages and disadvantages of interviews.

Recap: Interviews are planned conversations that reveal how work is really done. Choose interviewees across levels, set objectives, prepare questions, and read documents first. Mix open and closed questions, probe deeply, avoid leading questions, and pick a structure: pyramid (specific to general), funnel (general to specific) or diamond (both). Listen more than you talk, confirm understanding, and write the report the same day. Next lesson: questionnaires, observation and document analysis.
key_points: Fact-finding techniques include interviews, questionnaires, observation, document analysis, JAD and prototyping.
Interview people from different levels and roles, not only managers.
Plan each interview: objectives, prior reading, question list, time and place.
Open-ended questions give rich detail; closed-ended questions give precise, comparable facts.
Probes such as "why?" and "for example?" uncover the real requirements; avoid leading questions and jargon.
Pyramid goes specific to general, funnel goes general to specific, diamond combines both.
Listen more than you talk, confirm understanding, and write the interview report the same day.
lessons.tip: Before any interview, write your three most important questions at the top of the page. If time runs short, you will still leave with what you came for.
lessons.task: Interview a family member or shopkeeper for 15 minutes about how they keep track of money or stock. Use a funnel structure, write down at least two open and two closed questions you asked, and list three facts you would not have guessed without asking.

quiz.q: Which is an open-ended question?
options: How many sales did you make yesterday?
Do you check expiry dates, yes or no?
How do you decide which medicines to reorder?
quiz.explain: An open-ended question lets the person answer freely in their own words.

quiz.q: An interview that starts with broad, general questions and narrows down to specific ones uses which structure?
quiz.explain: The funnel goes from general open questions to specific closed ones.

quiz.q: Why should an analyst avoid leading questions?
options: They take too long to answer
They push the person toward an answer instead of revealing the truth
They are only allowed in questionnaires
quiz.explain: Leading questions bias the answer toward what the interviewer wants to hear.

quiz.q: When is a pyramid structure most useful?
options: When the interviewee loves to talk at length
When you need the answers to be anonymous
When there is no time to prepare
When the interviewee is reluctant and needs warming up with easy specific questions
quiz.explain: Starting with concrete, easy questions helps a hesitant person open up.

quiz.q: What is a probe in an interview?
options: A follow-up question that digs deeper into an answer
quiz.explain: Probes like "why?" or "can you give an example?" reveal details behind the first answer.

lessons.title: Fact-Finding II: Questionnaires, Observation and Documents
lessons.content:
Suppose ShasthoPharma has 12 branches and 80 counter staff. Interviewing every single person for 45 minutes would take 60 hours of talking, plus travel across Dhaka traffic. Yet the owner wants to know what all of them think. And even after many interviews, the analyst still wonders: do people really work the way they described? These two problems, reaching many people cheaply and checking what really happens, are solved by three other fact-finding techniques: questionnaires, observation and document analysis.

What this lesson covers: Last lesson we studied interviews in depth. Now we look at questionnaires (written questions sent to many people), observation (watching the work as it happens) and document analysis (studying existing forms, reports, files and records). At the end we compare all the main techniques so you know which one to pick in which situation.

Questionnaires, what they are: A questionnaire, or survey, is a set of written questions given to many people, who answer on their own, on paper or online. It is the best tool when the people are many, spread out, or when you need numbers to support a decision, for example "62 percent of counter staff say billing is the slowest step". Questionnaires are cheap per person, allow anonymous answers (which can make people more honest), and give results that are easy to count and compare.

Limits of questionnaires: You cannot ask a follow-up question when an answer is unclear. Many people do not return them, so the response rate can be low. People may misunderstand a question and you will never know. And a badly designed questionnaire gives confident-looking but useless numbers. That is why questionnaires are usually used after some interviews, when the analyst already knows the right questions to ask.

Question types: Like interviews, questionnaires use open and closed questions, but closed questions dominate because they are easy to answer and count. Common closed forms are yes/no questions, multiple choice ("Which step takes longest? Searching / Billing / Packing / Payment"), ranking ("Rank these four problems from 1 to 4"), and fill-in numbers ("How many customers per hour at peak time?"). Keep one or two open questions at the end, such as "What one change would make your work easier?". They often give the best ideas.

Likert scales: A Likert scale measures attitude by asking how strongly the person agrees with a statement, usually on five points: strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree. Example statement: "Finding a medicine on the shelf is quick." If 40 staff answer and you score the points from 1 to 5, you can compute an average. Say the scores add up to 92; the average is 92 / 40 = 2.3, between disagree and neutral, which tells you searching is a real problem. Keep the scale the same direction throughout so people do not get confused.

Writing good questions: Use simple words in the respondent's language; for counter staff in Bangladesh that usually means Bangla. Ask one thing per question. "Is the system fast and easy to use?" is a double question; split it. Avoid leading wording such as "Don't you agree that the register is outdated?". Avoid vague words like "often"; give ranges instead, such as "0, 1-2, 3-5, more than 5 times a week". Make choices cover all possibilities and not overlap: ranges 0-5 and 5-10 overlap at 5.

Layout and order: Start with a short note explaining the purpose, how long it takes and whether it is anonymous. Begin with easy, non-threatening questions. Group questions by topic. Put sensitive questions, such as about mistakes or salaries, later. Keep it short: a questionnaire that takes more than 10 to 15 minutes loses many respondents. Today free online form tools make it easy to share a survey link through WhatsApp or email and see the totals automatically.

Sampling: Often you do not need everyone; you can ask a sample, a smaller group that represents the whole population. Random sampling gives every person an equal chance, like picking names from a box. Systematic sampling picks every k-th person from a list, for example every 4th name from the staff list of 80, giving 20 people. Stratified sampling splits the population into groups (strata) and samples from each, for example a few staff from every branch, so small branches are not missed. Convenience sampling just uses whoever is easy to reach; it is quick but can be biased. For ShasthoPharma, stratified sampling by branch makes sense.

Pilot testing: Before sending a questionnaire to everyone, give it to three or four people first. Watch where they hesitate, which questions they misunderstand and how long it takes. Imagine the pilot shows that staff read "stock-out" as "stock taken out for sale" rather than "no stock left". Fixing that one word before the real survey saves every answer to that question.

Response rate: The response rate is the number of completed questionnaires divided by the number sent, times 100. If 80 are sent and 58 come back, the rate is 58 / 80 x 100 = 72.5 percent. A low rate is dangerous, because the people who reply may not be typical; often only the very happy or the very angry bother to answer. To raise it, keep the survey short, explain why it matters, get a manager to support it, send one polite reminder, and share the results afterwards so people see their answers were used.

Observation, what it is: Observation means the analyst goes to the workplace and watches people do their jobs. Interviews tell you what people say they do; observation shows what they actually do. At a ShasthoPharma branch, the analyst stands near the counter from 6 to 9 pm, the busiest hours, and notes every step: customer asks, staff searches, checks price on a paper list, writes in the register, takes cash or a mobile payment, gives change.

Types of observation: Observation can be passive, where the analyst only watches, or active, where the analyst asks questions or even does the job for a while. It can be announced, where people know they are being watched, or unannounced, though watching without telling people raises ethical problems and should follow the organization's rules. Analysts often time tasks: for example, observing 30 sales and finding that searching for a medicine took on average 70 seconds while billing took 25 seconds. That number points to the real bottleneck.

The Hawthorne effect: People often change their behaviour when they know they are being watched. They work faster, follow the rules more carefully and skip their usual shortcuts. This is called the Hawthorne effect, named after studies at the Hawthorne Works factory in the USA in the 1920s and 1930s. To reduce it, observe for longer periods so people get used to you, come several times, and be friendly rather than looking like an inspector.

Strengths and weaknesses of observation: It gives reliable, first-hand facts, reveals unofficial workarounds, and helps the analyst understand the physical setting, such as how little space the counter has for a computer. But it takes time, may catch an unusual day, can disturb the work, and only shows actions, not the reasons behind them. That is why observation is usually followed by a short interview: "I noticed you write the sale on a slip first. Why?"

Document analysis: Organizations are full of paper and files: forms, reports, invoices, manuals, policy circulars, organization charts, old system documentation and even spreadsheets on someone's laptop. Studying these is called document analysis, record review or sampling of existing documentation. It is usually the first thing an analyst does, because it is cheap and helps prepare better interview questions.

What documents reveal: A filled-in form shows exactly which data is captured and in what format. Comparing several filled forms shows what is often left blank, which suggests a field nobody needs, or what is written in the margin, which suggests a field that is missing. Reports show what managers actually look at. Error and complaint logs show where things break. At ShasthoPharma, studying 100 supplier challans shows that 18 percent have handwritten corrections to quantity, a clue that deliveries are often short and must be checked on arrival.

Cautions with documents: Documents can be outdated. A procedure manual from 2015 may describe steps nobody follows any more. Forms may have changed informally. So treat documents as a starting point and confirm with interviews and observation. Also handle documents carefully when they contain private data such as patient names; take only what you need and follow privacy rules.

Comparing the techniques: Interviews give depth and allow follow-up but are slow and expensive. Questionnaires reach many people cheaply and give numbers but lack depth and follow-up. Observation shows reality but is time-consuming and affected by the Hawthorne effect. Document analysis is cheap and gives the official picture but may be out of date. JAD sessions, covered next lesson, bring people together to agree quickly but need careful facilitation. No single technique is enough. A good analyst triangulates: uses two or three techniques on the same question and checks that the answers agree.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma combined approach: The analyst first studies registers, challans and the monthly report (documents). Then she interviews the owner and three branch managers. Next she sends a 12-question Bangla questionnaire to all 80 counter staff through a WhatsApp link, using a Likert scale for satisfaction with the current process; 58 reply. Finally she observes two branches during evening peak. All four sources agree on one finding: searching for medicines and checking stock by hand is the biggest time waster. That agreement gives her confidence to make fast search and live stock the top requirements.

Real life example 2, a garment factory canteen: An analyst asked to design a token system for a factory canteen in Gazipur sends a short questionnaire to a stratified sample of workers from each floor, asking about waiting time and food choice. Then he observes the lunch break and times the queue: about 18 minutes average wait. Old cash books show which items sell most. Together these lead to a simple design: pre-ordering by floor and separate counters for the three most popular meals.

Common mistakes: Sending a questionnaire before understanding the problem, so the questions miss the point. Writing double or leading questions. Making the questionnaire too long. Not pilot testing. Trusting a single day of observation. Ignoring the Hawthorne effect. Trusting old documents without checking. Using only one technique instead of combining several.

What exams ask: When should a questionnaire be used instead of interviews? Advantages and disadvantages of questionnaires, observation and document analysis. What is a Likert scale? Explain sampling methods (random, systematic, stratified, convenience). What is the Hawthorne effect? Compare fact-finding techniques in a table.

Recap: Questionnaires reach many people cheaply and give countable answers; design them with simple, single, unbiased questions, a Likert scale for attitudes, a good sample and a pilot test. Observation shows how work really happens; watch for the Hawthorne effect and follow up with questions. Document analysis is cheap and a great starting point but may be outdated. Combine techniques and check that they agree. Next lesson: group techniques such as JAD sessions and prototyping.
key_points: Questionnaires reach many people cheaply and give countable, comparable answers, but allow no follow-up.
Write simple, single, non-leading questions with non-overlapping choices, and pilot test first.
A Likert scale measures attitude, usually on five points from strongly disagree to strongly agree.
Sampling: random, systematic (every k-th), stratified (by group) and convenience.
Observation shows what people actually do and reveals workarounds and bottlenecks.
The Hawthorne effect: people change their behaviour when they know they are watched.
Document analysis is cheap and a good first step, but documents may be outdated.
No single technique is enough; combine several and check that they agree.
lessons.tip: Whenever you design a questionnaire, answer it yourself first and then give it to one friend. If either of you hesitates on a question, rewrite it.
lessons.task: Write a 6-question survey (with at least one Likert-scale item and one open question) about canteen or transport problems at your university. Pilot it with two classmates and note one question you had to rewrite and why.

quiz.q: When is a questionnaire usually better than interviews?
options: When you need to reach many people spread over many places
When you need to probe deeply into one person's feelings
When you want to watch the work being done
When there are only two users
quiz.explain: Questionnaires are cheap per person and good for large, spread-out groups.

quiz.q: What is the Hawthorne effect?
options: People change their behaviour when they know they are being observed
quiz.explain: Being watched makes people work differently, so observation may not show normal behaviour.

quiz.q: Picking a few staff from every branch for a survey is an example of:
options: Random sampling of the whole list
quiz.explain: Stratified sampling divides the population into groups and samples from each one.

quiz.q: "Is the system fast and easy to use?" is a poor questionnaire item because it:
options: Asks two things in one question
quiz.explain: A double question cannot be answered clearly when one part is true and the other is false.

quiz.q: What is a main weakness of document analysis?
options: It always requires the users to stop working
Documents may be outdated or not match how work is really done
It cannot show any data formats
quiz.explain: Manuals and forms may describe old procedures, so findings must be confirmed with other techniques.

lessons.title: Fact-Finding III: JAD, Brainstorming and Prototyping
lessons.content:
Imagine planning a family wedding by phone. You call the bride's mother, then the groom's father, then the decorator, then the caterer. Each call changes something, and by the time you call the first person back, the plan has shifted again. Weeks pass. Now imagine everyone sits in one room for a full afternoon with a whiteboard, decides the date, the menu, the budget and the guest list, and leaves with one agreed plan. That second way is the idea behind group fact-finding techniques like JAD. When many people must agree, getting them together saves enormous time.

What group techniques are: Interviews and questionnaires collect information from people one at a time. Group techniques collect it from several people at once and, more importantly, let them discuss, disagree and settle differences on the spot. The main ones are joint application development (JAD) sessions, brainstorming, and prototyping used as a requirements tool. This lesson explains each and when to use it.

The problem JAD solves: In a traditional analysis, the analyst interviews the owner, then the accountant, then the branch manager. Their answers often conflict. The accountant wants every sale to record the VAT detail; the counter staff want billing to take fewer clicks. The analyst becomes a messenger, running between people for weeks. Misunderstandings creep in. JAD replaces that slow back-and-forth with structured group meetings where the decision makers and users settle requirements together.

What JAD is: Joint application development (JAD), also called joint application design, is a structured, facilitated group workshop where users, managers and IT people work together intensively to define and agree on system requirements, and sometimes high-level design. It was developed at IBM in the late 1970s and became popular because it greatly shortened the time needed to gather and agree on requirements. A JAD project may hold one session or a series of sessions, each lasting from half a day to several days.

JAD roles, the sponsor: The project sponsor or executive sponsor is a senior manager who supports the project, gives people time off their normal jobs to attend, and has the authority to make final decisions when the group is stuck. At ShasthoPharma, that could be the owner or the operations director. The sponsor usually opens the first session to show it matters, but may not attend every hour.

JAD roles, the facilitator: The facilitator, or session leader, runs the meeting. This person plans the agenda, explains the rules, keeps the discussion on track, makes sure quiet people get heard and loud people do not dominate, and resolves conflicts. A good facilitator is neutral: they do not push their own solution. Often the facilitator is a trained analyst, sometimes from outside the organization so that nobody suspects favouritism.

JAD roles, the scribe and others: The scribe records everything: decisions, requirements, open issues, and diagrams drawn on the board. Today the scribe often types directly into a shared document or draws models with a tool so everyone can see them projected. Users are the people who will use the system, such as branch managers, counter staff and the stock keeper; they are the most important participants because they know the work. Managers explain business goals and rules. IT staff, such as developers or a database designer, answer questions about what is technically possible, and some may attend only as observers.

Planning a JAD session: Preparation is everything. The analyst defines the purpose and scope ("agree the requirements for sales and stock in branches"), chooses participants, studies documents and holds a few interviews beforehand, prepares an agenda, and sends background material to participants before the session. A common guideline is to keep the group small enough to discuss, often somewhere around 10 to 20 people including support staff.

Location and setup: JAD sessions are often held away from the normal workplace, for example a hotel meeting room or a training centre, so that participants are not pulled back into daily work by phone calls and customers. The room is usually set up in a U shape so everyone can see each other and the whiteboard or projector. Phones on silent. Refreshments help a long session go smoothly; in Bangladesh, tea and snacks are almost compulsory.

Ground rules: The facilitator sets rules at the start: everyone participates, one person speaks at a time, criticise ideas not people, stay on the agenda, and the sponsor or a vote settles deadlocks. Topics that cannot be settled in the session go to a "parking lot" list to be handled later, so the meeting does not get stuck on one argument.

A JAD session in action: Suppose the agenda item is "how a sale is recorded". The facilitator asks a counter staff member to walk through a sale. The accountant interrupts: "We need the VAT amount on every receipt." The stock keeper adds: "And the batch number, so we know which batch is expiring." The counter staff object: "If I type all that, the queue will reach the road." Discussion follows, and the group agrees: scanning the barcode on the strip fills the medicine and batch automatically, and the system calculates VAT, so the staff only enter quantity and payment type. The scribe records the requirement, the reason, and an open issue: "Not all medicines have barcodes; decide on manual lookup." In one hour, a conflict that might have taken two weeks of emails is resolved.

After the session: The scribe's notes become a formal JAD document within a day or two and are sent to all participants to confirm. Open issues from the parking lot are assigned to named people with deadlines. This document feeds directly into the requirements specification we will see in the next lesson.

JAD advantages and disadvantages: JAD gathers requirements much faster than serial interviews, settles conflicts immediately, builds shared ownership of the system so users are more likely to accept it, and gives better quality requirements because users and IT talk directly. On the other hand, it is expensive to take many people away from work for days, it depends heavily on a skilled facilitator, strong personalities or senior managers may silence juniors, and if the wrong people attend, the whole group can agree on the wrong thing.

When to choose JAD: JAD fits best when many departments share the system and their needs conflict, when the schedule is tight, and when the organization's culture allows juniors to speak in front of seniors. It fits poorly when the key users cannot leave their work, such as a single-pharmacist branch that would have to close, or when the problem is small enough that two interviews would do. A practical mix is common: a few interviews first to understand the ground, then JAD to settle and agree, then follow-up interviews for details.

Brainstorming: Brainstorming is a group technique for generating many ideas quickly, especially for new solutions rather than describing current work. The classic rules are: no criticism during the idea phase, quantity matters more than quality, wild ideas are welcome, and build on other people's ideas. Only after the idea phase does the group evaluate and select. For example, asked "how can we reduce expired medicine losses?", a ShasthoPharma group might list 25 ideas in 15 minutes: expiry alerts, transfer stock between branches, discount near-expiry items, ask suppliers to take back stock, first-expiry-first-out shelving, and so on. The group then votes on the best three. A useful variation is to have each person write ideas silently first, then share them in turn, so shy members are not drowned out.

Prototyping for requirements: A prototype is an early, simplified working model of a system or part of it, such as a few screens. Many users struggle to describe what they want in words but immediately react when they see something: "No, the price must be bigger", "Where is the button to return a strip?". Prototyping turns vague ideas into concrete feedback. The analyst builds a quick prototype, shows it to users, collects comments, improves it, and repeats.

Throwaway vs evolutionary prototypes: A throwaway prototype is built only to learn requirements and then discarded; the real system is built properly afterwards. It can be as simple as screens drawn on paper or clickable mock-ups made in a design tool. An evolutionary prototype is improved step by step until it becomes the real system. Throwaway prototypes are cheap and safe for exploring ideas. Evolutionary prototypes save time but can carry weak quick-and-dirty code into production if not handled carefully. The SDLC lesson already introduced prototyping as a development approach; here we use it purely to discover requirements.

Risks of prototyping: Users may think a nice-looking prototype is nearly finished and expect delivery next week. They may focus on colours and fonts instead of business rules. And it is easy to keep adding features in endless rounds. Set expectations clearly: "This is a sketch to check the idea, not the real system."

Modern sources of requirements: Today analysts also use online surveys shared by link, chat groups with users, and, when an older system or website already exists, usage data: which pages are visited most, where users abandon a form, what people search for. For ShasthoPharma's planned home-delivery app, search logs from its Facebook page messages could show which medicines customers ask about most. These sources supplement, not replace, talking to people.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma JAD: The owner sponsors a two-day JAD at a meeting room in Gulshan. Participants: the operations director, the accountant, four branch managers, three counter staff, the stock keeper, two developers, a facilitator and a scribe. Day one covers sales and returns; day two covers stock receiving, transfer between branches and reports. By the end the group has agreed on 46 requirements, ranked them, and listed 7 parking-lot issues. Doing the same through separate interviews would likely have taken several weeks.

Real life example 2, a ride-sharing feature: Imagine a ride-sharing company in Dhaka wanting a feature for booking a CNG auto-rickshaw. The team brainstorms with drivers and support staff, then shows paper prototypes of the booking screen to a handful of riders at a bus stop. Riders immediately ask for the fare estimate to appear before confirming, something none of the team had prioritised. One afternoon of prototyping changed the design.

Common mistakes: Inviting too many people or the wrong people to JAD. Letting the facilitator push their own design. Skipping preparation so the session becomes a chat. Not writing up and confirming the results. In brainstorming, judging ideas too early. In prototyping, letting users believe the prototype is the finished system, or polishing the prototype too much.

What exams ask: What is JAD? Describe the roles in a JAD session. Advantages and disadvantages of JAD compared with interviews. Rules of brainstorming. What is prototyping and how does it help requirements gathering? Distinguish throwaway and evolutionary prototypes.

Recap: Group techniques gather requirements from many people together and resolve conflicts on the spot. JAD is a structured workshop with a sponsor, a neutral facilitator, a scribe, users, managers and IT staff, usually off-site, with clear ground rules and a parking lot for unresolved issues. Brainstorming generates many ideas with no early criticism. Prototypes let users react to something concrete; throwaway prototypes are discarded, evolutionary ones grow into the system. Next lesson: organizing all the requirements we have collected.
key_points: Group techniques collect requirements from many people at once and settle conflicts on the spot.
JAD is a structured, facilitated workshop of users, managers and IT staff that defines and agrees requirements.
JAD roles: sponsor (authority), facilitator (neutral leader), scribe (records), users, managers and IT staff.
JAD is often held off-site with a U-shaped room, ground rules and a parking lot for unresolved issues.
JAD is fast and builds shared ownership, but is costly and depends on a skilled facilitator.
Brainstorming rules: no early criticism, many ideas, wild ideas welcome, build on others, evaluate later.
Prototypes turn vague wishes into concrete feedback; throwaway ones are discarded, evolutionary ones grow into the system.
lessons.tip: When you practise facilitation, your job is to ask questions and summarise, not to give answers. Count how many sentences you speak; if you speak more than the group, step back.
lessons.task: With three or four friends, run a 15-minute brainstorm on "How could our department notice board work better?". Follow the no-criticism rule, list every idea, then vote for the top three and sketch one of them as a paper prototype.

quiz.q: Who runs a JAD session, keeps it on track and stays neutral?
quiz.explain: The facilitator plans the agenda, leads the discussion and resolves conflicts without pushing a solution.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of JAD over a long series of individual interviews?
options: Conflicts are resolved together, so requirements are agreed much faster
quiz.explain: Bringing decision makers and users together lets them settle differences on the spot.

quiz.q: In a JAD session, what is the "parking lot" used for?
options: Issues that cannot be settled now and will be handled later
quiz.explain: Unresolved topics are parked so the meeting does not get stuck.

quiz.q: Which is a rule of brainstorming?
options: Limit the group to three ideas
Do not criticise ideas during the idea phase
quiz.explain: Criticism is held back until the evaluation phase so that many ideas appear.

quiz.q: A prototype built only to learn requirements and then discarded is called:
quiz.explain: Throwaway prototypes are for learning; the real system is built properly afterwards.

lessons.title: Organizing Requirements: Priorities, the SRS and Traceability
lessons.content:
After weeks of interviews, questionnaires, observation and a JAD workshop, the analyst at ShasthoPharma has a pile of notes: 46 agreed requirements from JAD, 30 more from interviews, survey results, photos of registers, and a list of open issues. Some requirements repeat. Some contradict each other. Some are vital, others are nice ideas. If this pile goes to the developers as it is, they will build the wrong things first, miss important rules, and argue later about what was promised. Like a tailor who measures a customer, writes the numbers on scraps of paper and then loses half of them, all the earlier hard work can be wasted. This lesson is about turning that pile into a clean, agreed, trackable set of requirements.

What organizing requirements means: It means four things. First, give every requirement a unique identity and a clear wording. Second, decide which matter most, called prioritization. Third, collect them into one agreed document, usually called the software or system requirements specification (SRS). Fourth, check that they are right (validation) and keep track of them, and of changes, throughout the project (traceability and change management).

Unique IDs: Each requirement gets an ID such as FR-12 for functional requirement 12 or NFR-03 for non-functional requirement 3. Grouping helps: SAL-01 to SAL-15 for sales, STK-01 to STK-20 for stock, REP-01 to REP-08 for reports. IDs let everyone refer to a requirement precisely. In a meeting, "STK-07 is not done" is far clearer than "that stock thing the manager mentioned".

Rewriting into clear statements: Raw notes like "manager wants to see expiry stuff" become a clear statement: "STK-07: The system shall list all batches that expire within 60 days, by branch, every morning." Recall from the requirements lesson that a good requirement is clear, specific, testable and says what, not how. The word "shall" is commonly used for mandatory requirements. Each statement should contain one requirement; split sentences joined by "and" when they describe separate needs.

Removing duplicates and conflicts: The analyst merges duplicates, such as three people asking for "search medicine by name" in slightly different words. Conflicts are listed and resolved with the stakeholders. For example, REP-03 says "the daily sales report shall be emailed at 9 pm" while a branch manager wanted it "after closing", and some branches close at 11 pm. The resolution might be: "after each branch closes its day in the system". Never resolve a business conflict silently on your own; the owners of the requirement must agree.

Why prioritize: There is never enough time or money to build everything at once. Prioritizing tells the team what to build first and what can wait or be dropped. It also protects the project when the deadline or budget is cut: low-priority items go first, not random ones.

The MoSCoW method: MoSCoW is a simple and widely used prioritization technique. The capital letters stand for four categories. Must have: without it the system is useless or illegal, such as recording a sale or calculating VAT correctly. Should have: important but the system can work without it for a while, perhaps with a manual workaround, such as stock transfer between branches. Could have: nice to have if time allows, such as SMS reminders to customers for monthly medicines. Won't have this time: agreed to be out of scope for this release, such as a customer mobile app. The small o's are just there to make the word readable.

A worked MoSCoW example: Suppose ShasthoPharma has 60 requirements and a 6-month budget. After a prioritization meeting: 24 Must, 18 Should, 12 Could, 6 Won't. A common guideline is that Must haves should not take up most of the available effort, so that there is room for surprises. If the developers estimate that the 24 Musts alone need almost the whole six months, the team must either push some Musts into Should, or extend time or budget. MoSCoW makes that conversation visible instead of hidden.

Other ways to prioritize: Some teams use a simple high/medium/low ranking, or numbered ranks from 1 to n. Some score each requirement on business value and on cost or effort, then favour high value, low effort items first. Whatever method you use, prioritization must involve the business owners, not just the analyst or the developers.

The SRS document: The requirements specification is the single official document that describes what the system must do and the constraints it must meet. It becomes the basis for design, for testing and often for the contract with a vendor. A well-known structure was given in the IEEE 830 standard, later replaced by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148. You do not need to memorize a standard; you should know the typical contents.

Typical SRS contents, part 1: An introduction, giving the purpose of the document, the scope of the system, definitions of terms and abbreviations (for example, what "batch", "challan" and "reorder level" mean), and references. An overall description, giving the product perspective (is it new, or replacing something?), the main functions in summary, the user classes (counter staff, branch manager, head office, accountant), the operating environment, constraints (such as "must run on the existing Windows PCs" or "must follow the drug regulator's rules"), and assumptions.

Typical SRS contents, part 2: The specific requirements: all functional requirements with their IDs and priorities, grouped by feature; external interface requirements, such as screens, printers, barcode scanners and links to a payment system; and non-functional requirements, such as performance ("a sale must be saved within 2 seconds"), security ("only pharmacists can approve prescription-only medicines"), availability, and usability. Appendices may hold models such as the context diagram, DFDs and the data dictionary that we will build in coming lessons.

Qualities of a good SRS: Commonly listed qualities are: correct (every requirement is truly needed), unambiguous (each statement has only one meaning), complete (nothing important is missing), consistent (no requirements contradict each other), ranked for importance, verifiable (each can be tested), modifiable (easy to change in a structured way) and traceable (you can follow each requirement back to its source and forward to design and tests).

Validation: Validation means checking that the requirements are the right ones, that they truly reflect what stakeholders need. Common techniques: a requirements review or walkthrough, where stakeholders read the SRS together and question each item; prototypes, where users try screens built from the requirements; and writing test cases early, because a requirement you cannot write a test for is usually too vague. For example, NFR-02 "the system shall be fast" fails, because no test can prove "fast"; rewriting it as "searching a medicine by name shall show results within 1 second for 95 percent of searches" makes it testable.

Validation vs verification: These two words are often confused. Validation asks "are we building the right system?", meaning do the requirements match real needs. Verification asks "are we building the system right?", meaning does the design or product match the written requirements. A requirement review is mainly validation; checking that screen R-4 really shows batches expiring within 60 days is verification.

Requirement attributes: Besides ID and text, each requirement usually carries a few attributes: its source (who asked), its owner (who can approve changes to it), its priority, its status (proposed, approved, built, tested, delivered) and a version number. A spreadsheet is enough for a small project like ShasthoPharma; larger organizations use requirements management tools. Keeping these attributes up to date makes progress reports honest: "52 of 64 requirements built, 40 tested".

Sign-off: When the stakeholders agree, the key people formally approve the SRS, often by signing it. Sign-off does not mean the requirements can never change; it means everyone agrees on the starting point, so later changes are visible and managed.

The traceability matrix: A requirements traceability matrix is a table that links each requirement to where it came from and where it goes. Typical columns: requirement ID, description, source (which interview or JAD session), priority, design element (screen or module), test case ID, and status. Example row: "STK-07 | expiry list within 60 days | JAD day 2, stock keeper | Must | Report module, screen R-4 | TC-31, TC-32 | built". With this, if a test fails you know which requirement is affected, and if a requirement changes you know which screens and tests to update. It also shows at a glance whether any requirement was forgotten, because its design or test column is empty.

Managing change: Requirements change because businesses change, laws change, and people understand more as they see the system take shape. Change is normal; uncontrolled change is the danger. Scope creep is the slow, unplanned growth of requirements: "while you are at it, can you also add...". Ten small additions can blow the schedule. A change control process handles this: anyone can submit a change request; the analyst studies its impact on cost, time and other requirements using the traceability matrix; a decision body, often called a change control board, approves, rejects or postpones it; and the SRS, matrix and plan are updated with a new version number.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma: The analyst writes 64 requirements with IDs, runs a half-day MoSCoW session with the owner, the accountant and two branch managers, and produces a 30-page SRS in Bangla and English. In the review, the accountant spots that two requirements calculate VAT differently, a consistency error caught before any code was written. Three months later, the government changes a rule about recording prescriptions for certain medicines. The change request goes through the control board, the matrix shows that it affects SAL-04, two screens and five test cases, and the change is planned properly instead of being patched in a panic.

Real life example 2, a citizen service portal: Imagine a city corporation building an online trade licence renewal portal. Hundreds of ideas arrive from officials and business associations. Using MoSCoW, online application and payment become Must, SMS status updates Should, a chatbot Could, and integration with every other government service Won't for this phase. A traceability matrix links each requirement to the relevant regulation, so when auditors ask why a field exists, the answer is one row away.

Common mistakes: Leaving requirements without IDs. Marking everything as Must, which makes prioritization meaningless. Writing vague requirements that cannot be tested. Mixing design decisions into requirements, such as "use a dropdown with blue text". Treating the signed SRS as frozen forever, or the opposite, accepting every change without impact analysis. Forgetting non-functional requirements entirely.

What exams ask: Explain the MoSCoW method with examples. List the contents of an SRS. What are the characteristics of a good SRS? What is requirements validation and how is it done? What is a traceability matrix and why is it useful? What is scope creep and how is it controlled?

Recap: Organizing requirements turns a pile of notes into a clean, agreed set. Give each requirement an ID and clear, testable wording; merge duplicates and resolve conflicts with stakeholders; prioritize with MoSCoW; collect everything in an SRS with introduction, overall description and specific requirements; validate through reviews, prototypes and early test cases; get sign-off; link everything in a traceability matrix; and control change to prevent scope creep. Next lesson: process modeling with data flow diagrams.
key_points: Give every requirement a unique ID and a clear, single, testable statement.
Merge duplicates and resolve conflicts with the stakeholders, never silently.
MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time.
The SRS is the single official document of requirements: introduction, overall description, specific functional, interface and non-functional requirements.
A good SRS is correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked, verifiable, modifiable and traceable.
Validation checks the requirements are the right ones, through reviews, prototypes and early test cases.
A traceability matrix links each requirement to its source, design and test cases.
Scope creep is uncontrolled growth of requirements; a change control process manages it.
lessons.tip: For every requirement you write, try to write one test for it immediately. If you cannot, the requirement is not finished yet.

quiz.explain: Won't have this time means agreed to be out of scope for this release.

quiz.explain: A verifiable requirement needs a measurable target, such as a response time.

options: Each requirement with its source, design elements and test cases
Only the screens and their colours
