quiz.explain: Validation uses reviews, prototypes and test cases to confirm the requirements are the right ones.

lessons.title: Process Modeling I: Data Flow Diagrams and the Context Diagram
lessons.content:
Think about how a parcel travels from a Daraz seller in Old Dhaka to a customer in Sylhet. It goes from the seller to a pickup point, gets sorted at a hub, rides a truck, reaches a local hub and finally a delivery rider. If you wanted to explain this to a new employee, you would not write ten pages. You would draw a picture: boxes for the places where something happens to the parcel, arrows for its movement, and labels saying what moves. A data flow diagram does exactly this, but for data instead of parcels. It is the most famous picture in systems analysis.

What process modeling is: A process model is a picture of what a system does: which activities take place, what data goes in and out of each, and where data is kept. The most common process model in structured analysis is the data flow diagram, or DFD. Requirements written as sentences in the SRS are hard to see as a whole; a DFD shows the whole system on one page, then lets you zoom in step by step.

What a DFD is: A DFD is a graphical model that shows how data enters a system, how it is transformed by processes, where it is stored, and how it leaves. It shows the flow of data, not the flow of control. That means a DFD does not show decisions like "if stock is low", loops, or the order and timing of steps. It answers "what data goes where and what happens to it", not "in what sequence". That is a key difference from a flowchart.

Why DFDs exist: DFDs became popular with structured analysis in the late 1970s, through the work of people like Tom DeMarco, Ed Yourdon, Chris Gane and Trish Sarson. Analysts needed a way to show users and developers the same picture of a system, simple enough for a pharmacy owner to understand, yet precise enough for designers. A DFD uses only four symbols, so non-technical users can read it after a few minutes of explanation, and they can point to mistakes: "No, the prescription does not go to the accountant."

Symbol 1, external entity: An external entity, also called a source or sink or terminator, is a person, organization or other system outside the system boundary that sends data into the system or receives data from it. Examples for ShasthoPharma: Customer, Supplier, Owner, Mobile Payment Provider. The system does not control what happens inside an external entity; it only exchanges data with it. Entities are named with nouns.

Symbol 2, process: A process is work done on data: it transforms input data into output data. Examples: "Record sale", "Check stock", "Generate reorder list". Processes are named with a strong verb plus an object. Each process gets a number, such as 1, 2, 3, which becomes important when we break processes down in the next lesson. A process must change data in some way: calculate, sort, combine, check, or produce something new.

Symbol 3, data flow: A data flow is an arrow showing data moving between symbols. It is named with a noun phrase describing the data, such as "medicine request", "receipt", "purchase order" or "delivery challan". A data flow represents data in motion: a form, a message, a screen entry, a report. Every arrow must have a name, except sometimes flows into or out of a data store where the content is obvious.

Symbol 4, data store: A data store is data at rest, kept for later use: a file, a table, a register, a folder of challans. Examples: "Medicine stock", "Sales", "Suppliers". Data stores are named with nouns, often plural. A process writes to a store with an arrow pointing into the store, and reads from it with an arrow pointing out of it.

Two notations: The same four ideas are drawn in two common styles. In the Gane and Sarson notation, a process is a rectangle with rounded corners, a data store is a rectangle open on one side, an external entity is a square, often shaded, and a data flow is an arrow. In the DeMarco and Yourdon notation, a process is a circle (often called a bubble), a data store is drawn as two parallel lines, an external entity is a rectangle, and a data flow is an arrow. Both mean exactly the same thing. Pick one and use it consistently throughout a project; never mix them in one diagram.

DFD rules, part 1, processes: Every process must have at least one input and at least one output. A process with inputs but no outputs is called a black hole; one with outputs but no inputs is called a miracle. Both are errors, and we will look at them more in the next lesson. Also, the outputs of a process must be possible to make from its inputs.

DFD rules, part 2, flows: Data cannot move directly between two external entities on your diagram; that conversation happens outside the system, so it is not shown. Data cannot move directly from an external entity to a data store or from a data store to an entity; a process must sit in between, because something has to receive, check and record it. Data cannot move directly from one data store to another; again, a process must do the moving. In short: at least one end of every data flow must be a process.

DFD rules, part 3, names and neatness: Processes: verb plus object. Flows, stores and entities: nouns. Avoid crossing lines where possible. An external entity may be drawn more than once on the same diagram to avoid long crossing arrows; it is usually marked to show it is a duplicate. Keep each diagram to a manageable number of processes so that it fits on one page and stays readable.

The context diagram: The context diagram is the highest-level DFD. It shows the entire system as a single process, usually numbered 0, surrounded by all the external entities and the main data flows between them and the system. It does not show data stores, because all the stores are inside the system and hidden in that one process. The context diagram answers two questions at a glance: where is the boundary of the system, and who does it talk to?

Why the context diagram matters: It fixes the scope. When the owner looks at it and sees no arrow to the bank, the analyst can ask, "Should the system send deposits to the bank, or is that out of scope?". Arguments about scope are cheaper on a one-page diagram than after six months of coding. It is often the first diagram shown to the sponsor and appears in the SRS.

Worked example, ShasthoPharma context diagram, entities: First list the external entities. Customer: buys medicines. Supplier: provides stock. Owner (management): receives reports and sets prices and policies. Mobile Payment Provider: confirms digital payments. Note that the counter staff are not external entities: they work inside the system, using it, so they are part of the system rather than outside it.

Worked example, the flows: Customer to system: "medicine request", "prescription", "payment". System to customer: "receipt" and "availability information". System to Supplier: "purchase order". Supplier to system: "delivery challan" and "supplier invoice". System to Supplier: "payment advice". Owner to system: "price updates" and "reorder approval". System to Owner: "daily sales report", "reorder list" and "expiry report". System to Mobile Payment Provider: "payment request"; provider to system: "payment confirmation".

Worked example, drawing it: In the centre, one rounded rectangle labelled "0 ShasthoPharma Sales and Stock System". Customer on the left, Supplier on the right, Owner at the top, Mobile Payment Provider at the bottom. Each named arrow connects one entity to the central process, pointing in the direction the data travels. No arrows between Customer and Supplier, because that is outside our system. No data stores. That is the entire diagram: a dozen or so arrows, four entities and one process.

How to build a context diagram, step by step: One, read the requirements and list every source and destination of data outside the system. Two, for each, list what data it sends and what it receives. Three, draw the system as one process in the centre. Four, place entities around it and draw named arrows. Five, show it to stakeholders and ask "what is missing?". Typically something is: perhaps the drug regulator needs a periodic report of certain controlled medicines, which adds an entity and a flow, or the owner decides it is out of scope for now.

Real life example 1, a university library: Context diagram for a library system: the external entities are Student, Book Vendor and Accounts Office. The librarian operates the system, so she is inside it, not an external entity. Flows: student sends "borrow request" and "return", receives "due date slip" and "fine notice"; vendor receives "book order" and sends "invoice"; Accounts Office receives "fine collection report". One look tells the head librarian what the system is responsible for.

Real life example 2, a bKash-style cash-out at an agent: Think of an agent shop's cash-out service as a system. External entities: Customer (sends "cash-out request" and "PIN confirmation", receives "cash" as a physical flow, which we do not show, plus an "SMS confirmation"), and the Mobile Financial Service Provider (receives "transaction request", sends "approval"). Only data is shown, not the physical cash.

DFD vs flowchart: A flowchart shows the sequence of steps and decisions in one program or procedure: start, do this, if yes go here, loop back. A DFD shows many processes that may run at different times, connected only by the data they share. In a flowchart, an arrow means "next step". In a DFD, an arrow means "this data moves". If you find yourself drawing a diamond or writing "yes" and "no" on arrows in a DFD, you have slipped into flowchart thinking. That distinction, data only, is something students often forget.

Common mistakes: Drawing control logic such as decisions and loops inside a DFD; that belongs in flowcharts or the logic tools in later lessons. Connecting two data stores or two entities directly. Leaving arrows unnamed. Naming processes with nouns, such as "Sales", instead of "Record sale". Putting data stores on the context diagram. Treating internal staff who operate the system as external entities. Showing physical items, such as medicine boxes or cash, instead of data about them.

What exams ask: Define DFD and list its symbols in both notations. State the rules of a DFD. Differentiate DFD and flowchart. What is a context diagram and what does it show and not show? Draw a context diagram for a given case, such as a library, hospital or online shop.

Recap: A DFD shows how data flows into, through and out of a system, using four symbols: external entity, process, data flow and data store. Gane-Sarson and DeMarco-Yourdon are two drawing styles of the same idea. Every flow must touch a process; processes need inputs and outputs; names follow verb-object for processes and nouns for the rest. The context diagram shows the whole system as one process with all external entities and main flows, and no data stores. Next lesson: breaking the context diagram down into level 0 and level 1, and keeping the levels balanced.
key_points: A DFD shows how data moves into, through and out of a system; it shows data flow, not control or sequence.
Four symbols: external entity, process, data flow and data store.
Gane-Sarson: rounded rectangle process, open-ended rectangle store; DeMarco-Yourdon: circle process, parallel-line store.
Name processes with verb plus object; name flows, stores and entities with nouns.
At least one end of every data flow must be a process: no entity-to-entity, entity-to-store or store-to-store flows.
Every process needs at least one input and one output.
The context diagram shows the whole system as one process (0) with all external entities and main flows, and no data stores.
The context diagram fixes the system boundary and scope.
lessons.tip: When you draw a DFD, put your finger on each arrow and ask "is at least one end a process, and does this arrow have a name?". Two seconds per arrow catches most exam mistakes.
lessons.task: Draw a context diagram for your university's exam result system. List the external entities first (students, departments, the controller of examinations office, and so on), then draw one process in the centre with named data flows to and from each entity.

quiz.q: What does a DFD mainly show?
options: The order and timing of every step
How data flows into, through and out of a system
The physical layout of the office
quiz.explain: A DFD models data movement and transformation, not control flow or timing.

quiz.q: Which data flow is allowed in a DFD?
options: From an external entity to a process
From one data store directly to another data store
From one external entity directly to another
From an external entity directly to a data store
quiz.explain: At least one end of every data flow must be a process.

quiz.q: In DeMarco-Yourdon notation, a process is drawn as:
quiz.explain: DeMarco-Yourdon uses a circle (bubble) for processes; Gane-Sarson uses a rounded rectangle.

quiz.q: What is NOT shown on a context diagram?
options: The whole system as one process
quiz.explain: Data stores are inside the system, hidden within the single process of the context diagram.

quiz.q: Which is the best name for a process?
quiz.explain: Processes are named with a verb plus an object.

lessons.title: Process Modeling II: Levelled DFDs, Balancing and DFD Errors
lessons.content:
Open Google Maps and look at Bangladesh. You see the whole country and the divisions. Zoom in on Dhaka and the main roads appear. Zoom in again on Dhanmondi and you can see individual lanes and shops. Each view is correct, and each one fits on your screen, because it shows only the detail you need at that level. Levelled data flow diagrams work the same way. The context diagram is the country view. Level 0 is the city view. Level 1 and below zoom into individual neighbourhoods. And just like a map, the roads entering Dhanmondi on the close-up must match the roads entering it on the city view. That matching is called balancing.

What levelling is: Levelling, or decomposition, means breaking a process into smaller sub-processes, each shown on its own lower-level diagram. The context diagram shows the whole system as process 0. A level 0 diagram, sometimes called the diagram 0, breaks process 0 into the main processes of the system. A level 1 diagram breaks one level 0 process into its parts, and so on. This lets us describe a large system without drawing one giant, unreadable picture.

Why levelling matters: A real system may have 50 or 100 processes. On one page, that is a spider's web nobody can read. Human readers handle a small number of items at once, so analysts often aim for roughly five to nine processes per diagram. Levelling also lets different readers stop at the level they need: the owner looks at level 0, the developer building the sales screen studies level 1 of the sales process.

Numbering: Numbers show where each process came from. Level 0 processes are numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. If process 3 is decomposed, its children on the level 1 diagram are 3.1, 3.2, 3.3. If 3.2 is decomposed further, its children are 3.2.1, 3.2.2. From any number you can trace back up to its parent. The number does not mean order of execution; process 2 does not necessarily happen after process 1.

What appears where: Data stores usually first appear at level 0, because the context diagram hides them. External entities appear on the context and level 0 diagrams; on lower levels, analysts often show only the flows to and from the outside without redrawing every entity, though many textbooks still draw them for clarity. A process that is not broken down any further is called a primitive or functional primitive. Its exact logic is then described with a process specification, using the structured English, decision trees and decision tables that we will study in the next two lessons.

Worked example, the ShasthoPharma level 0, processes: Starting from last lesson's context diagram, we identify five main processes. 1 Process sale. 2 Receive stock. 3 Manage purchasing. 4 Maintain price list. 5 Produce reports. We also identify the data stores: D1 Medicines (names, prices, reorder levels), D2 Stock (quantity per batch per branch, with expiry dates), D3 Sales, D4 Purchase orders.

Worked example, level 0 flows: Process 1, Process sale: receives "medicine request", "prescription" and "payment" from Customer, sends "availability information" and "receipt" back; sends "payment request" to Mobile Payment Provider and receives "payment confirmation"; reads prices from D1, reads and updates D2, writes to D3. Process 2, Receive stock: receives "delivery challan" and "supplier invoice" from Supplier, reads D4 to compare against what was ordered, and updates D2. Process 3, Manage purchasing: reads D1 and D2 to find items below reorder level, receives "reorder approval" from Owner, sends "purchase order" and "payment advice" to Supplier, writes D4. Process 4, Maintain price list: receives "price updates" from Owner and updates D1. Process 5, Produce reports: reads D2 and D3 and sends "daily sales report", "reorder list" and "expiry report" to Owner.

What balancing means: Balancing is the rule that a child diagram must have exactly the same inputs and outputs, to and from the outside, as its parent process. Nothing may appear from nowhere, and nothing may vanish. Internal flows between child processes and new internal data stores are fine, but every external flow on the parent must appear on the child, and the child must not add new external flows.

Worked balancing check, context vs level 0: List the context flows: from Customer, medicine request, prescription, payment; to Customer, receipt, availability information; from Supplier, delivery challan, supplier invoice; to Supplier, purchase order, payment advice; from Owner, price updates, reorder approval; to Owner, daily sales report, reorder list, expiry report; to provider, payment request; from provider, payment confirmation. That is 15 flows. Now tick each one on level 0: medicine request, prescription, payment, receipt and availability on process 1; challan and invoice on process 2; purchase order, payment advice and reorder approval on process 3; price updates on process 4; the three reports on process 5; payment request and confirmation on process 1. All 15 appear and no new external flows were added. The diagrams are balanced.

Worked example, level 1 of process 1: Now we zoom into Process sale. 1.1 Check availability: takes "medicine request", reads D2, outputs "availability information" to the Customer and an "available item list" to 1.2. 1.2 Verify prescription: takes "prescription" and the item list, outputs "approved item list". 1.3 Calculate bill: takes the approved list, reads prices from D1, outputs "bill". 1.4 Collect payment: takes "bill" and the Customer's "payment"; for digital payment it sends "payment request" to the provider and gets "payment confirmation"; outputs "paid sale". 1.5 Record sale: takes "paid sale", writes D3, updates quantities in D2, and outputs "receipt" to the Customer.

Checking level 1 balance: The parent, process 1, had inputs medicine request, prescription, payment, payment confirmation, and outputs availability information, receipt, payment request, plus access to D1, D2 and D3. On level 1: medicine request enters 1.1, prescription enters 1.2, payment and payment confirmation enter 1.4; availability information leaves 1.1, payment request leaves 1.4, receipt leaves 1.5. D1, D2 and D3 are used. Internal flows such as "available item list", "approved item list", "bill" and "paid sale" are new, but they are internal, so that is fine. Balanced.

Splitting a flow: Sometimes a parent flow is split on the child diagram. For example, the context flow "payment" might appear on a child as "cash payment" and "card or mobile payment". This is still balanced if the data dictionary defines payment as consisting of those parts. We will see that notation in the data dictionary lesson.

DFD error 1, black hole: A process that has inputs but no outputs. Data goes in and disappears. Example: a process "Record customer complaint" with an input from Customer but no output to any store or entity. Where did the complaint go? Either a store "Complaints" is missing, or the process is not needed.

DFD error 2, miracle: A process that has outputs but no inputs. Data appears from nothing. Example: "Produce expiry report" sending a report to the Owner but reading no store. It cannot know the expiry dates without reading D2. Fix: add the flow from the Stock store.

DFD error 3, gray hole: A process whose inputs are not enough to produce its outputs. It has inputs and outputs, so it looks fine, but it is impossible. Example: "Calculate bill" receives only the medicine names, yet outputs a total in taka. Without quantity and price, the bill cannot be computed. Fix: add the quantity on the incoming flow and a read from D1 for prices.

Other common errors: Unbalanced levels, where a child gains or loses an external flow. Data flowing directly between two stores, or between an entity and a store, without a process. Unnamed flows. A data store that is only written to and never read, which usually means a missing report or process, or one that is only read and never written, which means nothing ever fills it on any diagram.

Logical vs physical DFDs: A logical DFD shows what the business does, independent of how it is done: "Record sale", "Stock". A physical DFD shows how it is actually done or will be done, including people, technology, documents and files: "Write sale in counter register", "Type sale into POS screen", "Stock table in the central database", "Copy challan to head office by courier". Logical DFDs help you understand and improve the business; physical DFDs help you design and implement.

Current vs proposed: Combining the two ideas gives a classic sequence. First, draw the current physical DFD: how ShasthoPharma works today, with paper registers and phone calls. Second, abstract it into the current logical DFD, removing technology and people names to see the essential business processes. Third, create the new logical DFD by adding new requirements and removing problems, such as adding "Transfer stock between branches". Fourth, draw the new physical DFD, which shows how the new system will implement it, such as barcode scanners and a central database. Many modern projects skip some of these steps to save time, but the idea of separating "what" from "how" stays essential.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma review: The analyst shows the level 0 diagram to branch managers in a short walkthrough. One manager notices that returned medicines have no process at all. That is a missing requirement, not just a drawing error. Process 6 Handle returns is added, with flows from Customer and updates to D2 and D3, and the context diagram is updated with a new "return request" flow so that the levels stay balanced.

Real life example 2, a hospital outpatient department: In a government hospital's outpatient system, the level 0 might have processes for Register patient, Assign doctor, Record consultation, Issue medicine and Produce daily statistics. A student drawing this often adds "Produce daily statistics" with no store to read from, a miracle. Spotting it in the exam earns easy marks.

Common mistakes: Adding a new flow on a child diagram and forgetting to add it to the parent, which breaks balance. Thinking process numbers show the order of steps. Decomposing too much, until processes are single keystrokes, or too little, so level 0 has twenty processes. Putting physical details such as "MySQL" or "Ramesh types it" into a logical DFD. Drawing data stores on the context diagram. Forgetting that a store must be both written and read somewhere in the set of diagrams. And redrawing a lower level with different names for the same flows, so readers cannot tell they match.

What exams ask: Draw context and level 0 DFDs for a case. Explain levelling and numbering. What is balancing? Show a balanced and an unbalanced example. Define black hole, miracle and gray hole. Differentiate logical and physical DFDs. Explain the four-model sequence of current physical, current logical, new logical and new physical.

Recap: Levelling breaks a system into context, level 0, level 1 and lower diagrams, numbered 1, 1.1, 1.1.1 to show parentage. Balancing means each child has exactly the same external inputs and outputs as its parent. Check every process for black holes (no output), miracles (no input) and gray holes (insufficient input). Logical DFDs show what; physical DFDs show how; analysts move from the current system to the proposed one. Next lesson: describing the logic inside primitive processes with structured English and decision trees.
key_points: Levelling breaks the context diagram into level 0, then level 1 and lower diagrams.
Processes are numbered to show parentage: 3, then 3.1, then 3.1.2; numbers do not show order.
Data stores usually first appear at level 0; a process not broken further is a primitive.
Balancing: a child diagram must have exactly the same external inputs and outputs as its parent.
Black hole: inputs but no output. Miracle: outputs but no input. Gray hole: inputs not enough for the outputs.
A logical DFD shows what the business does; a physical DFD shows how it is done with people, technology and files.
Classic sequence: current physical, current logical, new logical, new physical.
lessons.tip: When checking balance, list every parent flow in a column on scrap paper and tick each one as you find it on the child. Unticked or extra flows jump out immediately.
lessons.task: Take the context diagram you drew for your university result system. Draw its level 0 with four or five processes and the data stores, then do a written balancing check by listing each context flow and the level 0 process where it appears.

quiz.q: What does balancing between DFD levels mean?
options: Every diagram has the same number of processes
A child diagram has the same external inputs and outputs as its parent process
Data stores appear on the context diagram
Processes are executed in numeric order
quiz.explain: Balancing ensures nothing appears or disappears when a process is decomposed.

quiz.q: A process that has inputs but produces no output is called a:
quiz.explain: Data goes into a black hole and disappears.

quiz.q: A process numbered 4.2.1 is:
options: The first process to run in the system
quiz.explain: Numbers show parentage: 4.2.1 is a sub-process of 4.2, which is a sub-process of 4.

lessons.title: Logic Modeling I: Structured English and Decision Trees
lessons.content:
Ask the counter manager at a ShasthoPharma branch how discounts work and you might hear this: "Well, regular customers get something, and if they buy a lot we give a bit more, unless it is a controlled medicine, but the owner said senior citizens always get at least five percent, except on insulin... I think." Every word of that is a business rule. But if a programmer tries to code from that sentence, she will guess, and her guesses will be wrong in at least one case. Logic modeling is the set of tools an analyst uses to turn messy, spoken rules into clear, exact, checkable descriptions.

What logic modeling is: In the previous two lessons we drew data flow diagrams. A DFD shows that a process called "Calculate bill" exists, what data goes into it and what comes out. It does not show what happens inside the bubble. Logic modeling describes the inside: the steps, the conditions and the decisions a process follows. For the lowest-level processes in a DFD, called primitive or functional primitive processes, the analyst writes a process description, and logic modeling tools are how that description is written.

Why ordinary language is not enough: Everyday English and Bangla are wonderful for talking, but they are full of traps for precise rules. Words like "a lot", "usually" and "regular customer" have no exact meaning. "And" and "or" get mixed up: "customers who are students and senior citizens" could mean people who are both, or both groups. Sentences with "unless" and "except" hide which rule wins. And long paragraphs make it easy to forget a case entirely. Logic modeling forces the analyst to remove these ambiguities before code is written, when fixing them is cheap.

Three common tools: Most SA&D textbooks teach three tools for process logic: structured English, decision trees and decision tables. In this lesson we study the first two. Next lesson is entirely about decision tables. All three describe the same thing, the logic of a process, but in different shapes, and each suits a different kind of logic.

Structured English: Structured English is a restricted, carefully formatted form of English used to describe process logic. It uses a small set of action verbs (such as READ, COMPUTE, ADD, SET, PRINT, SEND), names of data items exactly as they appear in the data dictionary, and only three kinds of structure: sequence, decision and repetition. It avoids adjectives, adverbs and vague words. It looks a bit like pseudo-code, but it is written for users and analysts to read, not for a compiler. The aim is that a pharmacy manager can read it and say "yes, that is our rule" or "no, you missed something".

Structure 1, sequence: A sequence is simply steps done one after another, in order. For example: READ prescription details. FIND medicine in stock list. COMPUTE line total = quantity x unit price. ADD line total to bill total. Each line starts with a verb and does one thing. There is no choice and no loop.

Structure 2, decision: A decision chooses between paths based on a condition. Structured English writes it with IF, THEN, ELSE and END IF, and the inside lines are indented. Example: IF medicine type is "controlled" THEN check prescription is attached; IF prescription is not attached THEN reject sale; END IF; ELSE continue sale; END IF. For a choice among many values, some textbooks use a SELECT CASE or "DO one of the following" block: SELECT CASE customer type: CASE "regular": set discount rate to 5 percent; CASE "staff": set discount rate to 10 percent; OTHERWISE: set discount rate to 0; END CASE.

Structure 3, repetition: Repetition repeats steps while or until a condition holds. Structured English uses DO WHILE ... END DO, REPEAT ... UNTIL, or FOR EACH ... END FOR. Example: FOR EACH item on the bill: COMPUTE line total; ADD line total to bill total; END FOR. The difference between DO WHILE and REPEAT UNTIL is the same as in programming: DO WHILE checks the condition first and may run zero times; REPEAT UNTIL runs the body at least once and then checks.

Rules of good structured English: Use data names exactly as defined in the data dictionary, often written in capitals or underlined, so there is one meaning. Start every statement with a strong verb. Indent nested blocks so the structure is visible. Do not use vague words like "some", "usually" or "a lot"; replace them with numbers. Keep each process description short; if it grows beyond about a page, the process probably needs to be split in the DFD. And write so a user can check it, not so a programmer can copy it.

A worked example, the discount rule: After interviewing the owner and checking old bills, the analyst writes the confirmed rule. Customers with a loyalty card get a discount. If a loyalty customer's bill is 2,000 taka or more, the discount is 10 percent; otherwise it is 5 percent. Customers without a card get 5 percent only if the bill is 5,000 taka or more; otherwise no discount. In structured English: IF customer has loyalty card THEN IF bill total is at least 2000 THEN set discount rate to 10 percent ELSE set discount rate to 5 percent END IF ELSE IF bill total is at least 5000 THEN set discount rate to 5 percent ELSE set discount rate to 0 END IF END IF. Then: COMPUTE discount = bill total x discount rate. COMPUTE amount payable = bill total minus discount.

Checking it with numbers: Card holder, bill 2,500 taka: discount 10 percent, 250 taka, pays 2,250. Card holder, bill 800 taka: 5 percent, 40 taka, pays 760. No card, bill 6,000 taka: 5 percent, 300 taka, pays 5,700. No card, bill 1,200 taka: no discount, pays 1,200. Four paths, four test cases. Notice that writing the logic precisely immediately gives you a set of test cases. That is one hidden benefit of logic modeling.

Decision trees: A decision tree is a diagram that shows the same logic as a branching picture. It is usually drawn left to right. You start at a root on the left. Each branching point (a node) asks one condition, and each branch leaving it is one possible answer. You follow the branches according to the facts of the case, and at the far right end of each path, the leaf, you find the action to take. A decision tree is one of the easiest logic tools for non-technical users to understand, because they can trace their finger along a path.

Drawing the discount tree: The root asks "Loyalty card?". The "Yes" branch leads to a node asking "Bill at least 2,000?": "Yes" leads to the leaf "10 percent discount", "No" leads to "5 percent discount". The "No" branch from the root leads to a node asking "Bill at least 5,000?": "Yes" leads to "5 percent discount", "No" leads to "No discount". Four leaves, the same four paths we tested above. If you count the leaves, you count the distinct cases the rule handles.

Steps to build a decision tree: First, list all the conditions involved and the possible values of each (yes/no, or ranges like "under 2,000", "2,000 to 4,999", "5,000 or more"). Second, list all the possible actions. Third, decide the order of conditions; usually the condition that splits cases most clearly or that a user thinks of first goes nearest the root. Fourth, draw branches for every value of each condition. Fifth, write the action at each leaf. Sixth, check: does every combination reach exactly one leaf? Are there leaves with impossible combinations that can be removed?

Why the order of conditions matters: The same logic can make a small or a big tree depending on which question you ask first. If a condition only matters on one branch, like "bill at least 2,000" which only matters for card holders, put it on that branch only. Good ordering keeps the tree small and readable. A tree that branches on every condition for every path grows like 2 x 2 x 2 for three yes/no conditions, which gives 8 leaves, and many of them may say the same thing.

Structured English vs decision tree, when to use which: Structured English is best when the logic has many sequential steps, loops and calculations, such as "for each item, compute, add, print". It handles repetition well, which a tree cannot show. A decision tree is best when the logic is mainly a few decisions in sequence and you need users to verify it quickly. When there are many conditions combining in complex ways, with many rules, the decision table of the next lesson is usually the best tool, because it guarantees you have checked every combination. Many analysts use a tree to talk with users and a table to check completeness.

Real life example 1, a mobile phone recharge offer: A Bangladeshi mobile operator runs a recharge offer: if you recharge 99 taka or more you get a data bonus; if you are a new SIM user you get an extra minute bonus; recharge below that gets nothing extra. A customer care agent confused by the long SMS terms could be given a decision tree: root "Recharge at least 99 taka?", then "New SIM?". Each leaf states exactly which bonus applies. The same rule, written as structured English, goes into the specification for the billing system so programmers implement exactly the same logic that customer care explains.

Real life example 2, university scholarship eligibility: A private university gives a tuition waiver based on the previous semester's GPA and a credit load. Suppose the rule is: GPA 3.90 or more with at least 12 credits gets a 50 percent waiver; GPA 3.75 to 3.89 with at least 12 credits gets 25 percent; anyone with fewer than 12 credits gets no waiver. An analyst writes this as structured English for the accounts system: IF credits taken is less than 12 THEN set waiver to 0 ELSE IF GPA is at least 3.90 THEN set waiver to 50 percent ELSE IF GPA is at least 3.75 THEN set waiver to 25 percent ELSE set waiver to 0 END IF END IF END IF. A student with GPA 3.80 and 15 credits follows the path to 25 percent; a student with GPA 3.95 and 9 credits gets nothing. Showing the tree to the accounts office quickly reveals whether they intended the credit rule to come first.

Common mistakes: Writing structured English like an essay, with vague words such as "large order" instead of "bill total at least 5,000". Mixing up "at least" (>=) and "more than" (>), which changes who gets the discount at exactly 2,000 taka; ask the user and write the boundary explicitly. Forgetting the ELSE path, so some customers fall through with no rule. Drawing a decision tree with leaves that never say what action to take. Using structured English for logic that is really a big combination of conditions, where a decision table would catch missing cases. And copying programming syntax, such as braces and semicolons, which users cannot read.

What exams ask: What is structured English and what are its three basic structures? Write structured English for a given business rule. Draw a decision tree for a given policy, for example an insurance premium or a discount. Compare structured English, decision trees and decision tables, with when to use each. Explain why natural language is not good enough for specifying process logic.

Recap: DFDs show what processes exist; logic modeling shows what happens inside the lowest-level processes. Structured English uses strong verbs, data dictionary names and only sequence, decision and repetition. Decision trees show the same logic as branches from a root to leaves, which users find easy to check. Write boundaries exactly and cover every path; each path becomes a test case. Next lesson: decision tables, the tool that guarantees you have covered every combination of conditions.
key_points: Logic modeling describes what happens inside a DFD process, especially the lowest-level (primitive) processes.
Natural language is ambiguous: vague words, mixed "and/or", hidden exceptions and forgotten cases.
Structured English uses action verbs, data dictionary names and only three structures: sequence, decision and repetition.
Decisions use IF-THEN-ELSE or CASE; repetition uses DO WHILE, REPEAT UNTIL or FOR EACH.
A decision tree shows conditions as branching nodes from a root and actions at the leaves.
Order conditions so the tree stays small; count leaves to count distinct cases.
Structured English suits steps and loops; trees suit a few sequential decisions; tables suit many combined conditions.
Every path through the logic becomes a test case, and boundaries like "at least" must be exact.
lessons.tip: When a user states a rule, immediately ask "What happens at exactly the boundary?" and "What happens otherwise?". Those two questions catch most logic errors before they reach the code.
lessons.task: Write the rules for a real offer you have seen (a mobile recharge offer, a Daraz coupon or a restaurant deal) first in structured English and then as a decision tree on paper. Then list one test case for every leaf of your tree.

quiz.q: What does logic modeling describe that a DFD does not?
options: The steps and decisions inside a process
quiz.explain: A DFD shows processes and data movement; logic modeling describes the internal logic of a process.

quiz.q: Which three structures does structured English use?
quiz.explain: Structured English is limited to sequence, decision (IF/CASE) and repetition (loops).

quiz.q: In a decision tree, where are the actions written?
options: In a separate data dictionary only
At the leaves, the ends of the paths
quiz.explain: Branch points hold conditions; the action for each path is shown at its leaf.

quiz.q: A rule has many conditions combining in complex ways and you must be sure every combination is covered. Which tool fits best?
quiz.explain: Decision tables list every combination of conditions, so missing cases are easy to spot.

quiz.q: In the discount example, a customer with a loyalty card buys exactly 2,000 taka. What discount applies if the rule says "at least 2,000 gets 10 percent"?
quiz.explain: "At least 2,000" includes exactly 2,000, so the 10 percent branch applies.

lessons.title: Logic Modeling II: Decision Tables
lessons.content:
Think of the routine chart pinned on the wall of a school staff room. Rows list the classes, columns list the days, and every box tells you exactly who teaches what and when. Nobody needs to read a paragraph; you just find the row and the column. If a box is empty, everyone notices at once that a class has no teacher. A decision table does the same thing for business rules. It lays every combination of conditions out in a grid, so you can see the action for each one, and an empty or conflicting box jumps out immediately.

What a decision table is: A decision table is a tabular way of showing process logic: which actions to take for each combination of conditions. It is the third logic modeling tool, after structured English and decision trees from the last lesson. Its special strength is completeness. Because the table lists every possible combination, the analyst can prove that no case has been forgotten and that no case has two conflicting answers. That makes it the best tool when many conditions combine in complicated ways.

The four parts: A decision table is divided into four quarters. The condition stub, top left, lists the conditions, one per row, such as "Customer has loyalty card?". The action stub, bottom left, lists all possible actions, one per row, such as "Charge 60 taka delivery". The condition entries, top right, hold the values of each condition for each rule, such as Y or N. The action entries, bottom right, mark with an X which actions happen for that rule. Each column on the right side is called a rule: one specific combination of condition values and the actions it triggers.

How many rules: If every condition has only two values, Y or N, and there are n conditions, the full table has 2^n rules. Two conditions give 4 rules, three give 8, four give 16, five give 32. If conditions have more values, multiply the number of values of each. For example, bill size with three ranges and card with two values gives 3 x 2 = 6 rules. This formula is how you know the table is complete before you even fill in actions.

Limited, extended and mixed entry: In a limited-entry table, every condition entry is just Y or N, and every action entry is X or blank. In an extended-entry table, the stub holds only part of the condition and the entry completes it, for example the stub says "Bill total" and the entries say "under 1,000", "1,000 to 4,999", "5,000 or more". A mixed-entry table uses both styles in different rows. Limited entry is easiest to check; extended entry is shorter to read.

Step 1, list conditions and actions: Let's build a real one. ShasthoPharma is starting home delivery. After interviews, the analyst confirms three conditions: C1, does the customer have a loyalty card; C2, is the order total at least 1,000 taka; C3, is the address inside Dhaka city. The possible actions are: A1, free delivery; A2, charge 60 taka; A3, charge 120 taka.

Step 2, count and fill the condition entries: Three yes/no conditions give 2^3 = 8 rules. A standard pattern fills them so that no combination is missed. For the first condition, write half the columns Y and half N: Y Y Y Y N N N N. For the second, alternate in groups of two: Y Y N N Y Y N N. For the last, alternate one by one: Y N Y N Y N Y N. Reading each column top to bottom now gives all 8 distinct combinations, from YYY to NNN.

Step 3, fill the action entries: The owner's policy is: inside Dhaka, an order of at least 1,000 taka is always free; a smaller order inside Dhaka is free for card holders and 60 taka for others. Outside Dhaka, card holders with an order of at least 1,000 pay 60; everyone else pays 120. Now go column by column. Rule 1 (card Y, big Y, Dhaka Y): free. Rule 2 (Y, Y, N): 60. Rule 3 (Y, N, Y): free. Rule 4 (Y, N, N): 120. Rule 5 (N, Y, Y): free. Rule 6 (N, Y, N): 120. Rule 7 (N, N, Y): 60. Rule 8 (N, N, N): 120. Each column has exactly one X in the action rows. The full table is complete: every combination has one answer.

Step 4, simplify with indifference: Some conditions do not matter in some rules. Look at rules 1 and 5: they differ only in C1 (card), and both give free delivery. That means for big orders inside Dhaka, the card does not matter. We merge them into one rule with C1 written as a dash, "-", which means "indifferent" or "does not matter": (-, Y, Y) free delivery. Similarly rules 4 and 8 differ only in C1 and both charge 120, so they merge into (-, N, N) 120. The simplified table has 6 rules instead of 8: (-, Y, Y) free; (Y, Y, N) 60; (Y, N, Y) free; (-, N, N) 120; (N, Y, N) 120; (N, N, Y) 60.

The rule to merge: Two rules can be merged into one only when they have identical actions and differ in exactly one condition. The condition where they differ becomes a dash. You can repeat the process on the new table if more pairs qualify. Merging never changes the logic; it only makes the table shorter and shows the user which conditions truly matter in each case.

Checking the simplified table: Here is a neat check. A rule with no dashes covers 1 combination; a rule with one dash covers 2; with two dashes, 4. In general a rule with d dashes covers 2^d combinations. Add them up: our table has two rules with one dash (2 + 2) and four rules with none (1 + 1 + 1 + 1), total 8. That equals 2^3, so the simplified table still covers every combination exactly once. If the total is less, a case is missing; if more, some rules overlap.

Three errors decision tables catch: Incompleteness: some combination has no rule, or has no action marked; the count check reveals it. Redundancy: two rules cover the same combination with the same actions; harmless but untidy, so remove one. Contradiction: two rules cover the same combination but with different actions; this is a real bug in the business policy, and the analyst must go back to the user and ask which is correct. Finding contradictions early, on paper, is one of the most valuable things an analyst does.

Impossible combinations: Sometimes a combination cannot happen in reality. For example, if one condition is "Customer is under 18" and another is "Customer is a senior citizen", both Y is impossible. Many analysts still keep the column but mark it as impossible, often with an X across the action entries or a note, so readers know it was considered and not forgotten. Others remove it and note why.

From table to tree to English: The three tools describe the same logic, so you can translate between them. Each rule in a decision table is one path in a decision tree and one branch in nested IF statements of structured English. A good working habit is: build the full table to make sure the logic is complete and consistent, simplify it, then draw a tree from the simplified rules to show users, and finally write structured English for the specification that also contains the surrounding steps and loops.

Decision tables for testing: Each rule of a decision table is also a ready-made test case. In our example, the 6 simplified rules give 6 test cases, or 8 if you test every original combination. Testers use exactly this technique, often called decision table testing, to make sure the program handles every combination. Your Software Engineering course covers testing techniques in more depth; here simply notice that good analysis also produces good tests.

When to use which logic tool: Use a decision table when there are many conditions, many combinations and you need to be sure nothing is missed or contradictory, such as pricing, insurance, loan approval or exam grading policies. Use a decision tree when there are a few conditions in a natural order and you need users to check the logic quickly. Use structured English when the logic has sequences of steps, calculations and loops. In real projects you will often use two or all three for the same process.

Real life example 1, a microfinance loan: A microfinance organization in rural Bangladesh decides on small loans using three conditions: has the member attended at least 80 percent of group meetings, has she repaid any previous loan on time, and is the requested amount within her limit. Actions: approve, approve a smaller amount, or refer to the branch manager. Writing this as an 8-rule decision table, the analyst may find that the field officers' manual says one thing for "repaid on time but poor attendance" and the head office circular says another. That is a contradiction, found on paper before it became two different behaviours in a mobile app used by hundreds of officers.

Real life example 2, a university grading policy: A department's policy for retake exams depends on whether the student failed the course, whether attendance was at least 60 percent, and whether the student has an approved medical certificate. Actions: allow retake, allow retake with a fee waiver, or not allowed. Building the table with 2^3 = 8 rules reveals that the written policy never says what happens to a student who passed but has a medical certificate. Does that student need a retake at all? The answer is probably "not applicable", and the analyst marks that rule as impossible or irrelevant, which is far better than letting the software guess.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to count rules first, so some combinations are never written. Filling condition entries randomly instead of with the halving pattern, which creates duplicates and gaps. Merging two rules that differ in more than one condition, which changes the logic. Merging rules with different actions. Writing vague conditions like "big order" instead of "order total at least 1,000 taka". Leaving a column with no action marked. And treating a contradiction as a typing mistake instead of a policy question for the user.

What exams ask: Name and explain the four parts of a decision table. How many rules does a table with n binary conditions have? Construct a decision table for a given policy, then simplify it using indifference. Explain incompleteness, redundancy and contradiction. Convert a given decision table to a decision tree or structured English. Compare the three logic tools.

Recap: A decision table shows logic as a grid of condition stub, action stub, condition entries and action entries; each column is a rule. With n yes/no conditions there are 2^n rules, filled with a halving pattern so none is missed. Merge rules that differ in exactly one condition and share actions, using a dash for "does not matter", and check that the covered combinations still add up to 2^n. Tables expose missing, redundant and contradictory rules, and every rule doubles as a test case. Next lesson: the data dictionary, where every data name used in our DFDs and logic gets an exact definition.
key_points: A decision table shows which actions happen for each combination of conditions.
Its four parts are condition stub, action stub, condition entries and action entries; each column is a rule.
With n yes/no conditions a full table has 2^n rules; with multi-valued conditions, multiply the number of values.
Fill entries with a halving pattern (YYYYNNNN, YYNNYYNN, YNYNYNYN) so no combination is missed.
Two rules may merge only if they differ in exactly one condition and have identical actions; the condition becomes "-".
A rule with d dashes covers 2^d combinations; totals must still equal 2^n.
Tables reveal incompleteness, redundancy and contradiction before coding.
Each rule is also a ready-made test case.
lessons.tip: Always do the count check after simplifying: add 2 to the power of the dashes in each rule. If it does not equal the full number of combinations, stop and find the mistake before showing the table to anyone.
lessons.task: Choose a rule set you know well, such as how your family decides who goes to the bazar, or a mobile data pack offer. Pick three yes/no conditions, build the full 8-rule decision table on paper, fill the actions, then simplify it and do the count check.

quiz.q: In a decision table, what does each column on the right side represent?
options: A rule: one combination of condition values and its actions
quiz.explain: Each column is a rule, combining specific condition values with the actions they trigger.

quiz.q: How many rules does a full decision table with four yes/no conditions have?
quiz.explain: The number of rules is 2^n, and 2^4 = 16.

quiz.q: When can two rules be merged using a dash ("-")?
options: When they differ in exactly one condition and have the same actions
When they differ in all conditions
Whenever the table has more than 8 rules
quiz.explain: Only rules with identical actions that differ in exactly one condition can merge; that condition becomes "does not matter".

quiz.q: Two rules cover the same combination of conditions but specify different actions. This is called:
quiz.explain: Same conditions with different actions is a contradiction, a real policy error to resolve with the user.

quiz.q: A simplified table for 3 yes/no conditions has two rules with one dash each and four rules with no dash. What is the total coverage?
quiz.explain: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8, which equals 2^3, so every combination is covered once.

lessons.title: The Data Dictionary
lessons.content:
Walk into any office in Bangladesh and ask three people what "customer ID" means. The accountant says it is the number on the invoice. The branch manager says it is the customer's phone number. The IT person says it is an auto-increment number in the database. All three are using the same words for three different things, and nobody notices until a report shows the wrong totals. A data dictionary exists to stop this. It is the one place where every piece of data in the system gets a single, exact, agreed definition.

What a data dictionary is: A data dictionary is a central catalogue of all the data used in a system: what each item is called, what it means, what it is made of, what values it may hold, and where it is used. In structured analysis, it is the companion of the data flow diagram. The DFD shows that a flow called "Sales receipt" moves from the "Process sale" bubble to the customer. The dictionary tells you exactly what a sales receipt contains. Data about data like this is called metadata, so a data dictionary is a store of metadata.

Why it exists: Without a dictionary, every analyst, programmer and user carries their own private meaning in their head. In a small project that might survive. In a system with hundreds of data items and many people, it causes duplicated fields, mismatched formats, wrong calculations and endless arguments. The dictionary gives the team a shared vocabulary, helps check that diagrams are consistent, makes designing the database and screens faster, and gives future maintenance staff a reference. It also supports validation: if the dictionary says a quantity must be between 1 and 999, the programmer knows exactly what to check.

Where it fits: The data dictionary sits alongside the other analysis models. The DFD names flows and stores. The logic tools of the last two lessons use data names, such as "bill total" and "discount rate". The ER diagram of the next lesson names entities and attributes. All of these names should be defined in the dictionary. In modern practice, CASE tools and modelling tools keep this information in a shared repository, but the idea is the same whether it is a software tool, a spreadsheet or a binder of paper forms.

What gets an entry: A typical dictionary has entries for six kinds of things: data elements, data structures, data flows, data stores, processes and external entities. The first two are the building blocks of data; the last four are the parts of the DFD. Let's go through each with ShasthoPharma examples.

Data elements: A data element, also called a data item or field, is the smallest piece of data that has meaning on its own and is not broken down further, for example medicine code, unit price or expiry date. A typical element entry records: the name, any aliases (other names users call it), a description, the data type (number, text, date), the length, the format or pattern, the allowed values or range, a default value if any, the source (where it comes from) and who may see or change it. Example: Name: unit_price. Alias: MRP, rate. Description: the maximum retail price of one unit of a medicine, in taka. Type: decimal number. Range: 0.01 to 99,999.99. Source: supplier price list, entered by the head office stock officer.

Discrete and continuous values: Some elements may only take a fixed list of values, called discrete values, such as payment method: Cash, Card or bKash. Others can take any value in a range, called continuous values, such as unit price between 0.01 and 99,999.99. Writing down which kind an element is, and the exact list or range, directly becomes a validation rule for the input screen.

Data structures: A data structure is a group of data elements, and possibly smaller structures, that belong together, such as a customer address or a line on a bill. Structures are described using a short algebra-like notation, which is the heart of the classic data dictionary.

The notation: The equal sign "=" means "is composed of". The plus sign "+" means "and", joining items that appear together. Square brackets with a bar, "[ A | B | C ]", mean "either A or B or C", exactly one of them. Curly braces "{ }" mean "repeated", an iteration; numbers outside give limits, so "1{ line_item }20" means at least 1 and at most 20 line items. Parentheses "( )" mean "optional", the item may be present or absent. Asterisks "* *" enclose a comment. Some books also use "@" or underlining to mark the key of a store.

Worked structure examples: customer_name = first_name + (middle_name) + last_name. Here the middle name is optional. mobile_number = "01" + 9{ digit }9, meaning a Bangladeshi mobile number is "01" followed by exactly nine digits, eleven digits in total. payment_method = [ "Cash" | "Card" | "bKash" ]. line_item = medicine_code + medicine_name + quantity + unit_price + line_total. And the receipt: sales_receipt = receipt_number + sale_date + branch_code + 1{ line_item }n + bill_total + (discount) + amount_payable + payment_method. *n has no fixed upper limit.* Read aloud, it says: a sales receipt is made of a receipt number and a date and a branch code and one or more line items and a bill total and an optional discount and the amount payable and a payment method.

Data flow entries: For every arrow on the DFD there is an entry that records its name, a description, where it comes from (source process, store or entity), where it goes (destination), its composition (usually a data structure, written in the notation above) and its volume, such as "about 400 per branch per day". Example: Data flow: sales_receipt. From: process 2.0 Process Sale. To: external entity Customer. Composition: as defined above. Volume: around 4,800 per day across 12 branches.

Data store entries: For every data store there is an entry with its name, description, the data structure of one record, the key (how a record is identified), the flows that write into it and read from it, the expected volume and growth, and access rules. Example: Data store: D1 Stock. Description: current quantity of every medicine at every branch. Record: branch_code + medicine_code + batch_number + expiry_date + quantity_on_hand + reorder_level. Key: branch_code + medicine_code + batch_number. Inflows: received goods, stock adjustment. Outflows: stock level for reorder report, availability check. Volume: about 3,000 medicines x 12 branches, with several batches each.

Process entries: For each process on the DFD, the dictionary or a separate process description records its number and name, a short purpose, its input and output flows, and its logic. For lowest-level processes, the logic is written using structured English, a decision table or a decision tree, exactly as in the last two lessons. Example: Process 2.3 Compute Discount. Inputs: bill_total, loyalty_status. Output: discount. Logic: see decision table DT-2.

External entity entries: Each external entity, such as Customer, Supplier or Bank, gets a short entry: name, description, and the flows it sends and receives. This keeps the system boundary clear and helps later when designing interfaces with outside systems.

Linking the dictionary and the DFD: The two are checked against each other. Every flow, store, process and entity on the DFD must have a dictionary entry, and every entry should appear somewhere on a DFD; an entry used nowhere is suspicious. When a level 0 flow is split into several level 1 flows, the dictionary shows that the parts add up to the whole, which supports balancing. For example, if "order details" at level 0 = customer_info + 1{ order_line }n, then the two level 1 flows "customer info" and "order lines" together match it exactly.

The dictionary feeds design: Later, during design, the dictionary becomes the basis of the database tables, the field lengths and types, the input validation rules, the report layouts and even the help text on screens. A field defined as mobile_number = "01" + 9{ digit }9 tells the database designer to store 11 characters and tells the screen designer to reject "1712345678" because it is only ten digits.

Building and keeping it alive: The dictionary is not written in one sitting at the end. The analyst starts it during fact-finding, adding an entry every time a new form, report or data name appears, and refines it as the DFDs and ERD grow. One person or a small team should own it, so that changes are reviewed and names stay consistent. Whenever a requirement changes, for example a new payment method such as Nagad is added, the dictionary entry is updated first, and every diagram, screen and table that uses that item is then checked. A dictionary that nobody updates quickly becomes a source of confusion instead of a cure for it.

Real life example 1, national ID numbers: In Bangladesh, people may hold an older 13-digit or 17-digit national ID number or a newer 10-digit smart card number. A bank analyst who writes nid_number = 10{ digit }10 would wrongly reject many valid customers. A careful dictionary entry would record all the formats the bank must accept, with a description of each, after checking current official guidance. This is exactly the kind of detail a dictionary forces the analyst to confirm instead of guess.

Real life example 2, an online food delivery service: A food delivery app in Dhaka has "delivery address" flowing between the customer, the restaurant and the rider. Without a dictionary, one team stores it as a single text box and another splits it into house, road, area and landmark. The rider app then cannot show the landmark, and riders call customers on every order. A dictionary entry delivery_address = house_number + road + area + (landmark) + (instructions), agreed by all teams, prevents this mismatch from the start.

Common mistakes: Defining only elements and forgetting flows and stores, so the DFD cannot be checked. Using different names for the same thing in different diagrams, such as "cust_id" in one place and "customer_number" in another, without recording them as aliases. Writing structures in prose instead of notation, which hides optional and repeating parts. Forgetting ranges and formats, which then become missing validation. Mixing up "[ | ]" (choose one) with "{ }" (repeat). And letting the dictionary go out of date after changes, which makes it worse than useless.

What exams ask: Define a data dictionary and explain why it is needed. List the components or entries of a data dictionary. Explain the notation symbols =, +, [ | ], { }, ( ) and * * with examples. Write a dictionary entry for a given data flow or store, for example a student registration form or a bank deposit slip. Explain how the data dictionary relates to the DFD.

Recap: The data dictionary is the single agreed catalogue of all data in a system, a store of metadata. It has entries for data elements, structures, flows, stores, processes and external entities. Structures are written with = for "is composed of", + for "and", [ | ] for "one of", { } for repetition, ( ) for optional and * * for comments. Every DFD part needs an entry, and the dictionary later drives database, input and report design. Next lesson: data modeling with ER diagrams, seen from the analyst's side.
key_points: A data dictionary is a central catalogue of every data item in a system: names, meanings, composition, values and use.
It is metadata: data about data, and the companion of the DFD.
Entries cover data elements, data structures, data flows, data stores, processes and external entities.
Element entries record name, aliases, description, type, length, format, allowed values or range, source and access.
Notation: = composed of, + and, [ A | B ] one of, { } repetition with optional limits, ( ) optional, * * comment.
Every DFD flow, store, process and entity should have an entry, and composite flows must add up across levels.
The dictionary later drives table design, field types, validation rules and report layouts.
lessons.tip: Whenever two people use different words for what seems the same data, stop and write a dictionary entry with aliases right away. Most data bugs in real systems start as a vocabulary problem.
lessons.task: Take a real paper form you have, such as a university admission form, a bank deposit slip or a mobile SIM registration form. Write its full data structure in dictionary notation, marking optional fields with ( ), choices with [ | ] and repeating parts with { }.

quiz.q: In data dictionary notation, what does "{ }" mean?
quiz.explain: Curly braces show that the enclosed items repeat, optionally with lower and upper limits.

quiz.q: Which is the best description of a data dictionary?
options: A catalogue of metadata defining every data item used in a system
A list of all users and their passwords
A diagram showing processes and data flows
quiz.explain: The dictionary holds data about data: names, meanings, composition, formats and use.

quiz.q: "customer_name = first_name + (middle_name) + last_name" means:
options: Only one of the three names is stored
The customer name is a comment
quiz.explain: Parentheses mark an optional item; + joins items that appear together.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT normally a kind of data dictionary entry?
quiz.explain: Entries cover elements, structures, flows, stores, processes and external entities, not floor plans.

quiz.q: A level 0 flow "order details" is split into two level 1 flows. How does the dictionary help?
options: It shows the two level 1 flows together make up exactly the level 0 flow
It removes the need for level 1 diagrams
It decides the order of processes
It assigns programmers to each flow
quiz.explain: The composition of the parent flow in the dictionary lets you check that the child flows add up, supporting balancing.

lessons.title: Data Modeling for Analysts: ER Diagrams
lessons.content:
Before a family builds a house in Bangladesh, someone draws a plan on paper: how many rooms, which room connects to which, where the stairs go. Nobody pours concrete before the family agrees on the plan, because moving a wall later costs a fortune. A data model is the plan for an organization's data. It shows what things the business needs to remember and how those things connect. The analyst draws it with the users, early, on paper or a whiteboard, so that the database built later holds the right data in the right shape.

What a data model is: A data model is a formal way of describing the data an organization needs, independent of any particular database product. The most common tool for this is the entity relationship diagram (ERD). Your Database Management Systems course teaches the ER model, mapping to tables and normalization in depth. In this lesson we look at it from the analyst's side: how to discover entities from interviews and documents, how to express business rules as relationships, and how the ERD fits with the DFDs and data dictionary we already built.

Why analysts model data: DFDs show how data moves; they say little about the structure of the data that sits in the data stores. Logic models show rules, not data. Yet in most business systems, the data lasts much longer than any program. ShasthoPharma may rewrite its sales screen three times in ten years, but it will still need to know which medicine was sold to whom, when and at which branch. Getting the data model right early prevents painful database changes later and exposes business rules that users never think to mention.

Entities: An entity is a person, place, object, event or concept about which the organization wants to keep data. Examples at ShasthoPharma: BRANCH (place), CUSTOMER and SUPPLIER (people or organizations), MEDICINE (object), SALE and PURCHASE ORDER (events), and DISCOUNT SCHEME (concept). An entity type is the category, written in capitals and singular, such as MEDICINE; an entity instance is one specific member, such as "Napa 500 mg tablet". A useful test: an entity should have many instances, each needing several facts stored. "The ShasthoPharma company" is only one thing, so it is usually not an entity in its own system.

Finding entities from nouns: A practical starting method is to read interview notes, forms and reports and underline the nouns. From the sentence "Each branch sells medicines to customers and records every sale on a receipt", we underline branch, medicines, customers, sale and receipt. Then we filter: some nouns are entities (BRANCH, MEDICINE, CUSTOMER, SALE); some are just outputs or another name for an entity (the receipt is a document showing one SALE); some are attributes (price, date). This noun method is rough, but it gives a first list to discuss with users.

Attributes: An attribute is a fact about an entity, such as a medicine's generic name, strength, unit price or a customer's mobile number. Attributes come straight from the data dictionary of the last lesson. A composite attribute can be split into parts, such as address into house, road and area. A multivalued attribute can have several values for one instance, such as several phone numbers. A derived attribute can be calculated from others, such as a customer's age from date of birth, so it usually does not need to be stored.

Identifiers: An identifier, or key, is an attribute or combination of attributes whose value is unique for each instance, such as medicine_code for MEDICINE or branch_code for BRANCH. A good identifier never changes and is never empty. Names are poor identifiers because two customers can share a name, and people change names. Mobile number is tempting for CUSTOMER, but numbers get recycled by operators and people change them, so many systems create their own customer_id instead. The analyst asks users: "Is this value ever missing? Can it ever change? Can two of them be the same?"

Entity or attribute: A common question is whether something should be an entity or just an attribute. Take "manufacturer" of a medicine. If the business only needs the company's name printed on a report, it can be an attribute of MEDICINE. If the business needs the manufacturer's address, contact person and a list of all its medicines, it should become its own entity, MANUFACTURER, related to MEDICINE. The rule of thumb: if you need to store several facts about it, or it is shared by many instances, make it an entity.

Relationships: A relationship is a meaningful association between entities, usually named with a verb: BRANCH makes SALE, SALE includes MEDICINE, SUPPLIER supplies MEDICINE. Relationships are where business rules hide. "Can a sale happen without a customer record?" "Can one sale be split across two branches?" "Can a medicine come from more than one supplier?" Each answer becomes a precise part of the diagram.

Cardinality and modality: For each relationship, the analyst records two things at each end. Cardinality, or maximum, says how many instances can be related: one or many. Modality, or minimum, says whether the relationship is required: zero (optional) or one (mandatory). Together they read like a sentence in both directions. For example: "Each SALE is made at exactly one BRANCH" and "Each BRANCH makes zero or many SALES" (a newly opened branch may have none yet).

Crow's foot notation: Most business analysts draw ERDs in crow's foot notation. An entity is a rectangle with its name and attributes. A relationship is a line. At each end of the line two marks are drawn. The mark nearest the entity shows the maximum: a single bar for one, a three-pronged "crow's foot" for many. The mark farther from the entity shows the minimum: a bar for one (mandatory) or a small circle for zero (optional). So "bar-bar" next to BRANCH means exactly one, and "circle-crow's foot" next to SALE means zero or many. Other notations, such as Chen notation with diamonds that your DBMS course uses, express the same ideas.

Three kinds of relationships: One-to-one (1:1): each BRANCH has exactly one BRANCH MANAGER and each manager runs one branch. One-to-many (1:N): one BRANCH makes many SALES; each SALE belongs to one BRANCH. Many-to-many (M:N): one SALE can include many MEDICINES, and one MEDICINE appears in many SALES. M:N relationships cannot be stored directly in relational tables, so analysts usually resolve them into an associative entity.

Associative entities: Between SALE and MEDICINE we add SALE LINE. Each SALE has one or many SALE LINES; each MEDICINE appears in zero or many SALE LINES; each SALE LINE belongs to exactly one SALE and refers to exactly one MEDICINE. And the associative entity holds the facts that belong to the pair, not to either side alone: quantity and the price charged on that day. Similarly STOCK sits between BRANCH and MEDICINE, holding batch number, expiry date and quantity on hand for that medicine at that branch.

The ShasthoPharma ERD in words: BRANCH (branch_code, name, address, phone) makes zero or many SALES. CUSTOMER (customer_id, name, mobile_number) makes zero or many SALES; each SALE has zero or one CUSTOMER, because walk-in customers are not registered. SALE (receipt_number, sale_date, payment_method) includes one or many SALE LINES. MEDICINE (medicine_code, brand_name, generic_name, strength, unit_price, controlled_flag) appears in zero or many SALE LINES and zero or many STOCK records. SUPPLIER supplies many MEDICINES and a MEDICINE may come from several SUPPLIERS, resolved through a SUPPLY or PURCHASE ORDER LINE entity. PRESCRIPTION is linked to SALE when a controlled medicine is sold. Drawing this on one page lets the owner confirm, rule by rule, that it matches how the business really works.

Linking the ERD and the DFD: The two models must agree. Every data store on a DFD should correspond to one or more entities on the ERD; the "D1 Stock" store matches STOCK, and "D2 Sales" holds SALE and SALE LINE. Every entity on the ERD should be created, read, updated or deleted by some process on the DFD; an entity that no process ever touches is either unnecessary or a sign of a missing process. Many analysts check this with a CRUD matrix: a grid with processes as rows, entities as columns, and letters C, R, U, D in each cell for what the process does. A column with no C means nothing ever creates that data, which is a real gap.

Normalization in brief: Once the ERD is drafted, it is checked for redundancy using normalization, which your DBMS course covers in depth. In one sentence each: first normal form removes repeating groups so each field holds one value; second normal form removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite key; third normal form removes attributes that depend on another non-key attribute. For an analyst, the practical sign is simple: if the same fact, such as a supplier's phone number, would be typed in many places, the model needs another entity.

Real life example 1, a hospital appointment system: A private hospital in Chattogram wants online doctor appointments. Interview notes mention patients, doctors, departments, chambers, schedules and appointments. The analyst identifies PATIENT, DOCTOR, DEPARTMENT, SCHEDULE SLOT and APPOINTMENT. The question "Can a doctor belong to more than one department?" turns out to be yes for some senior consultants, so DOCTOR to DEPARTMENT becomes many-to-many, a rule the first draft got wrong. "Can a patient book without an account?" turns out to be yes, using only a mobile number, which changes the identifier choice for PATIENT. Each discovered rule is a line and two marks on the ERD.

Real life example 2, a school result system: A high school in Rajshahi keeps results in Excel files, one per class. The analyst's ERD finds STUDENT, CLASS, SECTION, SUBJECT, EXAM and RESULT, where RESULT is the associative entity between STUDENT, SUBJECT and EXAM holding the marks. Drawing it shows why the Excel approach breaks: when a student moves from section A to B mid-year, her marks are split across two files. In the ERD, a STUDENT's enrolment in a SECTION for a year is its own entity, and the problem disappears.

Common mistakes: Making a report or a form into an entity (the receipt is a view of SALE, not a separate entity). Using names as identifiers. Leaving M:N relationships unresolved when the pair has its own facts, such as quantity. Getting the crow's foot marks backwards, putting the minimum next to the entity. Forgetting optionality, so a walk-in sale becomes impossible because "every sale must have a customer". Storing derived attributes like age without reason. And drawing the ERD alone at a desk instead of checking every relationship sentence with users.

What exams ask: Define entity, attribute, identifier and relationship with examples. Explain cardinality and modality, and draw crow's foot notation for given rules. Draw an ERD for a given case, such as a library, a hospital or an online shop, resolving M:N relationships. Explain associative entities. Explain how the ERD relates to the DFD and the data dictionary, and what a CRUD matrix is.

Recap: A data model describes what an organization needs to remember, and the ERD is its main tool. Entities are things with many instances; attributes are their facts; identifiers make each instance unique. Relationships carry business rules, recorded as cardinality (one or many) and modality (zero or one) at both ends, often in crow's foot notation. Resolve M:N relationships into associative entities, and check the ERD against the DFD's data stores and with a CRUD matrix. Next lesson: object-oriented analysis and use case modeling.
key_points: A data model describes the data a business needs, independent of any database product; the ERD is the main tool.
An entity is a person, place, object, event or concept with many instances; attributes are its facts.
An identifier is unique, never empty and should never change; names and phone numbers are risky identifiers.
Relationships carry business rules; each end has cardinality (one or many) and modality (zero or one).
