In crow's foot notation the mark nearest the entity is the maximum and the farther mark is the minimum.
Many-to-many relationships are resolved into associative entities that hold facts about the pair, like quantity.
Every DFD data store should map to ERD entities, and every entity should be created and used by some process (CRUD matrix).
Normalization, covered in DBMS, removes repeated facts; repeated typing of the same fact signals a missing entity.
lessons.tip: Read every relationship aloud as two sentences, one in each direction, such as "Each sale is made at exactly one branch" and "Each branch makes zero or many sales". Then ask a user if both sentences are true. This catches most ERD mistakes.
lessons.task: Draw an ERD on paper for your university's course registration: STUDENT, COURSE, SECTION, TEACHER and the registrations. Use crow's foot marks, resolve any many-to-many relationship, and write both direction sentences for each relationship.

quiz.q: Which of these is best modeled as an entity at ShasthoPharma?
quiz.explain: Medicine has many instances, each with several facts; price and expiry date are attributes.

quiz.q: In crow's foot notation, a small circle next to the crow's foot at one end means:
quiz.explain: The circle is the minimum (zero, optional) and the crow's foot is the maximum (many).

quiz.q: What is the usual way to handle a many-to-many relationship like SALE and MEDICINE?
options: Merge the two entities into one
Add an associative entity such as SALE LINE
quiz.explain: An associative entity resolves M:N and holds facts about the pair, like quantity and price charged.

quiz.q: Why is a customer's name a poor identifier?
options: Two customers can share a name and names can change
Names cannot be stored in databases
quiz.explain: An identifier must be unique and stable; names are neither.

quiz.q: In a CRUD matrix, an entity whose column has no "C" in any row shows that:
options: No process ever creates that data, so a process may be missing
The entity has too many attributes
quiz.explain: If no process creates an entity's data, something is missing in the process model or the entity is unnecessary.

lessons.title: Object-Oriented Analysis and Use Cases
lessons.content:
When you go to a bKash agent shop, you do not care how the agent's phone app talks to the server or which database stores your balance. You care about your goal: "I want to cash out 2,000 taka." The agent cares about her goal too: "I want to earn my commission without making a mistake." A use case starts exactly there, from the goals of the people who use a system. It describes what the system must do for each of them, in their own words, before anyone thinks about screens or code.

Two ways to analyse a system: So far in this course we have used the structured approach: DFDs for processes, a data dictionary and an ERD for data, and logic tools for rules. Processes and data are modelled separately. Object-oriented analysis (OOA) takes a different view. It models the system as a set of objects that each combine data and behaviour, and it starts from how users interact with the system. Both approaches are used in industry, and many projects mix them. It is worth knowing both, because exam questions and real teams use both vocabularies.

Objects and classes, a quick recap: Your Object Oriented Programming course covered these in code. An object is a thing that has state (its data, called attributes) and behaviour (what it can do, called operations or methods). A class is the template for a set of similar objects. At ShasthoPharma, Medicine is a class; "Napa 500 mg" is an object of that class with attributes like strength and unit price and operations like checkStock(). Encapsulation means the object keeps its data together with the operations that use it, and others interact through those operations. In analysis we use these ideas to describe the business, not yet to write code.

UML: The Unified Modeling Language (UML) is the standard visual language for object-oriented modelling. It grew in the 1990s from the work of Grady Booch, James Rumbaugh and Ivar Jacobson, and is maintained by the Object Management Group (OMG). UML 2 defines more than a dozen diagram types, grouped into two families. Structure diagrams show what the system is made of, such as class, object, component and deployment diagrams. Behaviour diagrams show what the system does, such as use case, activity, state machine and sequence diagrams. An analyst rarely needs all of them; the most common in SA&D are use case, activity, sequence, class and state machine diagrams, which we cover in this and the next two lessons.

What a use case is: A use case is a description of how a user interacts with the system to achieve one goal of value. "Sell medicine", "Receive stock from supplier" and "Generate expiry report" are use cases. "Click the Save button" is not, because it is a tiny step, not a goal. A use case tells a story: who starts it, what steps happen between the user and the system, what can go wrong, and what is true at the end. Use cases were introduced by Ivar Jacobson and became part of UML.

Actors: An actor is anyone or anything outside the system that interacts with it: a role, not a specific person. At ShasthoPharma, actors include Counter Staff, Stock Keeper, Branch Manager, Head Office Manager, Supplier and a Payment Gateway system. The same human can play several roles: Rahim may act as Counter Staff in the evening and as Stock Keeper in the morning. A primary actor starts a use case to reach a goal; a supporting or secondary actor helps, like the payment gateway that confirms a card or mobile payment. Actors are drawn as stick figures, even when they are computer systems, although some teams use a box labelled "actor" for systems.

The use case diagram: A use case diagram gives a one-page picture of the system's scope. A rectangle is the system boundary, labelled with the system name. Use cases are ovals inside the boundary, each named with a verb and a noun. Actors stand outside the boundary. Lines (associations) connect each actor to the use cases it takes part in. That is the whole basic diagram. For ShasthoPharma: Counter Staff connects to "Sell Medicine" and "Check Availability"; Stock Keeper connects to "Receive Stock" and "Adjust Stock"; Head Office Manager connects to "View Reorder Report" and "View Expiry Report"; Supplier connects to "Receive Purchase Order".

Include relationship: When several use cases share the same chunk of behaviour, we pull it out into its own use case and connect them with a dashed arrow labelled include, pointing from the base use case to the included one. The included behaviour always happens as part of the base. Example: both "Sell Medicine" and "Check Availability" need to look a medicine up by name or barcode, so both include "Search Medicine". Include avoids writing the same steps twice.

Extend relationship: When some behaviour happens only under certain conditions, it can be written as a separate use case that extends the base. The dashed arrow is labelled extend and points from the extending use case to the base one. The base use case is complete on its own; the extension adds optional steps at a named extension point. Example: "Verify Prescription" extends "Sell Medicine" only when a controlled medicine is in the bill. "Apply Loyalty Discount" extends "Sell Medicine" only when the customer shows a loyalty card. A helpful memory: include is "always, and points to the shared part"; extend is "sometimes, and points back to the base".

Generalization: Actors and use cases can also be generalized. If a Branch Manager can do everything Counter Staff can do plus more, we draw a solid line with a hollow triangle from Branch Manager to Counter Staff, meaning Branch Manager is a specialised kind of Counter Staff and inherits its associations. This keeps the diagram from filling with repeated lines.

The use case description: The diagram is only a map. The real requirements live in the written use case description, sometimes called a use case specification. A common template has: use case name and ID; primary actor; stakeholders and their interests; brief description; trigger (the event that starts it); preconditions (what must be true before); postconditions (what is guaranteed after success); main success scenario (normal flow); alternate flows and exception flows; related use cases; and sometimes priority and frequency.

Worked description, Sell Medicine: ID UC-02. Primary actor: Counter Staff. Stakeholders: customer wants correct medicine and bill; owner wants accurate sales and stock. Trigger: a customer asks to buy medicine. Precondition: staff is logged in at a branch terminal. Main flow: 1. Staff scans or searches each medicine (include Search Medicine). 2. System shows name, strength, price and available stock. 3. Staff enters quantity. 4. System adds the line and updates the bill total. 5. Steps 1 to 4 repeat until all items are entered. 6. Staff selects payment method. 7. System records the sale, reduces stock and prints the receipt. Postcondition: the sale is stored and stock for each item is reduced by the quantity sold.

Alternate and exception flows: 2a. Medicine out of stock at this branch: system shows nearby branches that have it; staff informs the customer. 3a. Quantity exceeds stock: system warns and accepts only available quantity. 4a. Controlled medicine: extension point, Verify Prescription runs. 6a. Customer has loyalty card: Apply Loyalty Discount runs. 6b. Mobile payment fails: system keeps the bill open and asks for another payment method. Writing these "what if" paths is where the analyst finds most of the hidden requirements, and each one later becomes a test case.

How to find use cases: Start from the actors. For each actor, ask: what goals does this person want the system to help with? What information do they need to create, read, update or delete? What events from outside does the system need to react to, such as a supplier delivery or the end of the day? Also look at the DFD processes and the event list if you have them. Keep use cases at the level of a goal achieved in one sitting, often called user-goal level, and avoid breaking them into tiny screen steps.

Use cases and the rest of the analysis: Use cases connect naturally to other models. Each use case often becomes an activity diagram for its flow, a sequence diagram for its object interactions, and a set of test cases. The nouns in use case descriptions suggest classes for the class diagram, much like nouns suggested entities for the ERD. Use cases are also a good unit for planning: a team can deliver "Sell Medicine" first and "View Expiry Report" later. In agile teams, user stories play a similar but lighter role; your Software Engineering course covers them.

Real life example 1, a train ticketing app: Think of booking Bangladesh Railway tickets online. Actors: Passenger, Payment Gateway, and Station Staff. Use cases: Register, Search Trains, Buy Ticket, Cancel Ticket, Verify Ticket at the station. "Buy Ticket" includes "Search Trains" and "Make Payment"; an extension "Choose Seat" may apply only for some classes. The exception flows matter enormously here: what happens if payment succeeds but the seat was taken by someone else in the same second? A clear exception flow, such as "hold the seat for a few minutes during payment, then release it", must be agreed before code is written, or customers lose money and trust.

Real life example 2, a university library: Actors: Student, Teacher, Librarian. Use cases: Search Catalogue, Borrow Book, Return Book, Reserve Book, Pay Fine. Teacher generalizes Student for borrowing but with a longer loan period. "Pay Fine" extends "Return Book" only when the book is late. Writing the description for "Borrow Book" reveals a rule nobody had mentioned: a student with an unpaid fine above 200 taka cannot borrow. That rule goes into the precondition and an exception flow.

Common mistakes: Naming use cases as tiny steps ("Enter quantity") or as system functions ("Database update") instead of user goals. Drawing a person's name as an actor instead of a role. Putting actors inside the system boundary. Reversing the include and extend arrows. Using include and extend to draw a flowchart of steps, which UML use case diagrams are not for. Drawing a pretty diagram but never writing the descriptions, where the real requirements live. And ignoring alternate and exception flows.

What exams ask: Define object-oriented analysis and compare it with structured analysis. What is UML and what are its diagram families? Define actor and use case, and draw a use case diagram for a given system such as an ATM, a library or online shopping. Explain include, extend and generalization with examples. Write a use case description with main and alternate flows.

Recap: Object-oriented analysis models the system as objects that combine data and behaviour, and uses UML as its visual language. A use case describes how an actor reaches one goal with the system. The use case diagram shows the system boundary, actors, use cases and their associations, plus include (always, shared), extend (sometimes, optional) and generalization. The written description, with preconditions, main flow, alternate flows and postconditions, holds the real requirements. Next lesson: activity and sequence diagrams, which show the flow and the object interactions inside a use case.
key_points: Object-oriented analysis models a system as objects that combine data (attributes) and behaviour (operations).
UML is the standard modelling language, with structure diagrams and behaviour diagrams.
A use case is how an actor uses the system to achieve one goal of value.
An actor is a role (human or system) outside the system boundary, not a specific person.
Include: shared behaviour that always happens; arrow points from base to included use case.
Extend: optional behaviour under a condition; arrow points from the extension back to the base.
The written use case description (trigger, preconditions, main flow, alternate flows, postconditions) holds the real requirements.
Use cases feed activity diagrams, sequence diagrams, class discovery and test cases.
lessons.tip: For every step in a use case's main flow, ask "What could go wrong here?" and write an alternate flow numbered after that step (like 3a). Teachers and testers both love this, and it uncovers requirements users forget to mention.
lessons.task: Draw a use case diagram on paper for a bKash or Nagad-style mobile wallet: actors Customer, Agent and Bank; at least six use cases; one include and one extend. Then write the full description for "Send Money" with at least two alternate flows.

quiz.q: What is an actor in a use case diagram?
options: A step inside a use case
A role outside the system that interacts with it
quiz.explain: An actor is a role, human or system, outside the boundary that interacts with the system.

quiz.q: "Verify Prescription" happens during "Sell Medicine" only when a controlled medicine is sold. Which relationship fits?
quiz.explain: Extend is for optional behaviour under a condition; the arrow points from Verify Prescription to Sell Medicine.

quiz.q: Which of these is a well-named use case?
quiz.explain: A use case is a user goal named with a verb and noun, not a tiny step, a system function or a person.

quiz.q: Where do the detailed requirements of a use case mainly live?
options: In the written use case description with its flows
In the colour of the ovals
quiz.explain: The diagram is a map; preconditions, main flow, alternate flows and postconditions are in the description.

quiz.q: Both "Sell Medicine" and "Check Availability" always search for a medicine first. How should this be modeled?
options: Extend each use case from "Search Medicine"
Draw "Search Medicine" outside the system boundary
Both include a separate "Search Medicine" use case
quiz.explain: Include pulls out shared behaviour that always happens, with arrows from each base use case to the included one.

lessons.title: Activity and Sequence Diagrams
lessons.content:
Think about a wedding in a Bangladeshi family. One cousin draws the plan for the day: the groom's party arrives, then food is served while photos are taken at the same time, then the bride's family does the rituals, and if it rains, everything moves indoors. Another cousin writes down who talks to whom: the caterer calls the manager, the manager calls the decorator, the decorator replies "ready". The first is a flow of activities; the second is a conversation between people over time. UML gives analysts two diagrams for exactly these two views: the activity diagram and the sequence diagram.

Why two more diagrams: In the last lesson, a use case description told the story of a goal in numbered steps. That text is precise but hard to see at a glance, especially when there are decisions, loops and things happening in parallel. An activity diagram draws the flow of a use case or a business process as a picture. A sequence diagram shows which objects send which messages to each other, in time order, to carry out one scenario of a use case. Both are behaviour diagrams in UML.

Activity diagrams, what they are: An activity diagram models a workflow: the sequence of actions, the decisions that choose between paths, and actions that can run at the same time. It looks like a flowchart, and that is no accident; it extends the familiar flowchart idea with parallel flows and responsibility lanes. Analysts use it to model business processes (how an order moves through a company), the flow of one use case, or the logic of a complex operation.

The basic symbols: The initial node, a small filled black circle, marks where the flow starts. An action is a rounded rectangle containing a short verb phrase, such as "Scan medicine". Arrows called control flows connect actions in order. The activity final node, a filled circle inside a ring, like a bullseye, marks the end of the whole activity. A flow final node, a circle with an X, ends just one path while others continue. Object nodes, plain rectangles, can show data such as "Receipt" being produced or used.

Decisions and merges: A diamond with one arrow coming in and several going out is a decision node. Each outgoing arrow carries a guard condition in square brackets, such as [in stock] and [out of stock]. Guards must not overlap and should cover all cases, the same completeness idea as decision tables. A diamond with several arrows coming in and one going out is a merge node, where alternative paths join again. Loops are drawn with a decision that sends the flow back to an earlier action, for example [more items] back to "Scan medicine".

Fork and join, doing things in parallel: A thick black bar with one arrow in and several out is a fork: all outgoing paths start and may happen at the same time or in any order. A thick bar with several arrows in and one out is a join: the flow waits until all incoming paths have finished. For example, after the sale is confirmed, "Print receipt" and "Update stock" can happen in parallel, and the activity ends only after both are done. Do not confuse fork with decision: a decision chooses one path; a fork starts all of them.

Swimlanes: Activity partitions, usually called swimlanes, divide the diagram into vertical or horizontal lanes, one per actor, role, department or system. Each action is drawn in the lane of whoever is responsible for it. Swimlanes make handoffs visible: every time an arrow crosses from one lane to another, work changes hands, and that is often where delays and errors happen. Analysts love swimlanes for "as-is" business process analysis because they show who does what.

Worked activity diagram, Sell Medicine: Three swimlanes: Counter Staff, System and Customer. Start in Counter Staff: "Scan or search medicine". Into System: "Show price and stock". Decision: [out of stock] goes to "Show nearby branches" and then back to Counter Staff; [in stock] goes to Counter Staff: "Enter quantity". System: "Add line to bill". Decision: [more items] loops back to "Scan or search medicine"; [no more items] continues. Decision: [controlled medicine in bill] goes to Counter Staff "Check prescription"; [else] skips it; then a merge. Customer: "Pay". System: fork into "Record sale and update stock" and "Print receipt"; join; end. Drawn on one page, the owner can trace the whole sale with a finger and spot that, for example, no path handles a customer who changes her mind before paying.

Sequence diagrams, what they are: A sequence diagram shows how a group of objects interact to carry out one scenario, by listing the messages they send to each other in time order. Time runs from top to bottom. It answers questions the activity diagram does not: which object is responsible for which step, what information is passed, and in which order. It is the bridge between analysis and design, because each message usually becomes an operation of a class.

The basic symbols: Each participant appears at the top as a box with a name like ":Sale" (an unnamed object of class Sale) or an actor stick figure. Below each runs a dashed vertical line called a lifeline, showing that the participant exists over time. A message is a horizontal arrow from the sender's lifeline to the receiver's, labelled with the message name and parameters, such as checkStock(medicineCode). A synchronous message, where the sender waits for a reply, uses a solid line with a filled arrowhead. An asynchronous message, where the sender does not wait, uses an open arrowhead. A return is a dashed arrow back, often labelled with the returned value. A thin rectangle on a lifeline, called an activation or execution specification, shows when that object is busy doing work.

Combined fragments: Real scenarios have choices and loops. UML draws these with a rectangle around a group of messages, labelled in the top-left corner. "alt" means alternatives, like if-else, with sections separated by a dashed line and each section guarded, for example [in stock] and [else]. "opt" means an optional part that happens only if its guard is true, like a single if. "loop" means the enclosed messages repeat, for example loop [for each item]. Creating an object can be shown by a message pointing to the new object's box, and destroying one by an X at the end of its lifeline.

Analysis objects: When moving from a use case to a sequence diagram, many analysts sort participants into three kinds, an idea from Jacobson's approach. Boundary objects are where actors touch the system, such as the SalesScreen. Control objects coordinate the steps of one use case, such as a SaleController. Entity objects hold long-lived business data, such as Medicine, Stock and Sale, which usually match entities in the ERD. This simple split keeps responsibilities clear and stops screens from containing business rules.

Worked sequence diagram, Sell Medicine main scenario: Participants from left to right: Counter Staff (actor), :SalesScreen, :SaleController, :Medicine, :Stock, :Sale. 1. Staff sends scan(barcode) to SalesScreen. 2. SalesScreen sends addItem(barcode, qty) to SaleController. 3. SaleController sends getDetails(barcode) to Medicine; return name, price. 4. SaleController sends checkStock(medicineCode, branch) to Stock; return available quantity. 5. An alt fragment: [available >= qty] SaleController sends addLine(medicine, qty, price) to Sale; [else] SaleController returns "insufficient stock" to SalesScreen. All of steps 1 to 5 sit inside a loop [for each item] fragment. 6. Staff sends confirm(paymentMethod). 7. SaleController sends save() to Sale and reduceStock() to Stock. 8. SalesScreen shows and prints the receipt.

From use case to sequence diagram, step by step: Pick one scenario, usually the main success flow first. List the actor and the objects involved, using the boundary, control and entity idea. Go through the use case steps in order and turn each into one or more messages between participants. Add returns where a value comes back. Wrap repeated steps in a loop fragment and choices in alt or opt fragments. Then check: does every message have a sender and receiver who would sensibly know about each other? Does any object do too much? Each important alternate flow can get its own diagram, or an alt fragment if it is small.

Activity vs sequence, when to use which: Use an activity diagram to show the overall flow of work, especially across several people or departments, with decisions and parallel steps; users understand it easily. Use a sequence diagram to show how objects collaborate for one scenario, especially when you are preparing to design classes and operations; developers find it most useful. A related UML diagram, the communication diagram, shows the same messages as a sequence diagram but arranged around the objects instead of along time.

Real life example 1, a garment factory sample approval: A garment factory near Gazipur gets a sample order from a foreign buyer. The analyst draws an activity diagram with lanes for Merchandiser, Sample Section, Quality Control and Buyer. A fork shows that fabric sourcing and pattern making happen in parallel, joined before sewing. A decision after the buyer's review sends rejected samples back to the Sample Section. The diagram reveals that every rejection crosses four lanes and waits for an email, which explains the two-week delays management complained about.

Real life example 2, ride-hailing request: In a ride-sharing app in Dhaka, a sequence diagram for "Request Ride" shows: Rider sends requestRide(pickup, destination) to the app screen; the screen calls the RideController; the controller asks a pricing component for an estimated fare and a matching component for nearby drivers; inside a loop it sends offers to drivers one by one until one accepts; an alt fragment covers [driver accepted] and [no driver found]. Drawing this makes it clear where time-outs are needed and what the rider sees in each case.

Common mistakes: In activity diagrams: using a decision diamond where a fork was meant, or vice versa; forgetting guards on decision branches; guards that overlap, such as [qty > 5] and [qty > 3]; joins that wait for a path that may never come; and putting actions in the wrong swimlane. In sequence diagrams: drawing messages with no receiver, putting time running upwards, letting one "god" object do everything, mixing several scenarios in one diagram without fragments, and forgetting return values that later steps need.

What exams ask: Draw an activity diagram with swimlanes for a given process, such as online order processing or course registration. Explain the difference between decision/merge and fork/join. Draw a sequence diagram for a given use case scenario, such as withdrawing money from an ATM. Explain lifelines, activation, synchronous and asynchronous messages, and alt, opt and loop fragments. Compare activity and sequence diagrams.

Recap: Activity diagrams show the flow of work: initial and final nodes, actions, decisions with guards, merges, forks and joins for parallel work, and swimlanes for responsibility. Sequence diagrams show how objects collaborate in one scenario over time: lifelines, messages, returns, activations and combined fragments like alt, opt and loop. Turning a use case into these diagrams makes gaps visible and prepares the ground for class design. Next lesson: class diagrams and state machine diagrams.
key_points: An activity diagram models a workflow; a sequence diagram models object interactions in one scenario over time.
Activity symbols: initial node, rounded action, control flow, decision/merge diamond with guards, fork/join bar, final node.
A decision chooses one path; a fork starts several paths in parallel, and a join waits for all of them.
Swimlanes show who is responsible for each action and make handoffs visible.
Sequence symbols: participants with lifelines, messages (synchronous filled arrow, asynchronous open arrow), dashed returns, activation bars.
Combined fragments: alt for if-else, opt for optional, loop for repetition.
Boundary, control and entity objects help turn a use case into a clean sequence diagram.
Each message in a sequence diagram usually becomes an operation of a class in design.
lessons.tip: When drawing a sequence diagram, read your use case description aloud step by step and draw one message per step as you go. If a step has no obvious sender and receiver, that is a gap in your analysis, not just in your drawing.
lessons.task: Draw an activity diagram with three swimlanes (Student, Department Office, Accounts) for getting a transcript from your university, including at least one decision and one fork/join. Then draw a sequence diagram for withdrawing cash from an ATM with an alt fragment for [enough balance] and [else].

quiz.q: In an activity diagram, what does a fork (thick bar with one incoming and several outgoing flows) mean?
options: Choose exactly one path based on a condition
All outgoing paths start and can run in parallel
quiz.explain: A fork splits the flow into parallel paths; a decision diamond is the one that chooses a single path.

quiz.q: What do swimlanes show in an activity diagram?
options: Which actor, role or department is responsible for each action
The order of classes in code
quiz.explain: Swimlanes (activity partitions) assign each action to a responsible party and make handoffs visible.

quiz.q: In a sequence diagram, which direction does time flow?
quiz.explain: Time runs down the page; messages lower on the diagram happen later.

quiz.q: Which combined fragment represents if-else alternatives?
quiz.explain: "alt" holds alternative sections with guards; "opt" is a single optional part; "loop" repeats.

quiz.q: In the boundary-control-entity idea, which object would hold long-lived data like a medicine's price?
options: A boundary object such as SalesScreen
A control object such as SaleController
An entity object such as Medicine
quiz.explain: Entity objects hold long-lived business data and usually match ERD entities.

lessons.title: Class and State Diagrams: The Basics
lessons.content:
Think about the medicine counter at a ShasthoPharma branch. Every box on the shelf is a different thing, but they all share the same kind of details: a name, a generic name, a price, an expiry date, a quantity. And every customer order goes through the same journey: it is created, then paid, then packed, then delivered or cancelled. Use case, activity and sequence diagrams told us what the system does and in what order. Two more UML diagrams answer two different questions. The class diagram answers "what kinds of things does the system know about, and how are they connected?". The state diagram answers "what stages can one thing go through during its life?".

What a class diagram is: A class diagram is a picture of the classes in a system, the information each class holds, what each class can do, and how the classes relate to each other. It is a static view: it shows structure, not the order of events. In analysis we draw it to capture the important business concepts and the rules between them. Developers later turn the same picture into code and database tables.

Class and object, quick recap: A class is a template or category, such as Medicine. An object is one real example of that class, such as "Napa 500 mg, price 12 taka per strip, expiry March 2027". Your OOP course covered this in depth. In SA&D we use the idea to describe the business, not to write Java or Dart yet.

Analysis classes vs design classes: During analysis we draw only business things the users talk about: Customer, Medicine, Order, Prescription, Branch, Supplier. We do not draw technical classes like DatabaseConnection or LoginScreenController. Those belong to design. A good trick is to take the nouns from the use case descriptions and the requirements document, remove duplicates and vague words, and keep the ones that the system must remember information about.

The class box: A class is drawn as a rectangle split into three parts. The top part holds the class name, written as a singular noun with a capital letter, for example Medicine. The middle part lists attributes, the pieces of data each object holds, for example name, genericName, unitPrice, expiryDate. The bottom part lists operations, the things an object can do or that can be done to it, for example applyDiscount() or isExpired(). In analysis it is fine to leave out data types and most operations; focus on the important attributes.

Visibility, in brief: In design diagrams you may see a sign before each attribute or operation. A plus sign means public, a minus sign means private, a hash sign means protected, and a tilde means package. For example "- unitPrice : Decimal" means a private attribute called unitPrice of type Decimal. Analysts usually skip visibility; designers add it later.

Associations: An association is a line between two classes showing that their objects are connected. A Customer places an Order. An Order contains Medicines. You can write a verb phrase on the line, such as "places", and a small arrow showing which way to read it. An association is the class diagram version of a relationship in an ER diagram, which you studied in lesson 17.

Multiplicity: Multiplicity says how many objects on one side can be linked to one object on the other side. It is written near the end of the line. Common values are 1 (exactly one), 0..1 (zero or one), * or 0..* (zero or many), 1..* (one or more), and a fixed range such as 2..4. Read it like this: between Customer and Order, put 1 near Customer and 0..* near Order. That means one customer can place zero or many orders, and each order belongs to exactly one customer. A new customer who has never ordered is allowed, but an order without a customer is not.

A worked multiplicity check: Suppose the pharmacy rule is "every prescription is written by exactly one doctor, and a doctor may write many prescriptions, but we only store doctors who wrote at least one". Then near Doctor we write 1, and near Prescription we write 1..*. If you wrote 0..* instead, you would allow a doctor with no prescriptions, which breaks the business rule. Small numbers on a line carry real business rules, which is why analysts must confirm them with users.

Association class: Sometimes the link itself has data. An Order contains many Medicines, and a Medicine appears in many Orders, so this is many-to-many. But where do we store "quantity 3 strips, price 12 taka each" for Napa in order 1045? That data belongs to the link, not to the order alone or the medicine alone. UML lets you attach a class called OrderLine to the association with a dashed line. This is the same idea as the junction table you use when mapping an M:N relationship in DBMS.

Generalization (inheritance): Generalization shows an "is a kind of" relationship. It is drawn as a line with a hollow triangle pointing to the general class. In the pharmacy, PrescriptionMedicine and OverTheCounterMedicine are both kinds of Medicine. Common attributes such as name and price stay in Medicine. Special ones go in the subclasses: PrescriptionMedicine needs a field requiresPrescription or a schedule category, OverTheCounterMedicine might have a maximum quantity per sale. Test it by saying the sentence aloud: "A prescription medicine is a medicine." If the sentence sounds wrong, it is not generalization.

Aggregation: Aggregation is a weak "has a" or "whole and part" relationship. It is drawn with a hollow diamond at the whole end. A Branch has Pharmacists, but if a branch closes, the pharmacists still exist and can move to another branch. The parts can live without the whole and can even belong to more than one whole over time.

Composition: Composition is a strong "whole and part" relationship, drawn with a filled black diamond at the whole end. An Order is composed of OrderLines. If the order is deleted, its order lines make no sense alone and are deleted too. A part belongs to only one whole at a time. Exam rule of thumb: if the part dies with the whole, use composition; if the part survives, use aggregation. If you are not sure, a plain association is always acceptable and safer than a wrong diamond.

A small class diagram in words: Customer (name, phone) 1 ---- 0..* Order (orderNo, date, status). Order (filled diamond) 1 ---- 1..* OrderLine (quantity, unitPrice). OrderLine 0..* ---- 1 Medicine (name, unitPrice, expiryDate). Medicine has two subclasses, PrescriptionMedicine and OverTheCounterMedicine, with a hollow triangle. Branch (hollow diamond) 1 ---- 0..* Pharmacist. Reading this picture, a new programmer can understand the core of the business in a few minutes.

Building it step by step: First list candidate classes from nouns. Second, add two or three key attributes to each so you know why the class exists. Third, draw associations for every sentence in the requirements that links two nouns with a verb. Fourth, add multiplicities and check each one with a user. Fifth, look for "is a kind of" sentences for generalization and "is made of" sentences for diamonds. Finally, walk through one or two use cases and check that every piece of data they need lives somewhere in the diagram.

What a state diagram is:A state machine diagram, often just called a state diagram, shows the life of one object of one class: the states it can be in, the events that move it from one state to another, and any conditions or actions on the way. A class diagram shows many classes at one moment; a state diagram shows one class over time. We draw it only for classes with interesting lives, such as Order, Payment or Prescription, not for simple things like Supplier address.

State diagram symbols: A state is a rounded rectangle with a name, usually an adjective or a "waiting" phrase, such as Pending, Paid, Packed. The initial state is a small filled black circle; the final state is a filled circle inside another circle. A transition is an arrow from one state to another, labelled with the event that triggers it. A label can have three parts: event [guard] / action. The guard is a condition in square brackets that must be true. The action is something done quickly during the transition.

Worked state diagram for an order: Start at the black circle, then go to Created. On the event "payment received" the order moves to Paid. From Created, on "customer cancels" it moves to Cancelled. From Paid, on "items packed" it moves to Packed. From Packed, on "handed to rider" it moves to OutForDelivery. From OutForDelivery, on "delivered" it moves to Delivered, then to the final state. A guard example: from Paid, "customer cancels [not yet packed] / refund" moves to Cancelled and triggers a refund. Cancelled also leads to the final state.

What the state diagram reveals: Drawing this forces useful questions. Can a delivered order be cancelled? Can a customer cancel after the rider leaves? What if the delivery fails because nobody is home? Each question is a requirement that might otherwise be missed until a real customer complains. That is why analysts like state diagrams: they find gaps.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma home delivery: When ShasthoPharma adds home delivery in Dhaka, the analyst draws the Order state diagram with the operations team. They discover a missing state, ReturnedToBranch, for failed deliveries, and a rule that prescription orders must pass a PharmacistVerified state before Paid. The class diagram gains a Prescription class linked to Order with multiplicity 0..1, because some orders need one and some do not.

Real life example 2, a train ticket in Bangladesh: Think of an online train ticket. The ticket object moves through states such as Reserved (seat held for a short time while you pay), Purchased, Cancelled and Used. If payment does not arrive before the time limit, an event "timeout" sends the reservation back and the seat is freed. The class diagram would show Passenger, Ticket, Train, Seat and Journey with multiplicities like "one Ticket is for exactly one Seat on one Journey".

Common mistakes: Putting technical classes in an analysis diagram. Using plural class names like Medicines. Writing multiplicity at the wrong end of the line, so the rule is reversed. Using generalization for "has a" relationships. Drawing filled diamonds everywhere without checking whether parts really die with the whole. In state diagrams, students often name states with verbs ("Pay") instead of conditions ("Paid"), forget the initial state, or confuse a state diagram with an activity diagram. Remember: an activity diagram shows the steps of a process; a state diagram shows the conditions of one object.

What exams ask: Draw a class diagram for a library, hospital or shop with multiplicities. Differentiate aggregation and composition with examples. Explain generalization. Explain association class. Draw a state diagram for an order, ticket or bank account and label events and guards. Differentiate class and object, and state and activity diagrams.

Recap: Class diagrams show the static structure of the system: classes with names, attributes and operations, linked by associations with multiplicities, generalization triangles, and aggregation or composition diamonds. In analysis keep them to business concepts. State diagrams show the life of one object: states, events, guards and actions, from the initial to the final state, and they are great for finding missing rules. Next lesson: we move from analysis to design, choosing a strategy and an architecture for the new system.
key_points: A class diagram shows the static structure: classes, attributes, operations and relationships.
Analysis classes are business concepts taken from nouns in requirements; technical classes come later in design.
Multiplicity such as 1, 0..1, 0..* and 1..* records real business rules on each end of an association.
An association class holds data that belongs to the link itself, like quantity on an order line.
Generalization (hollow triangle) means "is a kind of"; aggregation (hollow diamond) is a weak whole-part; composition (filled diamond) means the part dies with the whole.
A state diagram shows the life of one object: states, transitions labelled event [guard] / action, initial and final states.
States are named as conditions (Paid, Packed), not as actions.
Drawing state diagrams exposes missing requirements such as failed deliveries or late cancellations.
lessons.tip: Read every multiplicity aloud as a full sentence ("one customer places zero or many orders"). If the sentence sounds wrong to the pharmacy owner, the diagram is wrong.
lessons.task: On paper, draw a class diagram for your university library with Member, Book, Copy and Loan, including multiplicities. Then draw a state diagram for one Copy of a book (Available, OnLoan, Reserved, Lost) with labelled events.

quiz.q: Which UML diagram shows the different stages one object goes through during its life?
quiz.explain: A state machine diagram shows the states of one object and the events that move it between them.

quiz.q: Between Customer and Order, "1" is written near Customer and "0..*" near Order. What does this mean?
options: Each customer places zero or many orders, and each order belongs to exactly one customer
Each customer must place exactly one order
quiz.explain: Multiplicity is read from one object to the far end: one customer to 0..* orders, one order to exactly 1 customer.

quiz.q: An Order is deleted and its OrderLines are deleted with it. Which relationship fits best?
quiz.explain: Composition is a strong whole-part relationship where parts cannot exist without the whole.

quiz.q: In the transition label "cancel [not yet packed] / refund", what is "[not yet packed]"?
quiz.explain: The part in square brackets is the guard, a condition that must be true for the transition to happen.

quiz.q: Which class should NOT normally appear in an analysis class diagram for the pharmacy?
quiz.explain: Analysis classes are business concepts; technical classes like DatabaseConnection belong to design.

lessons.title: Design Strategy and Architecture
lessons.content:
Suppose you have decided exactly what kind of house your family needs: three bedrooms, a kitchen with good air flow, a roof you can use for drying clothes. That was analysis. Now come new questions. Do you build it yourself with a contractor, buy a ready flat in a building, or rent one? Will the water come from a city line or a deep tube well? Where will the electricity meter sit? Those are design decisions. In SA&D, after the requirements and models are agreed, the analyst and designers must decide how the system will be obtained and how its pieces will be arranged across computers and networks. This lesson covers both: the design strategy and the system architecture.

From logical to physical: Everything we drew in analysis was mostly logical. A data flow diagram said "Record Sale" without saying whether it happens on a laptop, a phone or a cash register. An ER diagram said "Medicine" without saying which database product stores it. Design turns these logical models into physical decisions: which software, which hardware, which network, which programming platform, where data lives, and who runs it. The logical model is the "what"; the physical design is the "with what and where".

The three big strategies: There are three main ways to get a new system. First, custom development: build it in-house with your own developers. Second, buy a packaged system: purchase or subscribe to ready-made software and configure it. Third, outsourcing: pay an outside company to build, and sometimes also run, the system for you. Many real projects mix these, for example buying an accounting package and custom-building a small app on top of it.

Custom development: Building your own gives the best fit to unusual needs and full control over features and data. It can also build skills inside the organization. The costs are high: you need skilled people, it takes longer, and the project risk is bigger. You also own all future maintenance. Custom development makes sense when the system gives a real competitive advantage, or when no package fits.

Packaged software: Packages exist for common business jobs: accounting, payroll, inventory, point of sale, hospital management, school management, and large ERP (enterprise resource planning) systems that cover many departments in one product. Buying is usually faster and cheaper than building, and the package has already been tested by many customers. The problems: it rarely fits 100 percent. You may have to change your procedures to match the package, pay for customization, or write workarounds. Upgrades from the vendor can break your customizations. A useful rule: if the package fits most of your key requirements, change the process rather than heavily changing the package.

Outsourcing: An outside vendor builds or runs the system. It is useful when the organization has no IT team or needs special skills only for a short time. Bangladesh has a large software outsourcing industry serving both local and foreign clients, so this option is common. The risks are losing control, depending on one vendor, poor communication, and leaking confidential data. A clear contract with deliverables, deadlines, ownership of source code and data, and a support period is essential.

The request for proposal: When buying or outsourcing, the organization often writes an RFP (request for proposal). It describes the business, the requirements (often grouped as must-have and nice-to-have), technical constraints, the expected timeline, and how proposals will be evaluated. Vendors reply with proposals and prices. A smaller, simpler version that asks only for prices for a clearly defined product is often called a request for quotation (RFQ).

The alternatives matrix: How do you choose between, say, building, buying package A, or buying package B? A common tool is the weighted alternatives matrix. List the criteria, give each a weight that adds up to 100, score each option on each criterion, multiply and add. Worked example for ShasthoPharma, scores out of 5: criteria are functional fit (weight 40), total cost (30), vendor support in Dhaka (20), ease of use (10). Custom build scores 5, 2, 4, 3, giving 200 + 60 + 80 + 30 = 370. Package A scores 4, 4, 3, 4, giving 160 + 120 + 60 + 40 = 380. Package B scores 3, 5, 2, 5, giving 120 + 150 + 40 + 50 = 360. Package A wins narrowly. The numbers do not make the decision alone, but they make the discussion clear and honest.

What architecture means: System architecture is the high-level plan of how the parts of a system are arranged: where data is stored, where the program logic runs, where the user interface runs, and how they talk over the network. Every application has three basic functions. Data storage keeps the data. Data access logic reads and writes it. Application logic (business logic) applies the rules, like calculating discounts. Presentation logic shows screens and takes input. Architecture is about which computer does which of these jobs.

Server-based architecture: In the old style, one central computer (a mainframe or a central server) did everything, and users had simple terminals that only displayed text and sent keystrokes. It is easy to control and secure because everything is in one place, but the central machine can become a bottleneck and the interfaces were limited.

Client-based architecture: Here the user's own PC does almost all the work, and a file server simply stores shared files. A small office sharing an Access or Excel file over a network is an example. It is cheap and simple, but every PC pulls whole files across the network, so it gets slow and risky with many users, and file locking problems can corrupt data.

Client-server architecture: The work is split. The client (a PC app, a browser or a phone app) handles presentation and sometimes some logic; the server handles data storage and data access, and often the business logic. The client sends a request, the server does the work and sends back only the result. This is the most common style today. It scales better, keeps the data in one safe place, and lets different kinds of clients use the same server.

Two-tier, three-tier and n-tier: In a two-tier design, the client talks directly to a database server; business logic sits on the client or inside the database. In a three-tier design, there is a separate middle tier, an application server, between the clients and the database. The client handles presentation, the application server handles business logic, and the database server handles data. An n-tier design splits further, for example a web server, separate service servers for payment or SMS, and a database server. More tiers mean better separation, scaling and security, but also more complexity and more network hops.

Thin vs thick clients: A thin client does little more than presentation; most logic runs on the server. A web app in a browser is a typical thin client. Updates are easy because you change only the server. A thick (fat) client does a lot of processing itself, like a desktop accounting program that calculates everything locally. Thick clients can work faster and sometimes offline, but every PC must be updated when the program changes. Mobile apps sit in between; many keep some data locally so they keep working when the network drops.

Cloud computing: Instead of owning servers, an organization can rent computing over the internet. Three common service models: IaaS (infrastructure as a service) rents virtual machines, storage and networks, and you manage the operating system and software. PaaS (platform as a service) rents a ready platform where you just deploy your code and database, and the provider manages the servers. SaaS (software as a service) rents a complete application used through a browser or app, such as online email or an online accounting service. Cloud reduces upfront hardware cost and makes scaling easier, but needs reliable internet, has ongoing monthly costs, and raises questions about where data is stored and who can access it.

Choosing with non-functional requirements: Architecture is mostly decided by non-functional requirements, which you met in lesson 7. Operational needs: must the branch keep selling when the internet is down? Performance: how many sales per minute at peak, how fast must a screen respond? Security: who may see patient prescriptions, must data be encrypted? Cultural and political needs: must data stay inside the country, must screens support Bangla? Each answer pushes the design. For example, "keep selling during internet outages" pushes toward a client that stores sales locally and synchronizes later.

Hardware and software specification: The final part of architecture design is a document that lists what to buy or rent: number and type of PCs or tablets at each branch, barcode scanners, receipt printers, server or cloud plan, operating systems, database product, backup method, and network connections. It should state minimum specifications rather than brand names where possible, so vendors can compete fairly.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma's choice: The team chooses Package A, a pharmacy point-of-sale system, as a three-tier, cloud-hosted solution. Each branch has a tablet or PC client with a barcode scanner and a receipt printer. The client keeps the last day's sales and stock locally so the counter keeps working during internet outages, then synchronizes. Head office managers use the same service through a browser as a thin client to see stock across all branches. A small custom app for home delivery riders is outsourced to a local software firm and talks to the package through its API.

Real life example 2, a mobile financial service: Think of how bKash-style mobile money works at a high level. Millions of phones act as clients: the app or a USSD menu handles presentation. Behind them sit application servers that check PINs, balances and limits, and highly protected database servers that record every transaction. Separate services handle SMS notifications and links to banks. This is a clear n-tier client-server design built for very high volume and strong security. The exact internal design of any real company is private, so treat this only as the general shape.

Common mistakes: Choosing technology first and requirements later ("we will use the cloud") instead of letting requirements drive the choice. Forgetting the hidden costs of packages, like customization, training and yearly license fees. Treating outsourcing as "hand it over and forget it". Confusing tiers (logical layers of the software) with physical machines; several tiers can run on one machine. Ignoring offline and power-cut scenarios, which matter a lot in Bangladesh.

What exams ask: Compare custom development, packaged software and outsourcing with advantages and disadvantages. What is an RFP? Prepare a weighted alternatives matrix. Explain server-based, client-based and client-server architecture. Differentiate two-tier and three-tier architecture with a diagram. Differentiate thin and thick clients. Explain IaaS, PaaS and SaaS with examples.

Recap: Design begins by turning logical models into physical choices. The organization picks a strategy: build, buy or outsource, often using an RFP and a weighted alternatives matrix. Then it picks an architecture by deciding where data storage, data access, business logic and presentation run: server-based, client-based or client-server, in two, three or more tiers, with thin or thick clients, on its own servers or in the cloud. Non-functional requirements drive these choices. Next lesson: designing the outputs and inputs that users will actually see and type.
key_points: Design turns logical models (what) into physical decisions (with what and where).
The three strategies are custom development, packaged software (including ERP) and outsourcing; many projects mix them.
An RFP asks vendors for proposals; a weighted alternatives matrix compares options with criteria, weights and scores.
Every application has data storage, data access logic, application (business) logic and presentation logic.
Server-based, client-based and client-server architectures differ in which computer does these jobs.
Three-tier separates presentation, business logic and data onto separate tiers; n-tier splits further.
Thin clients keep logic on the server; thick clients do more work locally.
IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are cloud models; non-functional requirements like offline use, performance and security drive architecture choices.
lessons.tip: For any architecture question, draw four boxes (storage, data access, business logic, presentation) and then show which machine each box sits on. Most exam answers become clear from that one sketch.

lessons.title: Output and Input Design
lessons.content:
There is an old saying in computing: garbage in, garbage out. If a counter clerk types 100 strips instead of 10, every stock report after that is wrong, the reorder list is wrong, and the owner makes bad decisions with full confidence. And even when the data is perfect, a report that is twenty pages of tiny numbers is useless to a busy manager. Users judge a system mostly by two things they touch: what comes out of it and what they must put into it. That is why output design and input design are two of the most practical jobs of the analyst.

Why outputs come first: Many textbooks design outputs before inputs, and there is a good reason. Outputs are the whole point of the system: the receipt, the reorder list, the monthly profit report. Once you know exactly what outputs are needed, you know what data must be stored, and from that you know what must be captured as input. Working backwards from outputs avoids collecting data nobody uses.

What an output is: An output is any information the system produces for people or for other systems: a printed receipt, a screen of search results, an SMS, an email, a PDF report, a dashboard, or a data file sent to a supplier's system. Outputs can be internal (used inside the organization, like a branch sales report) or external (sent to outsiders, like a customer invoice or a VAT statement). External outputs often have legal or brand requirements, so they deserve extra care.

Detail reports: A detail report shows one line for each record or transaction, for example every sale at Branch 3 today with time, medicine, quantity and amount. It is useful for checking and auditing, but long. Detail reports should usually include control totals at the end, such as total number of sales and total taka, so that someone can check nothing is missing.

Summary reports: A summary report groups and totals data, for example total sales per branch for the month, one line per branch. Managers prefer these because they show the big picture in one glance. Summary reports often include subtotals and grand totals and comparisons, such as "this month vs last month".

Exception reports: An exception report shows only the records that need attention, for example medicines below their reorder level, or medicines that expire within 60 days. Everything normal is left out. This is powerful because it saves managers from searching through hundreds of normal lines to find the five that matter. For ShasthoPharma, the expiry exception report alone can save real money by moving near-expiry stock to busier branches.

Other kinds of output: Turnaround documents are outputs that later come back as inputs, for example an electricity bill with a tear-off slip that the customer returns with payment. Key-indicator or dashboard outputs show a few important numbers, often as charts, like today's sales and the number of low-stock items. Many textbooks also list ad hoc or on-demand reports, which a user runs only when needed, versus scheduled reports that are produced automatically, such as every night.

Choosing the output medium: The same information can be delivered on paper, on screen, by email, by SMS, or as a file. Ask who needs it, where they are, how fast they need it, how often, whether a permanent copy is needed, and how private it is. A receipt for a customer at the counter may need paper because many pharmacies and customers still expect it, and it can serve as proof of purchase. A low-stock alert for a branch manager who is always moving fits an SMS or app notification. A tax report may need a printable PDF with a fixed format.

Rules for a good report: Give it a clear title, the date and time it was produced, and the period it covers. Label every column and give units, such as "Amount (Tk)". Line up numbers to the right so digits line up. Sort the data in the order users will look for it. Put totals where people expect them. Keep only the columns users really need. Show page numbers on printed reports, like "Page 2 of 5". Avoid bias: for example, a chart whose vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0 makes a small change look huge. Always show a report mock-up to real users and ask them to find an answer using it.

What input design is: Input design decides how data enters the system: which data is captured, by whom, when, on which device, in which format, and how it is checked. The goals are simple: capture only the data that is needed, capture it once, capture it as close to where it is created as possible, and make errors hard to make and easy to catch.

Source documents: A source document is the paper or electronic form where data is first recorded, such as a doctor's prescription, a supplier's delivery challan, or a customer registration form. Good source documents have a logical flow from top to bottom and left to right, clear labels, enough space to write, boxes for each character when handwriting is unavoidable, and check boxes instead of free text where possible. In a modern system, the "source document" is often a screen form itself.

Batch vs online input: In batch input, data is collected over a period and entered or processed together, for example all paper delivery challans of the day typed in at night. In online input, data is entered and processed immediately, like a sale scanned at the counter that updates stock at once. Online input gives fresh data and immediate error checking. Batch input can still make sense for large volumes that do not need instant results, like monthly payroll. Many modern systems mix the two: they capture data online but run heavy calculations in a nightly batch.

Reducing input errors at the source: The best way to avoid typing errors is to avoid typing. Barcode scanners read the medicine code exactly. QR codes on bills, card readers, and data pulled automatically from other systems all reduce keystrokes. When typing is needed, use drop-down lists, radio buttons, date pickers and default values, such as today's date and the current branch filled in automatically. Every field you remove is an error you will never have to fix.

Validation checks: Even with good design, wrong data will be typed, so the system must check it. A completeness (presence) check makes sure required fields are not empty, such as the customer phone number for home delivery. A data type check makes sure a number field gets only digits. A range check makes sure a value falls between limits, such as quantity between 1 and 100 per sale. A format check makes sure the pattern is right, for example a Bangladeshi mobile number of 11 digits starting with 01. A consistency (combination) check compares fields, for example an expiry date must be after the manufacturing date. An existence (lookup) check makes sure a code exists, for example the medicine code is in the medicine table. A batch control total compares a total typed by hand with the total the system calculates.

Check digits, worked: A check digit is an extra digit calculated from the other digits and added to a code, so that common typing mistakes can be detected. One common method is modulus 11. Take the code 1234 and multiply its digits by the weights 5, 4, 3, 2: 1x5 + 2x4 + 3x3 + 4x2 = 5 + 8 + 9 + 8 = 30. Divide by 11: 30 = 2 x 11 + 8, so the remainder is 8. Subtract from 11: 11 - 8 = 3. The full code becomes 12343. If a clerk swaps two digits and types 21343, the system recalculates: 2x5 + 1x4 + 3x3 + 4x2 = 10 + 4 + 9 + 8 = 31, remainder 9, check digit 2, which does not match 3, so the error is caught. Barcodes, ISBNs and many card numbers use check digits (with different formulas), so you see this idea every day.

Coding schemes: Codes are short values that stand for longer data. A sequence code just counts: 1001, 1002, 1003. A block code reserves ranges for groups, for example 1000 to 1999 for tablets and 2000 to 2999 for syrups. A significant-digit or classification code puts meaning in parts of the code, for example DHK-03 for Dhaka branch 3. A mnemonic code is easy to remember, like PCM for paracetamol. Good codes are short, unique, stable over time and leave room for growth. Codes that pack too much meaning become a problem when the meaning changes, for example when a branch moves to a new area.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma's sale screen and reports: At the counter, the clerk scans the barcode; the medicine name and price appear automatically. Quantity has a range check of 1 to 100, and a warning appears if the item is a prescription medicine and no prescription has been recorded. The date, branch and clerk ID are filled in by the system. Outputs include a printed receipt for the customer, a nightly detail report of all sales per branch with control totals, a monthly summary report by branch for the owner, and two exception reports: low stock and medicines expiring within 60 days, sent to each branch manager's phone every morning.

Real life example 2, an online form for a national service: Think of an online application form for a government service in Bangladesh, such as one that asks for your national ID number, date of birth and mobile number. A format check rejects a mobile number that is not 11 digits starting with 01. A consistency check might compare the date of birth with the ID record. A one-time password sent by SMS checks that the mobile number really belongs to you. The output may be a downloadable PDF and an SMS confirmation. You have probably filled in such forms and met these checks without thinking about them as design.

Common mistakes: Designing screens before knowing what outputs are needed. Producing huge detail reports when a summary or exception report would do. Collecting data "just in case". Asking users to type what the system already knows. Validation that is too strict, such as rejecting names with a dot like "Md." or rejecting a valid new mobile prefix. Error messages that say only "Invalid input" without saying what is wrong and how to fix it. Mixing up validation (is it reasonable?) with verification (is it actually correct?, for example double entry or an OTP).

What exams ask: Differentiate detail, summary and exception reports with examples. What is a turnaround document? Explain factors in choosing output media. Explain batch vs online input. List and explain validation checks with examples. Calculate a modulus 11 check digit. Explain sequence, block, classification and mnemonic codes.

Recap: Design outputs first, because they define what data must be stored and captured. Use detail reports for checking, summary reports for the big picture and exception reports for what needs action, on the medium that fits the user. Design inputs to capture only needed data, once, at the source, preferably by scanning or selecting instead of typing. Protect data with validation checks, check digits and sensible codes. Next lesson: the user interface that wraps all of this into screens people enjoy using.
key_points: Garbage in, garbage out: wrong input makes every later output wrong.
Design outputs first; they decide what data must be stored and what inputs are needed.
Detail reports list every record, summary reports show totals and groups, exception reports show only what needs attention.
Choose the output medium (paper, screen, SMS, email, file) by who needs it, where, how fast, how often and how private.
Capture data once, at the source, with scanning, selection lists and default values instead of typing.
Batch input processes collected data together; online input processes each item immediately.
Validation checks include completeness, data type, range, format, consistency, existence and control totals; check digits catch typing mistakes.
Good codes (sequence, block, classification, mnemonic) are short, unique, stable and leave room to grow.
lessons.tip: When you design any report, ask the user one question: "What decision will you make after reading this?" Keep only what helps that decision.
