quiz.explain: Exception reports show only the records that need attention and leave out normal ones.

quiz.q: A rule that quantity must be between 1 and 100 is which kind of validation check?
quiz.explain: A range check makes sure a value falls between set limits.

quiz.q: Using weights 5, 4, 3, 2 and modulus 11, what is the check digit for the code 1234?
quiz.explain: 5 + 8 + 9 + 8 = 30, remainder 8 when divided by 11, and 11 - 8 = 3.

quiz.q: Why do many analysts design outputs before inputs?
options: Outputs show what data must be stored, so you capture only what is needed
quiz.explain: Working backward from outputs avoids collecting data nobody uses.

quiz.q: All delivery challans of the day are typed in together at night and processed then. This is:
quiz.explain: Batch input collects data over a period and processes it together.

lessons.title: User Interface Design
lessons.content:
Picture an evening rush at a ShasthoPharma branch. Eight customers are waiting, one is holding a crying baby, and the counter clerk has to find a syrup, check a prescription and take payment by mobile money. If the screen hides the search box behind three menus, uses tiny grey text and shows "Error 0x45" when something goes wrong, the clerk will hate the system and customers will leave. If the screen opens straight to a big search box, shows stock clearly and says "Only 2 bottles left at this branch, 14 at Dhanmondi branch", the same clerk feels like a hero. The user interface is where all the analysis and design finally meet a real person.

What a user interface is: The user interface (UI) is every part of the system that a user sees, hears or touches: screens, buttons, menus, forms, messages, sounds, printed receipts, even the barcode scanner beep. User interface design is the work of planning these parts so that people can do their tasks quickly, correctly and comfortably. A related term, user experience (UX), is wider: it covers the whole feeling of using the product, from first login to getting help. Your HCI/UX studies can go deeper; here we look at UI design from the analyst's side.

Why UI matters so much: For users, the interface is the system. They never see your elegant database or three-tier architecture. A bad interface causes slow work, data entry errors, training costs, frustration and, in the worst case, people refusing to use the system and returning to paper. A good interface reduces training time, errors and support calls, which saves real money.

Start from users and tasks: Before drawing any screen, the analyst asks: who are the users, and what tasks do they do? Counter clerks are busy, stand most of the time, may have little computer experience, and do the same few tasks hundreds of times a day. The owner uses the system rarely but needs clear reports. Delivery riders use a small phone outdoors in sunlight. Each group needs a different interface. A use case or a short scenario for each frequent task is a good starting point for screen design.

Golden rules, part 1: A well-known set of principles is Ben Shneiderman's "eight golden rules of interface design". The first is strive for consistency: the same action should look and work the same way everywhere. If "Save" is a green button at the bottom right on one screen, it should not be a blue link at the top on another. The second is seek universal usability: support both beginners and experts, for example menus for beginners and keyboard shortcuts for frequent users. The third is offer informative feedback: every action should get a visible response, such as "Sale saved, receipt printing".

Golden rules, part 2: The fourth is design dialogs to yield closure: a task should have a clear beginning, middle and end, so users know when they are done, like a "Payment complete" screen. The fifth is prevent errors: make mistakes hard, for example disabling the "Confirm" button until required fields are filled, or offering a list instead of free typing. The sixth is permit easy reversal of actions: let users undo or cancel, which reduces fear. The seventh is keep users in control: the system should respond to the user, not surprise them with unexpected pop-ups or jumps. The eighth is reduce short-term memory load: do not make users remember information from one screen to use on another; show it where it is needed.

Interaction styles: Textbooks list a few basic ways people talk to a system. Command language means typing commands, like a terminal; it is fast for experts but hard to learn. Menu selection means choosing from lists; it is easy to learn but can feel slow if menus are deep. Form fill-in means typing into labelled fields, which suits data entry. Direct manipulation means acting on visible objects, like dragging a file or tapping a medicine card. Natural language means typing or speaking ordinary sentences, like asking a voice assistant. Most real systems mix several styles; a pharmacy system will mainly use menus, forms and touch-based direct manipulation, with keyboard shortcuts for expert clerks.

Navigation design: Navigation is how users move between parts of the system. Common styles are menus (lists of choices), tabs, toolbars, a home dashboard with large tiles, and search. Keep menus shallow, so the most common tasks are one or two taps away. Group related options and use words the users use, not technical words: "Sell" and "Stock" rather than "Transaction Module" and "Inventory Entity". Always show where the user is, for example a highlighted tab or a page title, and give a clear way back.

Layout: A screen layout decides where things go. Put the most important information where the eye starts, usually the top left for left-to-right languages, which includes both English and Bangla. Group related fields together with spacing or boxes. Keep a consistent area for titles, the main work area, and buttons or status messages. Leave white space; a crowded screen is slow to read. Align fields and labels in neat columns. For touch screens, make buttons big enough to tap easily, and keep dangerous buttons like "Delete" away from common ones like "Save".

Form design: Forms are the most common input screens. Ask only what is needed. Order fields in the natural order of the task or of the paper source document. Put labels close to their fields. Mark required fields clearly. Use the right control: a date picker for dates, radio buttons for two to five choices, a drop-down list for many choices, a check box for yes or no. Show the expected format, like "01XXXXXXXXX". Validate as the user goes, next to the field, rather than only after they press submit.

Messages: Error, warning and confirmation messages need special care. A good error message says what happened, why, and how to fix it, in polite plain language. Compare "Invalid entry" with "Mobile number must be 11 digits starting with 01. You typed 10 digits." Do not blame the user. Use confirmation only for actions that are hard to undo, like deleting a customer; if every action asks "Are you sure?", users start clicking Yes without reading.

Colour, text and icons: Use colour to support meaning, not as the only signal. About one in twelve men has some form of colour vision deficiency, so a red "out of stock" word should also say "Out of stock", not only be red. Keep text large enough, with strong contrast. Use icons that are familiar, like a magnifying glass for search, and add text labels when the meaning is not obvious.

Accessibility: Accessible design lets people with different abilities use the system: low vision, colour blindness, limited hand movement, or hearing loss. Practical steps include adjustable text size, good contrast, full keyboard use without a mouse, labels that screen readers can read, and not relying on sound alone. Accessibility often helps everyone; large clear buttons also help a clerk in a hurry or a rider in bright sunlight.

Language and local context: In Bangladesh, users may prefer Bangla, English or a mix. Decide early which language the interface uses, and if it supports both, make switching easy and test that Bangla text displays correctly in every screen, report and receipt, including the printer. Show amounts in taka with the format users expect, and dates in a familiar format, such as day before month. Medicine names are usually printed in English on boxes, so a pharmacy search might stay in English even if menus are in Bangla. These choices are requirements to confirm with users, not guesses.

Storyboards and prototypes: Before coding, designers sketch screens. A storyboard is a series of sketches showing the screens a user goes through for one task, like frames in a comic. Wireframes are simple black-and-white layouts showing where things go without colours or images. A prototype is a clickable mock-up, made on paper or with a design tool, that users can try. Showing a paper prototype to a real counter clerk and watching them try to "sell" a medicine reveals problems in minutes, at almost zero cost.

Usability testing, in brief: Usability testing means watching real users perform real tasks with the interface and noting where they get stuck. You give a task, such as "Sell two strips of Napa and take payment by mobile money", stay quiet, and observe. Measure things like time taken, number of errors and whether they finished. Even testing with about five users usually finds the biggest problems. Fix them, then test again.

A worked redesign: The first version of the ShasthoPharma sale screen had seven fields: date, branch, clerk, customer name, medicine code, quantity and price. Testing showed clerks took about 40 seconds per item and often typed wrong codes. The redesign filled date, branch and clerk automatically, used the barcode scanner for the medicine, filled price from the database, made customer name optional, and showed a large running total. Time per item dropped sharply and wrong-code errors almost disappeared. Fewer fields, more automation, clearer feedback.

Real life example 1, the delivery rider app: ShasthoPharma's riders use cheap Android phones outdoors. The design uses large buttons, high contrast for sunlight, only three main screens (Today's deliveries, Navigate, Mark delivered), Bangla labels, and a "Call customer" button. If a delivery fails, the rider picks a reason from a short list instead of typing. Offline mode stores status changes until the network returns.

Real life example 2, mobile banking apps in Bangladesh: Popular mobile financial service apps show a home screen with large icons for Send Money, Cash Out, Mobile Recharge and Payment, which are the most frequent tasks. Before money moves, a confirmation screen shows the receiver, amount and charge, and the user must enter a PIN or hold a button: a deliberate step for an action that is hard to reverse. After success, a clear receipt screen and an SMS give closure and feedback. These are the golden rules in action.

Common mistakes: Designing for yourself instead of the real users. Copying a fancy design without testing it on the actual audience. Long forms with optional fields mixed in. Inconsistent buttons and words across screens. Using colour alone to show meaning. Error messages written in technical codes. Adding many features to one screen because "someone might need it". Skipping testing because "it looks fine to us".

What exams ask: Define user interface and explain why UI design matters. Explain Shneiderman's eight golden rules with examples. Give guidelines for screen layout, form design and error messages. What is a storyboard, wireframe and prototype? Explain usability testing. Discuss accessibility in interface design.

Recap: The user interface is the system as far as users are concerned. Start from users and their frequent tasks. Follow principles such as consistency, feedback, closure, error prevention, easy reversal, user control and low memory load. Design simple navigation, clean layouts, sensible forms and helpful messages, with accessibility and local language in mind. Sketch, prototype and test with real users before coding. Next lesson: implementation, when the designed system is built, tested and put into real use.
key_points: The user interface is everything users see, hear or touch; for them, the interface is the system.
Start UI design from the real users and their most frequent tasks.
Shneiderman's eight golden rules: consistency, universal usability, informative feedback, closure, error prevention, easy reversal, user control, low memory load.
Keep navigation shallow, use the users' words and always show where the user is.
Good forms ask only what is needed, use the right controls and validate next to each field.
Error messages should say what went wrong and how to fix it, in plain polite language.
Do not rely on colour alone; design for accessibility and the users' language (Bangla, English or both).
Storyboards, wireframes, prototypes and usability testing with real users catch problems cheaply before coding.
lessons.tip: Watch one real person use an app you think is easy, without helping them. Every pause or wrong tap you see is a UI lesson no textbook can give you.
lessons.task: On paper, sketch a wireframe for a pharmacy sale screen with as few fields as possible. Then ask a friend or family member to "sell" an item using your paper screen while you play the computer, and write down three things that confused them.

quiz.q: Which golden rule is followed when a "Sale saved, receipt printing" message appears after the clerk presses Save?
quiz.explain: Every action should get a visible response so the user knows what happened.

quiz.q: Which error message is best?
options: Mobile number must be 11 digits starting with 01. You typed 10 digits.
quiz.explain: A good message says what is wrong and how to fix it, politely and in plain language.

quiz.q: Why should "out of stock" not be shown by red colour alone?
options: Some users have colour vision deficiency and cannot rely on colour
Red is not allowed on screens
quiz.explain: Colour should support meaning, not be the only signal, for accessibility.

quiz.q: A simple black-and-white layout showing where elements go, without colours or images, is called a:
quiz.explain: Wireframes show layout only; prototypes can be clicked and tried.

quiz.q: The "Confirm" button stays disabled until all required fields are filled. Which rule is this mainly?
quiz.explain: The design makes it hard to submit incomplete data, preventing errors.

lessons.title: Implementation and Conversion
lessons.content:
Think of moving your family to a new flat. Buying the flat was the easy part. Now someone must pack, label boxes, decide what to throw away, move the fridge without breaking it, connect gas and internet, teach grandmother where the new light switches are, and make sure the family can still eat dinner on moving day. Moving an organization from an old system to a new one is very similar. The software can be perfect, yet the project still fails if the data is moved badly, the users are not trained, or the switch happens on the busiest day of the year. This stage is called implementation, and the most delicate part of it is conversion.

What implementation is: Implementation is the phase of the SDLC where the designed system is built, tested, installed and put into real use. From the analyst's side it has five big jobs: construction (programming or configuring the system), testing, preparing documentation, training users, and converting from the old system to the new one, including moving the data. After that comes a review to check whether the project actually delivered what was promised.

Construction, in brief: If the system is custom-built, programmers write the code following the design specifications. If it is a package, the team installs it, sets up the master data (medicine lists, branches, users), configures options and builds any customizations or interfaces. The analyst's role here is to answer questions about requirements, check that the design is followed, and control changes so the scope does not keep growing. Your Software Engineering course covers programming practice and process in detail.

Testing, in brief: Testing checks that the system works and meets requirements before real users depend on it. Unit testing checks small pieces, such as the discount calculation. Integration testing checks that pieces work together, such as the sale screen updating stock. System testing checks the whole system against the requirements, including performance and security. Acceptance testing is done by the users or owners themselves, often with real-looking data, to decide whether they accept the system. Alpha tests are done in-house and beta tests with selected real users. A test plan, prepared earlier from the requirements, lists what to test and the expected results. The Software Engineering course goes deep into test design; for the analyst, the key point is that every requirement should have at least one test.

Documentation: Two kinds of documents are produced. System documentation describes how the system works for those who will maintain it: design models, data dictionary, program notes, configuration settings, interfaces. User documentation helps people use it: a user manual, quick reference cards, help screens, FAQs and short videos. For busy counter staff, a one-page laminated quick guide next to the computer is often more useful than a 100-page manual.

Training: Different users need different training. Counter clerks need hands-on practice on selling, returns and searching. Branch managers need reports and stock transfers. IT staff need backup, user management and troubleshooting. Training methods include classroom sessions, one-to-one coaching, online tutorials and a "train the trainer" approach, where a few experienced users learn first and then teach others in their branch. Training should happen close to the go-live date, so people do not forget, and should use a practice copy of the system, never the live data.

Site preparation and installation: The physical side is easy to forget. Each branch needs a stable power supply, ideally with a UPS so a power cut does not lose a half-finished sale, network or mobile internet connection, a safe place for the computer, and printers and scanners tested with the real software. Someone must also create user accounts with the right permissions, so a clerk can sell but cannot change prices. In Bangladesh, planning for load-shedding and slow internet in some areas is part of realistic installation planning.

Data conversion: Before the new system can run, existing data must be moved into it. For ShasthoPharma that means the medicine list, current stock in every branch, supplier details and maybe customer records. Data conversion has three steps: extract the data from the old source, which may be paper registers, spreadsheets or an old database; transform it by cleaning, removing duplicates, fixing formats and mapping old codes to new ones; then load it into the new system. This is often called ETL (extract, transform, load). It is usually harder than expected, because old data is messy: the same medicine spelt three ways, stock counts that do not match the shelves, prices missing.

Checking converted data: After loading, verify. Compare record counts, such as 2,450 medicines before and 2,450 after. Compare control totals, such as total stock value in taka per branch. Spot-check sample records by hand. For stock, a physical count on the day of conversion is the safest base. Wrong opening data will make every later report wrong, so it is worth the effort.

Conversion strategies overview: Conversion (also called changeover or cutover) is the moment the organization stops using the old system and starts using the new one. There are four classic strategies: direct, parallel, pilot and phased. They differ in cost, risk and time. The right choice depends on how critical the system is, how different the new system is, and how much money and staff time are available.

Direct conversion: On a chosen date, the old system stops and the new system starts. Also called the "big bang" or "cold turkey" approach. It is the cheapest and fastest because you run only one system. It is also the riskiest: if the new system has a serious problem, there is no old system to fall back on. Direct conversion fits when the old system cannot keep running, when the systems are too different to compare, or when the system is not critical. Choosing a quiet time, such as a weekend or a holiday, reduces the risk.

Parallel conversion: The old and new systems run side by side for a period, for example one month. The same transactions are entered in both, and the results are compared. If they match and users are comfortable, the old system is switched off. This is the safest strategy because the old system is always there as a backup. It is also the most expensive: staff do double work, and comparing results takes time. It suits critical systems like payroll or accounting, where mistakes are costly. It is hard when the new system works very differently, so outputs cannot be compared directly.

Pilot conversion: The new system is first installed fully at one location or for one group, such as one branch, while the others continue with the old system. When the pilot works well, the system is rolled out to the rest. The risk is limited to one site, and lessons from the pilot improve the rollout. The pilot site itself may use direct or parallel conversion. The downside is that during the pilot, the organization runs two different systems at once, and data from pilot and non-pilot sites must be combined.

Phased conversion: The new system is introduced module by module or step by step, for example first the sales module, then stock, then purchasing, then reports. Each phase is smaller and easier to manage, and users learn gradually. But the full benefit comes only at the end, the conversion takes longer, and temporary links between new modules and the old system may be needed. Some textbooks call this modular or staged conversion.

Comparing the strategies: Think of two scales. On risk, from highest to lowest: direct is highest; pilot and phased are in the middle because problems are limited to one site or one module; parallel is lowest. On cost, roughly the opposite: parallel is highest because of double work; direct is lowest. Pilot and phased also take longer overall. Real projects often combine them: a pilot at one branch using parallel running for a month, followed by phased rollout to the other branches.

Worked choice for ShasthoPharma: The chain has 12 branches. Running two systems in all 12 for a month would exhaust staff. A pure direct switch everywhere on the same day is too risky for a business selling medicines. The team chooses a pilot at the Mirpur branch for three weeks, running the paper register in parallel for the first week to compare daily totals. After fixing problems found there, they roll out to three branches per week, each on a Friday morning when sales are lower, with a trainer on site and a physical stock count the night before.

Go-live readiness and support: Before switching, use a simple checklist: tests passed and signed off, data converted and verified, users trained, hardware installed, backups ready, a fallback plan written, and help available. In the first weeks after go-live, provide extra support: a help desk phone number, a trainer visiting branches, and a quick way to report problems. Many projects plan a short "hypercare" period with extra support right after go-live.

Post-implementation review: A few weeks or months after go-live, the team reviews the project. Did the system meet its requirements? Did it deliver the expected benefits from the cost-benefit analysis? Are users satisfied? Were costs and time as planned? What should be done differently next time? This review, sometimes called a post-implementation evaluation, feeds into maintenance and improves future projects.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma's go-live: At the Mirpur pilot, the first week of parallel running showed that daily sales matched within a few taka except on two days, traced to clerks forgetting to scan returns. The fix was a clearer "Return" button and a short refresher session. The conversion also revealed 180 duplicate medicine names in the old lists, which were cleaned before rollout to the other branches.

Real life example 2, a university result system: A Bangladeshi university replacing a spreadsheet-based result system cannot afford wrong grades. A sensible plan is parallel running for one semester: the exam office calculates results in both the old spreadsheets and the new system, compares every student's GPA, and investigates every difference before the new system becomes official. After that semester, the spreadsheets are retired.

Common mistakes: Treating implementation as "install and go". Underestimating data cleaning. Training too early or only once. Choosing direct conversion for critical systems to save money. Running parallel systems without actually comparing results. Going live on the busiest day of the month. Skipping the post-implementation review, so the same mistakes repeat in the next project.

What exams ask: What are the activities of the implementation phase? Differentiate system and user documentation. Explain data conversion and ETL. Explain direct, parallel, pilot and phased conversion with advantages and disadvantages, and compare their risk and cost. Recommend a conversion strategy for a given case. What is a post-implementation review?

Recap: Implementation builds or configures, tests, documents, trains and converts. Data conversion means extracting, cleaning and loading old data, then verifying it with counts and totals. The four conversion strategies trade cost against risk: direct is cheap and risky, parallel is safe and expensive, pilot and phased limit risk by site or by module. A post-implementation review checks whether the promised benefits arrived. Next and final lesson: maintenance, the long life of the system after go-live, and a recap of the whole course.
key_points: Implementation covers construction, testing, documentation, training, data conversion and the switch to the new system.
Every requirement should have at least one test; acceptance testing is done by the users or owners.
System documentation helps maintainers; user documentation helps people use the system.
Data conversion means extract, transform (clean) and load, followed by checks with record counts and control totals.
Direct conversion is cheapest and riskiest; parallel is safest and most expensive.
Pilot conversion tries the full system at one site first; phased conversion introduces it module by module.
Real projects often combine strategies, and choose quiet times and extra support for go-live.
A post-implementation review checks whether requirements and expected benefits were achieved.
lessons.tip: For any conversion question in an exam, first ask: how critical is the system, and can we compare old and new outputs? Those two answers usually point to the right strategy.
lessons.task: Your university library is moving from paper loan cards to software. Write a one-page conversion plan: which strategy you choose and why, what data must be converted, how you will check it, and who needs what training.

quiz.q: Which conversion strategy runs the old and new systems together and compares results?
quiz.explain: Parallel conversion runs both systems at the same time until the new one is trusted.

quiz.q: Which strategy is generally cheapest but riskiest?
quiz.explain: Direct conversion runs only one system, so there is no fallback if the new one fails.

quiz.q: ShasthoPharma installs the full new system at the Mirpur branch first, then rolls it out to the others. This is:
quiz.explain: Pilot conversion installs the whole system at one site first.

quiz.q: After loading data, 2,450 medicine records existed before and 2,450 after. What kind of check is this?
options: A record count check of converted data
quiz.explain: Comparing record counts before and after is a basic check that conversion lost nothing.

quiz.q: Which document mainly helps the IT staff who will maintain the system?
options: A quick reference card for clerks
quiz.explain: System documentation describes design, data and configuration for maintainers.

lessons.title: Maintenance, Support and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
A new motorbike runs beautifully on the day you buy it. But within weeks it needs fuel and air in the tyres, after a few months an oil change, after a year new brake pads, and one day you add a phone holder because you started doing deliveries. If you ignore all that, the bike becomes noisy, unsafe and finally useless. An information system is the same. Go-live is not the end of the story; it is the start of the longest phase of the system's life. This phase is called maintenance and support, and it usually lasts years, often far longer than it took to build the system.

What maintenance is: Systems maintenance is every change made to a system after it goes into use: fixing faults, adapting it to new conditions, improving it, and preventing future problems. Support is the related work of keeping users productive: answering questions, solving day-to-day problems, training new staff, and keeping the system running, backed up and secure. In the SDLC we met in lesson 3, this is the support or maintenance phase, and it loops back to planning whenever a big change is needed.

Why maintenance costs so much: Many textbooks and studies report that maintenance takes a large share, often well over half, of the total money spent on a system across its whole life. The reason is simple: building happens once, but the system is used for years, and the world around it keeps changing. Laws change, prices change, users ask for new features, hardware ages, and security threats appear. Good analysis and design reduce this cost, because a clear, well-documented system is easier to change.

Corrective maintenance: Corrective maintenance fixes errors found after go-live. For example, ShasthoPharma's daily report counts returned medicines twice, so stock looks lower than it is. A clerk reports it, the team finds the cause, fixes the program and tests it. Corrective work is often urgent, especially when it affects money, medicine safety or data. Errors that slipped through testing, or appear only with real data and real volumes, show up here.

Adaptive maintenance: Adaptive maintenance changes the system to fit a changed environment, even though nothing was "wrong" before. The government changes the VAT rule on certain items, so invoices must change. A new mobile payment method becomes popular and customers want to use it. The operating system on the branch tablets gets a major update. The business opens branches outside Dhaka with a different delivery fee. The system worked fine, but the world around it moved.

Perfective maintenance: Perfective maintenance improves the system's features, performance or usability based on new user requests. The owner wants a new report comparing sales of the same month last year. Clerks ask for a keyboard shortcut to repeat the last sale. The stock search becomes slow as data grows, so the team adds an index. Perfective requests are usually the largest group of change requests, because once users like a system, they always find new things they want it to do.

Preventive maintenance: Preventive maintenance reduces the chance of future failures. Examples: cleaning up old code that has become messy, archiving very old sales data so the database stays fast, replacing a server disk that shows warning signs, updating libraries that will soon stop getting security fixes, and checking that backups can really be restored. Nobody complains when preventive work is skipped, which is exactly why it gets skipped. Then one day the problem arrives all at once.

A quick classification exercise: Classify these four requests. One, "The receipt shows the wrong total when a discount and a return happen together": corrective. Two, "Add the new 2026 tax rate": adaptive. Three, "Add a graph of monthly sales to the owner's dashboard": perfective. Four, "Move sales older than five years to an archive to keep searches fast": preventive. Exams often ask exactly this kind of classification, so practise it with your own examples.

Handling change requests: Changes should not be made just because someone asks loudly. A typical process: the user submits a change request (a form or a ticket) describing what and why. The analyst reviews it, estimates the effort and the impact on other parts, and checks with the system owner. A small committee, sometimes called a change control board, approves, rejects or schedules it based on priority and budget. Approved changes are designed, built, tested, documented and released. Emergency fixes may skip the queue but are documented afterwards.

Releases: Instead of changing the live system every day, many organizations group changes into planned releases, for example a small update every two weeks and a larger one every quarter. Each release has a version number, such as 2.3, a list of what changed, and tested installation steps. This makes changes predictable, easier to test, and easier to roll back if something goes wrong. Urgent fixes can still be released as patches between planned releases.

Configuration management: Configuration management means keeping track of exactly which versions of programs, settings, database structures and documents are in use, and controlling how they change. With a version control system, every change to the code is recorded with who changed it, when and why, and older versions can be recovered. Without it, nobody knows which branch is running which version, and a fix in one place breaks something in another.

Keeping documentation alive: Every change should update the documentation: the data dictionary, diagrams, user guides and help screens. Otherwise, after two years, the documents describe a system that no longer exists, and every future change becomes guesswork. An analyst who writes "update DFD level 1 and data dictionary" into every change ticket saves the next analyst weeks of work.

Performance monitoring: Support teams watch how the system behaves: response time of the sale screen, how long the nightly reports take, database size, error logs, and how often the system goes down. A simple measure is response time at peak hours; if the sale screen took 1 second last year and takes 4 seconds now, something needs attention before users start complaining. Capacity planning uses these trends to predict when more storage, a faster server or a bigger cloud plan will be needed.

Measuring reliability, worked: Two simple numbers help. Mean time between failures (MTBF) is the average running time between breakdowns, and mean time to repair (MTTR) is the average time to fix one. Suppose in 90 days the ShasthoPharma server failed 3 times and was down for 2, 4 and 3 hours. Total downtime is 9 hours, so MTTR is 9 / 3 = 3 hours. Total time is 90 x 24 = 2,160 hours, so uptime is 2,160 - 9 = 2,151 hours, and MTBF is about 2,151 / 3 = 717 hours. Availability is uptime divided by total time: 2,151 / 2,160, about 99.6 percent. If the owner wants 99.9 percent, the team must reduce failures, repair faster, or both.

Security and backups: Security is not a one-time feature. Support staff must apply security updates, remove accounts of staff who leave, review who has access to sensitive data like prescriptions, and watch for suspicious activity. Backups must be taken regularly, kept in a separate place, and tested by actually restoring them. A backup that has never been restored is only a hope. Many organizations also keep a written disaster recovery plan describing how to restore service after a fire, flood or major failure.

User support: Users need a clear place to ask for help: a help desk phone line, a chat group, or a ticket system. Common questions become entries in an FAQ or the help screens. New staff need training when they join. Feedback from support is a goldmine for the analyst, because repeated questions often point to a confusing screen that perfective maintenance should fix.

System retirement: Eventually, maintaining the old system costs more than replacing it, or it can no longer adapt to what the business needs. Warning signs include very frequent breakdowns, rising maintenance cost, vendors stopping support, and simple changes taking weeks. At that point the organization starts a new SDLC cycle, and the old system is retired, with its data converted or archived. The life cycle really is a cycle.

Real life example 1, ShasthoPharma one year later: In the first year, the team handled about forty change requests. A few were corrective (a rounding error in VAT on receipts). Several were adaptive (a new mobile payment option and a new branch in Chattogram with its own delivery fee). Most were perfective (a sales-comparison report, faster medicine search, Bangla receipts). The IT officer also scheduled preventive work: archiving old data every quarter and a monthly backup-restore test. Releases went out every two weeks on Friday mornings.

Real life example 2, an online exam result portal: Think of a public exam result website in Bangladesh on result day, when a very large number of students try to check results at the same time. Before result day, support teams plan capacity and test the load; during the day they monitor response times; afterwards they review what slowed down and improve it for next year. That cycle of monitoring, adapting and improving is maintenance in action.

Common mistakes: Thinking the project ends at go-live. Treating maintenance as unimportant work for junior staff only. Making changes directly on the live system without testing or version control. Not updating documentation. Mixing up adaptive (the environment changed) and perfective (users want something better). Assuming backups work without testing them.

What exams ask: Define systems maintenance. Explain corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive maintenance with examples, and classify given requests. Why is maintenance costly? Describe the change request process. What is configuration management? Explain the role of performance monitoring, backups and security in support. When should a system be replaced?

Course recap: Let us look back at the whole journey. We began with what systems analysis and design is, the analyst's role and the six parts of an information system, then learned to see organizations as systems. We followed the SDLC: planning with project initiation, feasibility and cost-benefit analysis; analysis with requirements, interviews, questionnaires, observation, JAD and a well-organized specification; modeling of processes with DFDs, logic with structured English, decision trees and tables, data with the data dictionary and ERDs, and objects with UML use case, activity, sequence, class and state diagrams. Then design: strategy and architecture, outputs and inputs, and user interfaces. Finally implementation, conversion and maintenance. The single idea running through all of it: understand the real problem and the real users first, then design the simplest system that solves it.

What next: Practise on real cases. Pick a local business or a university office, interview one person, draw a context diagram and a level 0 DFD, and write five requirements. Your Software Engineering course will take you deeper into process models, testing and project management, Management Information Systems into how organizations use information for decisions, and DBMS into turning your ERDs into working databases. Analyst skills grow with every real conversation, so start listening to how people actually work. Keep your ShasthoPharma notes too; redoing them for a real organization is the best revision for the final exam.
key_points: Maintenance and support is the longest phase of a system's life and often the largest share of its total cost.
Corrective maintenance fixes errors; adaptive maintenance adjusts to a changed environment.
Perfective maintenance adds improvements users request; preventive maintenance reduces future failures.
Change requests should be reviewed, estimated, approved, built, tested, documented and released in planned releases.
Configuration management and version control track exactly which versions are in use and who changed what.
Documentation must be updated with every change, or it quickly becomes useless.
Support includes performance monitoring, capacity planning, security updates, tested backups and a help desk.
When maintenance costs more than replacement, the system is retired and a new SDLC cycle begins.
lessons.tip: For every change request you see, practise saying which of the four maintenance types it is and why. If you can classify ten real examples, that exam question is yours.
lessons.task: Write down ten things you wish your favourite app did differently or better. Classify each one as corrective, adaptive, perfective or preventive maintenance, and mark the three you would do first if you were the analyst.

quiz.q: The government changes the VAT rate and the invoice program is updated. Which type of maintenance is this?
quiz.explain: Adaptive maintenance adjusts the system to a changed environment such as new laws.

quiz.q: Archiving old sales data so searches stay fast, before anyone complains, is:
quiz.explain: Preventive maintenance reduces the chance of future problems.

quiz.q: Which practice keeps track of exactly which versions of programs and settings are in use?
quiz.explain: Configuration management, usually with version control, records and controls changes to every part of the system.

quiz.q: A user asks for a new graph of monthly sales on the dashboard. This request is mainly:
quiz.explain: Perfective maintenance adds improvements or new features requested by users.

quiz.q: Why is a backup that has never been restored risky?
options: It always doubles the database size
Nobody knows if it can actually bring the data back
Restoring is part of corrective maintenance only
quiz.explain: Only a tested restore proves a backup really works.
